News.title: Anak Krakatau eruption - live: All flights suspended at 8 airports as 150,000 stranded
News.content:
Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano has erupted, sending a cloud of ash as high as 50,000ft into the sky and forcing the cancellation of all flights at the country's main airport

More than 150,000 passengers have been left stranded after a massive volcanic eruption forced Indonesian authorities to suspend hundreds of flights at eight airports.

The eruption sent two large clouds of volcanic ash as high as 20,000ft on the Java side of the volcano and 50,000ft on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java.

Eight airports, including the country's busiest, Soekarno-Hatta International near the capital Jakarta, have halted operations and will remain closed until at least midnight local time (6pm UK time). The eruption has so far disrupted 712 flights across the country, with flights delayed, suspended or cancelled.

Indonesia's Geological Agency said Anak Krakatau, a volcanic island in Indonesia's Sunda Strait, had shown signs of activity since Friday before erupting twice this morning (Sunday).

The Anak Krakatau volcano - which translates to "child of Krakatoa" in Indonesian - was formed following the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883, one of the most violent volcanic events in recorded history.

News.title: Nurse took just 32 seconds to decide care home patient was dead before refusing to perform CPR
News.content:
Nurse took just 32 seconds to decide care home patient was dead before refusing to perform CPR

A tribunal found Melissa Papandrea relied on her own subjective judgement before refusing instructions from a 999 operator to begin resuscitation on a care home resident

View 2 Images The nurse took just 32 seconds to assess the patient before claiming there was 'no point' carrying out CPR (stock image) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A nurse has been suspended after refusing to perform CPR on a care home resident following an assessment which lasted just 32 seconds.

‌



Melissa Papandrea was working at Poplars Care Centre in Maidstone when the man stopped breathing and an ambulance was called on November 7, 2022. A tribunal heard the nurse decided the resident had already died before refusing instructions from a 999 call handler to begin resuscitation.

‌



During the call with the ambulance service, Ms Papandrea said: “I’m a qualified nurse and I can tell you by looking at the resident that he has passed. His heart has stopped.”

‌



View 2 Images Ms Papandrea refused a 999 operator's instruction (Image: Getty Images)

She was told to start CPR because the man “was still warm” and did not have a do-not-resuscitate order in place, but replied “there’s no point”. A transcript considered by the Nursing and Midwifery Council showed the nurse and emergency operator then disagreeing over whether the resident should be resuscitated instead of attempting resuscitation.

An emergency operator said: “If he’s still warm, you need to start CPR.” Ms Papandrea replied: “No, I’m sorry, that isn’t possible because he is deceased. I’ve had this argument before with the emergency services. There is no cardiac output. I’m not commencing CPR.”

‌



The man was subsequently pronounced dead. An inquest later found he died from bowel ischaemia, caused when the blood supply to the intestines is restricted or cut off. But a Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC)tribunal has now ruled Ms Papandrea did not carry out an adequate clinical assessment before deciding there were irreversible signs of death.

The Fitness to Practise Committee, chaired by Derek Artis, said: “The requirement to undertake a proper clinical assessment as to whether [the resident] had signs of irreversible death was a fundamental tenet of the nursing profession. Fellow professionals would consider a failure to follow guidelines in such circumstances to be appalling.”

The panel was particularly troubled by the fact Ms Papandrea’s conclusion had been based on her own subjective assessment. The NMC’s report added: “The panel was particularly concerned that Ms Papandrea’s decision that [the resident] had irreversible signs of death was based on her subjective opinion. She could not have known whether or not there might have been a different outcome had CPR been commenced.”

‌



The tribunal heard that when a first responder reached the care home, Ms Papandrea was asked to assist with resuscitation but witnesses said her chest compressions were not deep enough. Witnesses said she explained she “did not want to break his ribs,” before the responder took over.

Ms Papandrea has since acknowledged that her handling of the incident was wrong. In written submissions, Ms Papandrea described her actions as “a serious error in clinical judgement”.

She said: “I formed a subjective belief that they were deceased and that resuscitation would not be successful. I recognise now that this was an assumption rather than a clinical conclusion that I was appropriately qualified or authorised to make.”

Article continues below

Ms Papandrea was suspended for 12 months, with the sanction due to be reviewed. A separate 18-month interim suspension was also imposed to cover any appeal period. The Maidstone care home was rated ‘Good’ at its latest Care Quality Commission inspection in August 2024.

News.title: UK broadband provider with thousands of customers plunges into administration
News.content:
UK broadband provider with thousands of customers plunges into administration

UK broadband provider iTalk Telecom has fallen into administration after nearly two decades in business

View Image iTalk Telecom, which was founded in 2007, went into administration on August 28

A UK broadband provider has fallen into administration after nearly two decades in business.

‌



iTalk Telecom, which was founded in 2007 and is based in Brighton, is an internet service provider offering residential broadband and phone services.

‌



The company, which trades as iTalk Affiliate Telecommunications Ltd, formally entered administration on August 28.

‌



According to The Gazette, Andrew Pear and Richard Keley of Moorfields Advisory Limited have been appointed as administrators.

As Companies House notes, when a company enters administration, the process may be used to rescue a viable business that has become insolvent due to cashflow problems. It does not necessarily mean the company will stop trading.

‌



Administration puts in place a statutory moratorium - a "breathing space" - protecting the company from creditor enforcement action while plans are drawn up to restructure its finances and, where possible, rescue it. This may involve selling the business to an unrelated party.

Specialist outlet Thinkbroadband reports that UK-based holding company Telecom Acquisitions is a potential partner to take on the customer base of iTalk Telecom.

According to the outlet, Telecom Acquisitions is in discussions with the administrators about its options, with the intention of ensuring any migration to its services takes place without disruption to customers.

Article continues below

Nigel Barnett, CEO of Telecom Acquisitions, told the outlet: "This is a difficult situation, but we have assurances from the suppliers that no service should be affected in the short term. We are here to support Italk's customers and staff."

The Mirror has contacted ITalk Telecom, Moorfields Advisory Limited and Telecom Acquisitions for comment.

News.title: CrossCountry cancels nearly 70 trains over driver shortage - Manchester and Birmingham hit
News.content:
CrossCountry cancels nearly 70 trains over driver shortage - Manchester and Birmingham hit

CrossCountry has cancelled more than 70 trains today due to a driver shortage, with services between Manchester and Birmingham among those worst affected by the rail disruption

View Image Manchester Piccadilly to Birmingham is one of the affected routes (Image: Mark Waugh Manchester Press Photography Ltd)

Scores of CrossCountry train services have suddenly been axed today due to a shortage of drivers.

‌



Routes between Manchester Piccadilly and Birmingham are among the worst affected. At time of writing the CrossCountry website shows 69 cancelled services.

‌



Further cancellations over the course of the rest of the day include trains running from Leeds. Edinburgh, Bristol Temple Meads, Plymouth, Newcastle, Reading, Glasgow Central, Bournemouth and Paignton.

‌



In a statement posted on X, the company said: "Due to significant constraints on train crew availability, there will be disruption to services across our network today".

National Rail Enquiries said: "Constraints on train crew availability mean that there will be some late notice changes to the CrossCountry timetable across their network today. Some services will be cancelled or revised to only run part of their normal route.

‌



"This is with the exception of the route between Birmingham New Street, Leicester and Stansted Airport which is not expected to be impacted."

Replacement rail buses will operate between Birmingham and Manchester this evening. Three buses will depart Birmingham New Street for Manchester Piccadilly at 10.01pm, with stops at Stafford, Stoke-on-Trent, Macclesfield, and Stockport, before arriving at Manchester Piccadilly for drop-off only.

A single bus will travel in the opposite direction, departing Piccadilly at 10.04pm and making stops at Stockport, Macclesfield, Stoke-on-Trent, Stafford, Wolverhampton and Birmingham New Street for drop-offs only. A separate bus will also depart Wolverhampton bound for Manchester Piccadilly at 10.19pm.

Article continues below

These latest issues come just two weeks after CrossCountry was compelled to scrap almost all of its UK services following a power cut at its control centre. The outage in Birmingham triggered widespread disruption across the country.

News.title: Robert Jenrick reacts 'boohoo' to sickening clip of Reform conference protestor being dragged by hair
News.content:
Robert Jenrick reacts 'boohoo' to sickening clip of Reform conference protestor being dragged by hair

Robert Jenrick has told protesters at the Reform UK conference to 'get a life' and reacted to footage of a woman being dragged out by her hair by saying 'boohoo'

View 2 Images Police are examining footage of a woman being assaulted at Reform's conference (Image: X)

Robert Jenrick has reacted "boohoo" to footage of a woman being dragged out by her hair after heckling Nigel Farage's speech at Reform UK's party conference.

‌



Reform's Treasury spokesman - whose party claims to champion free speech - told protestors to “get a life” after disrupting the leader's keynote address on Friday.

‌



A sickening clip shows a woman being hit around the head with a crutch before her hair is pulled and a hand put over her mouth at the party conference. The grey haired man seen assaulting her was not a member of the event's security team. Another woman from the crowd can be seen pulling the protester's hair as guards escorted her from Birmingham's NEC. West Midlands Police has asked the protester to come forward in light of the footage.

‌



Asked about a "disturbing video" of a woman being dragged out by her hair and hit over the head, Mr Jenrick said: “Oh boohoo.” He told Sky News host Jon Sopel: “We’re now in a country, Jon, where somebody who is – whatever she is – a far-left protester, goes into a party conference, tries to wreck the leader’s speech, and cries foul if a pensioner knocks her over the head with their Zimmer frame, I mean, come on, get a life.

“This person knew what they were doing. They were trying to cause trouble, and they probably got more publicity out of it as a result of what happened.”

A Labour source said: “Funny how Robert Jenrick only champions free speech until someone exercises it in a way he dislikes - and then assault apparently becomes acceptable.” Replying to Mr Jenrick's comments on social media, Lib Dem MP Max Wilkinson said: "Reform: 'protect our women and girls.' Reform when a woman is attacked on their watch: 'oh boo hoo.' Horrible." And the Liberal Democrats also posted the footage of the woman on social media, captioning: "Don’t let Trump’s America become Farage’s Britain."

‌



Reform conference sees woman hit on head with crutch and hair pulled in sickening clip READ MORE :

View 2 Images Robert Jenrick has told protesters at the Reform UK conference to 'get a life' (Image: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock)

West Midlands Police said on Sunday: “Our enquiries are continuing and we would ask the woman involved to come forward. Anyone with any information should contact us on 101 quoting log number 924 of September 5.”

Mr Farage was interrupted four times during his keynote conference speech on Friday. He laughed as the first demonstrator was taken away and Reform fans chanted "out, out, out".

‌



The Reform leader said: “We’ve got a screamer. Oh dear.” And he added: "That poor young girl, she looked like she was going to do herself an injury,” before adding, “boring, boring, boring”.

Asked by The Mirror whether those involved should face consequences during a conference event about free speech, Nadine Dorries said those who disrupt speakers should not expect to be treated gently and said it was "shocking" that protesters had been there.

Ms Dorries, who was Tory Culture Secretary under Boris Johnson before defecting to Reform, said: “Somebody said to me it was shocking to see protesters being treated the way they were. I think what was also shocking was the way they thought they could come into the conference and try to derail Nigel Farage’s speech.”

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

And she went on: “If you’re going to come into a conference like this… of course you’re not going to get gentle treatment.” And she added: “It’s wrong, no one should be punched." She went on: "No one should attend this conference and try and disrupt it.”

Her remarks came after The Mirror asked if those who assaulted protesters should face consequences. Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf responded: “To the question from The Mirror about whether I condemn people punching people, yes I do condemn people punching people.”

‌



Reform's chairman Lee Anderson used his speech to make a joke about the incident and said the party would be having a “whip round” for an audience member who was seen hitting the protester with a walking stick. He told delegates: "A few nuisances we had in the hall yesterday, the protesters...

"I did see an old chap, a pensioner, somewhere with a walking stick... Look I don't condone any of that type of behaviour, but if anyone wants to have a quick whip around later we are collecting for a new walking stick. He's in here somewhere."

Mr Farage said on Saturday the criticism was “one-sided”, telling broadcasters: “It’s all one way, isn’t it? I can have milkshakes chucked in my face, be bashed over the head with placards and that’s all fine. That’s absolutely fine.

Article continues below

“Yet, well, we have a big event that people have paid a lot of money to come to and we get people there trying to disrupt it and we remove them. Suddenly we’re in the wrong. Utter nonsense.”

Activist group Climate Resistance claimed responsibility for the protest. In a comment, they said they were “horrified at the violence” from Reform conference audience members. The group also said the protester was considering whether to come forward to police.

News.title: Prince Harry's friend 'reveals' secret UK living arrangements as 18-month warning issued
News.content:
Prince Harry's friend 'reveals' secret UK living arrangements as 18-month warning issued

Harry and Meghan could face an 18-month wait for a permanent UK home after a friend revealed their secret living arrangements

View 4 Images Prince Harry and Meghan Markle (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's plans for their new life in Britain have been shrouded in uncertainty since their dramatic decision to spend more time in the UK.

‌



The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are understood to have chosen schools for their two children, Archie and Lilibet, as they prepare for a major change in their family life.

‌



But while the couple's plans for their children's education appear to be taking shape, a source close to Harry has now lifted the lid on where the family could be living in the meantime.

‌



Writing in the Mail on Sunday, Alison Boshoff said a friend of Prince Harry's has claimed the Sussexes are currently staying on the estate of another friend.

However, the temporary arrangement could last considerably longer than expected, with the friend warning that it may be up to 18 months before Harry and Meghan move into a permanent home.

"They are staying in a property on the estate of a friend," the source told Boshoff.

‌



View 4 Images Prince Harry and Meghan Markle (Image: Getty)

"But the truth is Harry feels they are highly unlikely to find somewhere that is just ready to move into."

He added: "He thinks it may be 12 to 18 months before they're into a new place, and that's if you are thinking about completing at the end of this year or early next year. So it could be even further away than that."

‌



The source said Harry and Meghan's reported budget of more than £8million means they are likely to be looking at historic properties, potentially making any move more complicated.

"It's likely that if you have the £8million-plus budget, which they do, that a house will be historic, which makes renovations more complicated because there are heritage issues."

He continued: "The kind of property they are looking for with the amount of land doesn't come up every week, so they know it might be a long search for the right place."

‌



The couple's children are also understood to have been enrolled in local schools.

According to Boshoff, Harry's friends say he wanted Archie, seven, to attend a traditional British prep school similar to Ludgrove in Berkshire, where Harry spent some of his own childhood.

Lilibet, five, is expected to attend the pre-prep section at the same school.

‌



View 4 Images Meghan and Harry in Australia (Image: Getty)

The arrangement would reportedly allow Harry to take on more of a full-time parenting role, while Meghan travels between Britain and the family's home in Montecito to continue her business and media ambitions.

Harry is expected to be seen supporting Archie from the sidelines as he takes up rugby, while Meghan has reportedly been adjusting to the prospect of school commitments including Saturdays.

‌



The Sussexes' return comes six years after they stepped down as working royals and moved to the US. They have since remained non-working royals.

Their plans to spend more time in Britain have raised fresh questions over security, with Harry previously arguing that it was unsafe for his wife and children to visit the UK under his current arrangements.

The Duke recently wrote to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood asking her to personally consider whether his family could receive close police protection.

‌



View 4 Images Prince Harry (Image: Getty)

Harry lost a legal challenge against the Home Office last year after his security arrangements were changed following his decision to step back from royal duties.

He has previously argued that he faces a greater threat than his late mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, citing "additional layers of racism and extremism".

Article continues below

The Sussexes have yet to publicly set out the full details of their plans for their new life in Britain.

News.title: Boy, two, killed in horror hit-and-run near his Limerick home as he played on toy tractor
News.content:
Boy, two, killed in horror hit-and-run near his Limerick home as he played on toy tractor

Peter Mulcaire was tragically pronounced dead after he suffered catastrophic injuries when he was struck by a Jeep in Rathkeale, Co Limerick

View Image Gardaí rushed to the scene in Limerick (stock image) (Image: PA)

A two-year-old boy has died after being struck by a car in a horror hit-and-run.

Little Peter Mulcaire had been playing on a toy tractor when he was struck by a Jeep near his home in Rathkeale, Co Limerick, the Irish Mirror reports. Gardaí (Irish Police) said the vehicle involved did not remain at the scene after the collision at 4pm on Saturday.

The boy was flown by air ambulance to University Hospital Limerick with serious injuries but was later pronounced dead.

A male driver of the vehicle, aged in his 30s, was arrested at a different location by Gardaí on suspicion of driving under the influence of an intoxicant.

He was taken to a Garda Station in County Limerick to provide a blood/urine sample and was later released pending analysis of that test.

A Rathkeale community fun day, which had been scheduled for Sunday, was cancelled by the organisers "out of respect" to the boy and his family and the "tragic circumstances" of his death.

Friends and relatives of the boy posted photographs of him on social media and shared their sympathies and shock with his family.

"Never in my life seen sadder, may u get best bed Peter only a baby…heartbreaking," stated a relative. Another stated: "Heartbreaking…rest in peace baby Peter."

Article continues below

A neighbour of the boy’s family, wrote: "l've never see sadder, rest in peace to our little neighbour Peter, may God comfort his family tonight. I'm so sorry for year loss, my heart breaks for his family, a little angel."

News.title: Minister to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
News.content:
JLR has not confirmed the scale of the job cuts, but said they would "simplify" the business and "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".

"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.

"We will share further information with our colleagues first." It did not rule out the prospect of some compulsory redundancies as part of the plans.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.

She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses.

Reynolds was asked about the impact on the car industry of the UK's electric vehicle sales target, which means manufacturers must ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.

He said one of the first things he had done as business secretary was give the industry more flexibility to work towards that and said there was a further consultation open on it.

"It's not where it needs to be and that's why we're willing to change the regulation to work with where consumer demand is and the industry," he added.

He said he had also spoken with West Midlands mayor Richard Parker about supporting the business and its staff.

JLR in July said fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.

It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.

The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.

That led to a 27% drop in overall production at the company, which is one of the West Midlands' biggest employers.

The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be Â£1.9bn.

In June, the firm announced it planned to cut about Â£1.7bn in costs over the coming years to help towards its recovery from the attack.

JLR had indicated at the time that it would make the savings through cuts in areas such as materials, warranty and fixed costs.

Additional reporting by Simon Jack

News.title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
News.content:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

News.title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
News.content:
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.

Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.

Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".

Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".

"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.

"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."

The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".

"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.

Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".

Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".

Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.

News.title: The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered
News.content:
Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way, external. But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right."

It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline, external Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet."

Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said, external on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy."

His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider, external who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussieâ¦"

The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career.

News.title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
News.content:
As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.

What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.

The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.

The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.

Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.

He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.

"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.

"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes withâ¦ to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".

Such a scenario, he thinks, would make the disruption for passengers caused by the incident in June seem relatively minor â and could even put lives at risk. But how likely is it?

News.title: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'
News.content:
When it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion.

"I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says.

"If I'm sat in a chair, I get nothing.

"So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"

Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.

Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.

On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause.

"It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness.

"I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."

Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger.

"You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'

"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."

News.title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
News.content:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

News.title: Why Munya Chawawa is 'jumping ship' from socials to Shakespeare
News.content:
Comedian, content creator and documentary maker Munya Chawawa became a star in the "golden era" of online video, but says his stage acting debut in Shakespeare is part of a move to "jump ship" from social media.

Recently, he has been immersing himself in footage of the UK's 1990s illegal rave scene.

It was a time of hedonism and freedom surrounded by political and media panic - and is the setting for a modern take on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, in which Chawawa will appear.

"I've obviously done a super-deep dive into rave culture and watched loads of rave footage from all these little free parties where they would find an empty field," he says.

While some footage exists of those illicit outdoor parties, they came before everyone had phones and cameras - and Chawawa, 33, feels a pang of nostalgia for that age of analogue abandon.

"I absolutely miss an era where we were dancing for ourselves and not for a digital world somewhere," he says.

News.title: Baby girl dies while camping with family in woods
News.content:
A three-month-old girl has died while camping in woodland with her family, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to land off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at 08:45 BST on Saturday, to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

"While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident," Det Insp Katie Gregory said. "The death is being treated as unexplained at this time."

People living in the close-knit community, a village of around 7,000 people, have been left shocked by the child's death.

The area is not an official camping site but locals said teenagers would often fish in two pools there and camp overnight.

The nature trail is also popular with dog walkers and runners.

A police cordon remained in place in the woodland on Sunday, and officers were in the area carrying out inquiries and providing reassurance.

A bunch of roses was also left nearby, in tribute to the little girl.

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Body-worn cameras given to school crossing wardens
News.content:
Lollipop men and women in Sheffield have been given body-worn cameras in an effort to combat abuse and aggressive behaviour from drivers.

Sheffield City Council said school crossing wardens at several unspecified locations across the city would be given the cameras, which will record interactions, as part of a new initiative.

The local authority said the measure would create a safer environment for families walking to school in the new academic year and provide reassurance to staff working alone.

Wardens have been subjected to "unacceptable behaviour" and dangerous driving by a "small" number of motorists, the council added.

Jefferson Nwokeoma, the authority's assistant director of city transport said: "These body-worn cameras will help protect our staff, provide valuable evidence when incidents occur and encourage motorists to follow the rules of the road.

"Ultimately, this is about making the journey to school safer for everyone."

Drivers who fail to stop for a school crossing warden can be fined up to Â£1,000 and have three penalty points added to their licence.

News.title: Royal Navy aircraft carrier departs for training
News.content:
HMS Queen Elizabeth has set sail with hundreds of sailors to take part in a pre-planned deployment around the UK and northern Europe.

The 65,000-tonne aircraft carrier, which was commissioned into service in 2017, left Portsmouth Naval Base at about 18:20 BST on Saturday.

Over the next three months, the Â£3.2bn warship and her crew of more than 800 sailors will take part in an intensive programme of training, the Royal Navy said.

The deployment marks the vessels first official sailing as Nato's command ship for the Allied Response Force - a designation it received in July this year.

As part of the operation, the carrier will rehearse how an Allied naval force would operate together in the event of a crisis, the Navy said.

This work, the Navy said, would aim to "enhance collective security, deterrence and readiness" among the UK and its allies.

News.title: Diana fountain shut all summer by technical fault
News.content:
The Diana Memorial Fountain in Hyde Park - which has long been a popular place to cool down in hot weather - has been kept dry all summer due to a technical fault.

Royal Parks, the charity that maintains the central London park, apologised to visitors who found it without water "particularly given the prolonged high temperatures we've been experiencing".

The fountain opened in 2004 in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales who died nearly seven years earlier.

The closure was initially triggered by a mechanical breakdown in the pump that draws water from the local borehole. The pump was fixed, but software used to control the system then failed, preventing the water supply from being restored.

The closure was publicly announced by Royal Parks on 1 July.

The charity's spokesperson acknowledged that the fountain had "remained dry for longer than we hoped" while specialist teams worked to resolve the software issue.

News.title: Police investigate Bielik fan clash at Portsmouth
News.content:
Police are investigating an incident between Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik and home supporters during Portsmouth's 2-0 Championship win on Saturday.

Bielik was involved in a physical altercation with a fan as he went to retrieve a ball from the crowd late in the second half.

Hampshire Police were notified of the incident during the match and launched an investigation immediately afterwards.

"We can confirm that we are investigating an incident in which a teenage boy was reportedly the victim of a common assault during the football match at Fratton Park. Our enquiries are ongoing," the police said.

Several Portsmouth supporters made gestures that indicated they believed the fan had been grabbed by the throat.

Cardiff head coach Brian Barry-Murphy claimed afterwards that Bielik "got slapped in the face", while clips circulating on social media appeared to show the Poland international grabbing a young fan around his upper body.

In the aftermath, another fan threw a ball at the head of Cardiff defender Perry Ng. Both supporters were ejected from the stadium.

After the game Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho apologised to Cardiff City's players.

Pompey added in a statement:, external "Portsmouth Football Club are aware of supporter concerns regarding the incident involving a young fan and an opposition player at yesterday's match at Fratton Park.

"As this remains a safeguarding matter and is currently under investigation by both the club and the police, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further on the circumstances at this time.

"However, we are aware that a number of claims and assertions are circulating on social media. We would urge caution against speculation while enquiries are ongoing.

"The welfare and safeguarding of young people are of paramount importance to Portsmouth Football Club. We will continue to liaise with the relevant parties as enquiries progress.

"No further comment will be made at this stage while investigations remain ongoing."

The Football Association is aware of the matter and will review the details in the referee's match report before deciding whether any action should be taken.

Cardiff City said: "We are satisfied with the way that match officials dealt with the situation during the game, having been in full view of it. Player protection will always be of paramount importance to us."

News.title: Heathrow Airport train services resume after trackside fire disruption
News.content:
Trains to and from Heathrow Airport were halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations.

National Rail said there was a "major disruption" to services following the incident which began shortly after 16:00 BST on Saturday.

A statement said all lines were blocked between London Paddington station and Heathrow's terminals, as well as Reading, due to "a failure of the electricity supply caused by a fire next to the track".

In an update on Sunday morning, rail operators said the fire had been extinguished and normal services had resumed.

Pictures on social media showed crowds of stranded passengers at Paddington, one of London's main rail hubs.

London Fire Brigade said six fire engines and around 40 crew members were tackling the blaze near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington.

Great Western Railway, external cancelled its services to Reading and no Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express services were running between Paddington and Heathrow on Saturday night.

The airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys, adding that the Piccadilly line, which runs services to the airport, also has delays.

Network Rail Western said some services on Sunday morning could face delays and cancellations, caused by trains being displaced by the disruption.

Earlier on Saturday, Heathrow's southern runway was closed while crews tackled a grass fire on the airfield.

It caused some disruption with at least two flights diverted elsewhere. Heathrow apologised for any disruption and said the fire was extinguished quickly.

That comes weeks after another grass fire near Heathrow's southern runway which forced 18 flights to divert and destroyed a large area of grassland.

While weather has cooled across much of the UK in recent days following record-breaking heat over the summer, fire crews have still been warning of wildfire risks.

The Met Office's Fire Severity Index, external shows that if a wildfire was to occur, it would have a "high" fire severity in most of south-east England and some of the Midlands.

The fire severity is "exceptional", the highest level on the index, in some parts of London including Heathrow, as well as on the Essex and Suffolk coasts.

News.title: Bodies of missing French fishermen recovered
News.content:
The bodies of two French fishermen who had been missing since their trawler sank in the English Channel have been found, French prosecutors have said.

The Maranello trawler sank off the coast of Plymouth on 29 August after reporting problems with its fishing gear, with three of the five crew members rescued by a nearby vessel.

A major search operation involving HM Coastguard, RNLI lifeboats from Devon and Cornwall, and French authorities was suspended after two days.

Alex Dehays, deputy prosecutor in Saint-Brieuc, said divers found and recovered the bodies on Saturday after weather conditions allowed searches to resume.

News.content:

Over the past year, Josh Loewen could hardly escape the charm offensive from American tourism organizations. Across billboards, banners, and digital platforms, US states and cities declared their fondness for Canada, promising tailored discounts to entice travelers from north of the border.

As a marketing executive based in Vancouver, Loewen said he understands the conciliatory overtures. Canadian travel to the United States plunged after President Donald Trump returned to office with remarks about making Canada the 51st state. An acrimonious trade war now is threatening to reinforce the informal boycott just as it appeared to be easing slightly.

"It’s such a big ask right now,” Loewen, 45, said of the attempts to woo Canadians like him back before a new president occupies the White House. “It’s just a wasted effort.”

Relations between the U.S. and Canadian governments have deteriorated sharply since their trade negotiations collapsed last month. Trump imposed import taxes of up to 50 percent on a range of Canadian products. Canada’s government responded in kind. Trump ordered the U.S. government to change the name of border-spanning Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed insults from members of Trump's Cabinet as childish and undignified.

The bilateral rift has not stopped state and local tourism officials and popular destinations like Graceland from trying to persuade Canadian visitors to return.

open image in gallery Canada traditionally sent more overnight international visitors to the United States than any other country ( AP )

New York state launched a “NY Loves Canada” promotion this summer, offering discounts at hotels, restaurants and attractions. Some downtown Las Vegas hotels are treating the Canadian dollar as equivalent to the U.S. dollar to give Canadian visitors more value for their money. Las Vegas tourism officials went to Canada last month to meet with travel advisers, tour operators and airline representatives.

“We’re here to make sure you know that we care about Canada," Steve Hill, president of the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority, said while in Vancouver.

The outreach is happening at the national level, too. Brand USA, the U.S. tourism industry’s marketing organization, is bringing its Travel Week trade-event series to Canada for the first time in October, expanding and rebranding an earlier program known as Canada Connect.

Travel to the U.S. from Canada remains well below 2024 levels

Canada traditionally sent more overnight international visitors to the United States than any other country. Amid last year's consumer-led backlash, both same-day trips and longer stays nosedived. Canadian residents made 25 percent fewer return border crossings and spent about $2.4 billion (CA$3.3 billion) less on travel to the U.S. in 2025 than they had the year before, according to Canada's national statistical agency, Statistics Canada.

The retreat coincided with other headwinds, including a weaker Canadian dollar that made traveling to the U.S. more expensive and rising prices for airfares and hotels. Canadian air travel to the U.S. started declining in September 2023, Statistics Canada data shows.

But the abrupt pullback in stateside travel that accompanied Trump's second presidency and extended into this year signaled “a persistent shift away from the United States by Canadian residents in their travel preferences,” agency analysts said in a July report.

open image in gallery People watch the sun set over Lake Ontario ( AP )

Tentative signs of improvement emerged in May, June and July, when border crossings picked up slightly, the agency reported. The latter two months coincided with the 2026 World Cup, which the U.S., Canada and Mexico cohosted. Canada’s national soccer team competed during the tournament's early weeks, giving some Canadians a reason to head south. Carney attended the final match in New Jersey alongside Trump.

Trips by car accounted for most of the uptick in cross-border traffic, while air travel to the U.S. fell from year-earlier levels in every month through June, Statistics Canada said. The U.S. National Travel and Tourism Office estimates that during the first six months of 2026, Canadians made even fewer overnight visits, which typically generate more tourism spending, than they did during the same period last year.

Snowbirds may provide a barometer of Canadian sentiment

A day after the World Cup ended, Trump announced that tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods would take effect in 30 days. The White House said the tariffs were intended to address U.S. complaints over Canadian barriers to American-made automobiles, alcohol and dairy.

“You went from this really high, exciting moment for the U.S. in terms of international attention, to the next week, it’s negative again,” said Deborah Friedland, a hospitality consultant at financial services firm Eisner Advisory Group. “It’s one step forward and two steps back.”

With the summer now winding down, some of the U.S. destinations most dependent on Canadian visitors are heading into their most important season. Large numbers of Canadian snowbirds typically flock to warm-weather locations in Florida, Arizona and California when temperatures drop at home, making the coming months a test of whether the grassroots boycott will extend into another winter.

open image in gallery Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, center, talks to Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey, right, and Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem ( AP )

“I’d be surprised if we’re talking a year from now and all of a sudden you see this huge uptick in Canadian travel over the winter months," Friedland said.

Not all tourism officials are worried. Jennifer Adams, tourism director for the Destin-Fort Walton Beach area in Florida’s Panhandle, said she never panicked when headlines about Canadians shunning travel to the U.S. first appeared last year.

“I felt our message was strong," she said, adding that “the thing for us is to let the Canadian family know that they are welcomed here and we are committed to giving them a great experience when they get here.”

Florida recorded a seven percent decline in Canadian visitors in 2025 compared to the previous year, according to state marketing organization Visit Florida. Visit California, citing data from global research and consulting company Tourism Economics, estimated that Canadian visitation to the Golden State fell 20 percent.

For some Canadians, a promise of a good vacation isn't enough

Loewen, the Vancouver marketing executive, said his family loved visiting the United States. He, his wife and their two children often traveled to San Diego, Portland and Seattle. This year, they chose Mexico instead.

The reluctance, Loewen said, has little to do with whether the U.S. can offer a good vacation. It’s about whether Canadians want to spend their money there while tensions between their country and the U.S. remain so high. Loewen said his family hasn't set foot in the U.S. since Trump’s inauguration and doesn't plan to until there's a new president.

Eileen March, a life coach from Calgary, said she made a similar decision. Trump's threats to make Canada the 51st state and his trade policies were part of it, as was a broader sense of no longer feeling safe or welcome in the United States, March said.

“As time has worn on, I was beginning to waver,” she said. The latest round of tariffs “reinforced my initial decision to not travel in the U.S. at all while he is in office." She refuses even to book flights with layovers in the U.S.

March, 41, knows that staying away for four years is a long time. She is prepared to go even longer.

“I think that’ll really depend on who is elected next, their values and the relationship they attempt to foster or repair with Canada,” she said.

The US war with Iran is likely to last another six months, according to former defence secretary Leon Panetta.

Six months after US-Israeli strikes against Iran, the war has reached a stalemate after a preliminary ceasefire plan unravelled.

Little progress has been made in diplomatic efforts to get the peace process back on track, after negotiations broke down in June.

Mr Panetta, who was defence secretary under President Barack Obama and has also served as director of the CIA, said in an interview that Donald Trump’s war in Iran risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”.

He told The Guardian: “It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end.”

He added: “I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved.”

open image in gallery Former US Secretary of Defence Leon E. Panetta ( AFP/Getty )

He said that reports of tensions between staff at the Pentagon were weakening the United States’ standing, saying: “Whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.”

“What I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries,” he said.

His comments come as Iran said it would step up efforts to counter the economic problems created by US sanctions.

US Central Command said it had hit three Iranian tankers on Saturday after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US navy ships.

open image in gallery Vessels at the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, September 6, 2026. Oil is getting through the waterway, US energy chief said ( Reuters )

Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Sunday that the US should understand that the rules of the game in the war against Iran have changed “before it is too late”.

He added: “From now on, any attack against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response.”

However three senior Iranian sources told Reuters that the US blockade of Iran’s oil exports was growing increasingly difficult to withstand.

US energy secretary Chris Wright said that despite Iran imposing a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz oil was getting through the waterway. He told CNN: “Our transits through the Strait are averaging over 9 million barrels a day now, and ​with the access pipelines that go around the Strait, we're probably two thirds or more of pre-conflict flows. So Iranians are still causing trouble, but the United ‌States Navy is winning that battle.”

Agencies contributed to this report.

News.title: Everton v Man United LIVE: Sesko superbly heads home vital late goal in dramatic Premier League clash
News.content:
Everton host Manchester United in the Premier League as David Moyes faces his former side following a dramatic deadline day that left him short of a striker.

The Toffees saw a late move for striker Folarin Balogun collapse after the transfer window had closed and Everton had already sold star forward Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City and striker Beto to Fiorentina. It leaves Everton with Thierno Barry as their only striker, although Jack Grealish has returned for another loan spell at the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

Everton fans were left in dismay after what had been a promising start to the season, with a home win over Crystal Palace followed by a late draw at Bournemouth, with Manchester United now arriving after Bruno Fernandes inspired Michael Carrick’s side to victory over Ipswich at Old Trafford thanks to the captain’s hat-trick.

In the weeks leading up to Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine, the headlines in a Kyiv newspaper looked much like they would anywhere else.

There was some debate over whether Russia would actually attack its neighbour. But then, outside of politics, there was everything else: the tourists stuck abroad, changes to school meals and the spread of the Omicron variant of Covid.

On 24 February 2022, everything changed as Russian tanks rolled across the border. Businesses closed or relocated, martial law saw hundreds of thousands of working-age men recruited for military service, and around one million people fled the country in the first week.

A brave few stayed behind to keep a record of what happened as the missiles rained down. Local journalists observed and asked questions as their communities were torn apart by the war.

“In one day, most of our journalists became war correspondents, especially in the frontline areas,” says Oksana Brovko, CEO of the Association of Independent Regional Press Publishers of Ukraine (AIRPPU). “And that was not a professional decision. It was the environment which changed, in February 2022.”

open image in gallery Regional journalist Maksym Zabelia brings printed newspapers to readers in the frontline city of Myrnohrad, Donetsk region, May 2026. Despite the ongoing war, local journalists continue to deliver news directly to their communities ( Maksym Zabelia / Supplied )

Brovko has spent the last four years organising support for Ukraine’s battered regional media industry. In the early days, she says, that comprised delivering bulletproof vests, first aid kits, generators and charging stations, so that reporters could continue to work.

Since then, AIRPPU has helped more than 180 outlets with material support, grants and business modelling to ensure they stay in print. Even now, the threats are very real. In July alone, Brovko says, eight local media outlets were destroyed by Russian missiles or drones. Upwards of 300 publications have closed since 2022, she adds.

UNESCO reported last summer that around 28 per cent of Ukrainian outlets had closed their doors since the start of the invasion, with 37 per cent of newsrooms partially or fully evacuated.

Internews International assessed that regional media has only seen a “clear deterioration in operating conditions” since then, exacerbated by the suspension of foreign aid programmes since Donald Trump took office.

open image in gallery AIRPPU’s Regional Media Support Hub distributing protective equipment, body armour and helmets to Ukrainian journalists, Lviv, April 2022. The initiative helped regional newsrooms continue reporting safely during the first months of Russia’s full-scale invasion ( AIRPPU / Supplied )

Beyond the immediate threat to life, newsrooms are desperately in need of staff, investment and psychological support.

Mobilisation has seen newsrooms shrink from an average of 10 to 20 reporters to just three to five, Brovko says, while the evacuation of residents has cut into subscription revenues and the relocation of businesses has dried up advertising money.

Nearly three-quarters of editors said a lack of funding was a primary challenge last year, up from 58 per cent a year prior. Almost half said staffing was a major concern, with mobilisation now the main cause of reporters leaving, ahead of stress and burnout.

Those journalists have crucially been among the first to parse and share the conflict as it moves through their communities.

The 0629 outlet from Mariupol was on the scene speaking to witnesses when Russia bombed a theatre sheltering civilians on 16 March 2022. Vhoru continued publishing from Kherson even through nine months of Russian occupation. Okana says their work is vital.

open image in gallery Oksana Brovko, CEO of the Association of Independent Regional Press Publishers of Ukraine (AIRPPU), at the Media Congress, an annual gathering of independent regional media from across Ukraine, which she has organised for 15 years ( AIRPPU / Supplied )

“They are writing history right now, and in 50 years we’ll come back and we will learn history – European history – from these newspapers, which I receive every week from the colleagues on the front line.”

But the strain of the conflict also threatens the other functions of a free press.

It took decades from Ukraine’s independence for the media to unshackle itself from government ownership, and the country is still negotiating a new relationship with its anti-corruption bodies. Brovko says the media plays an essential role in scrutinising the work of local government. And, as well as the war, reporters also face pressure from local officials to rein in their investigations.

“From one side, we fight with Russia, because we work under missiles, in a broken environment,” she says. “From another side, it’s the local government ... we start to be visible, and we start to feel pressure from local authorities, from local businesses, from local politicians.”

open image in gallery Burned copies of the Mezhivskyi Meridian newspaper after a Russian missile attack on the vehicle delivering the print run in Mezhova, Dnipropetrovsk region, August 2026. With AIRPPU’s support, the newspaper was reprinted to ensure residents continued to receive essential local information ( Mezhivskyi Meridian / Supplied )

She says the challenge going forward will be to move out of this constant struggle for survival and towards a new resilience.

“It’s important to remember that sometimes you need to fight for independence. Sometimes you need even to die protecting that. But at the same time we need to remember that the future is not just to think about survival, but also about the future.”

AIRPPU has partnered with OpenAI and the World Association of News Publishers to facilitate the adoption of artificial intelligence in newsrooms. The topic is sensitive in the industry, but Brovko believes that using AI to automate routine tasks and administrative so that the reporters can spend more time on the front lines gathering news.

“This programme will provide Ukrainian publishers with access to international expertise, practical tools and hands-on support that will help them turn those opportunities into tangible results. And most importantly – it should give journalists back time to do journalism,” she says.

open image in gallery Yevhen Khrypun, chief editor of Mezhivskyi Meridian, holding copies of the newspaper damaged by a Russian attack in Mezhova, Dnipropetrovsk region, August 2026 ( Yevhen Khrypun / Supplied )

Trudova Slava, a digital and print newspaper in Zaporizhzhia, said in a statement shared with The Independent: “Our newsroom is small, but we serve five communities in Zaporizhzhia region, most of whose territories are inaccessible to journalists because of the fighting, while our communities are dispersed across Ukraine and abroad.

“We need AI to continuously monitor social media and other sources, helping us find important stories, people and issues that we might otherwise miss.”

The Kremenchuk Telegraph said they planned to use the tools to help analyse large volumes of documents, asset declarations, court decisions, public procurement records and other open data, to generate leads for investigation faster than sifting through information manually.

News.title: Arsenal v Chelsea LIVE: Premier League champions host challengers in mouthwatering London derby
News.content:
Why Chelsea Are SERIOUS Title Contenders

Arsenal host Chelsea in an early London derby in the Premier League that could determine whether we have a title race this season.

Champions Arsenal flexed their muscles as they ground out an impressive win at Aston Villa on Monday and although a big-name attacking signing eluded them in the transfer window, Mikel Arteta’s side have the strength and depth to defend their title.

Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea have caught the eye, however, with Cole Palmer finding some early form and creating a formidable front three with Joao Pedro and Morgan Rogers that could fire the Blues towards a potential title challenge.

Chelsea have conceded goals at the other end, however, and have struggled to control games so far under Alonso, so a visit to champions Arsenal – who they have not beaten in five years – sets up a fascinating test of their credentials.

Follow updates from Arsenal v Chelsea with our live blog below:

News.title: ‘My child suffered heat exhaustion after nursery – Burnham must act on climate change’
News.content:
