We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

A mother whose daughter suffered heat exhaustion after a day at nursery during this year’s record-breaking summer weather has urged Andy Burnham to prioritise future generations over drilling in the North Sea.

Joanna Groves, 31, from Bristol, was forced to call an ambulance after her four-year-old Ivy’s temperature soared to 38.7C during the second heatwave in June, just days before the mercury would peak at 38C in parts of the country.

“It [was] really scary. We were pretty worried,” she said, as Ivy was left lethargic and refusing to drink after a day at her nursery, which was later forced to temporarily close due to the extreme temperatures.

The mother-of-two has urged the prime minister to “prioritise the safety of vulnerable people, especially kids, and to think about what they’re inheriting” as she attended a demonstration from Mothers Rise Up alongside a hundred more parents on Tuesday outside No 10 Downing Street.

“He’s got kids himself, so you’d hope that he’s having these same worries that we have,” she added.

open image in gallery Jo Groves called an ambulance for her daughter Ivy during the second heatwave ( Supplied )

The campaigners handed a letter in to No 10, signed by more than 28,000 people, urging Mr Burnham to adapt homes, schools and public infrastructure in line with recommendations from the Climate Change Committee’s A Well-Adapted UK report, invest more in affordable and renewable energy, and oppose new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.

The government is expected to give a go-ahead for the Jackdaw gas field off the coast of Aberdeen in a matter of weeks, it has been reported, despite concerns raised that its emissions could generate 36 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in greenhouse gas emissions over its lifetime, around 90 per cent of Scotland’s total emissions for 2023.

Ms Groves said that she was lucky Ivy was not hospitalised during the second heatwave, which saw the UK Health Security Agency issue a rare red heat-health alert for large parts of England across three days.

The UKHSA recorded 2,877 excess deaths caused by May and June heatwaves.

open image in gallery A giant melting-planet ice cream is displayed outside 10 Downing Street as Mothers Rise Up calls for urgent heat adaptation, clean energy and an end to new North Sea oil and gas ( Denise Laura Baker / Mothers Rise Up )

More than 1,000 UK schools closed for days or sent students home early in late June as the temperatures made them unsafe for children. Ms Groves’ nursery told parents that they’d worked hard to keep children hydrated and in the shade throughout the day, but was later forced to close due to the heat.

Mothers Rise Up told The Independent that now was the time to take action as the Met Office provisionally declared Summer 2026 the UK’s warmest on record, with a mean average temperature across June, July and August of 16.5C, beating the previous seasonal high of 16.1C set last year.

Maya Mailer, policy lead for the campaign group, said: “It’s only going to get hotter and we’re not set up for that as a country. We have the mindset of being in a cooler climate, and our buildings trap heat.”

open image in gallery Mothers and children with Mothers Rise Up gather outside 10 Downing Street with a giant melting-planet ice cream, calling for urgent action to protect children from extreme heat ( Denise Laura Baker / Mothers Rise Up )

She said this summer was “so difficult for so many kids, teachers, patients, doctors, nurses, so we need to adapt our infrastructure” and that in order to address the root cause of the crisis, the government needed to commit to no new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.

“The government is about to make a decision on whether it will green light the huge Rosebank oil field, the largest undeveloped oil field in the North Sea, and also the Jackdaw gas fields, and our view is that it would just be unimaginable to do that after such a summer.”

A government spokesperson said: “The UK continues to be a world leader in tackling the climate crisis and we are acting to protect people and places from the impacts of climate change.

“We are investing in clean power, building nine new reservoirs and investing £10.5 billion by March 2036 to construct new flood and coastal erosion schemes, as extreme weather becomes more frequent.”

News.title: VAR a scourge on the Premier League as Forest denied by off-field meddling
News.content:
“I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

“Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

“I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

“I just said he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us.”

Maresca said he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

News.title: Newcastle’s limitations exposed by Bournemouth before hosts fight back for draw
News.content:
A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

In truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a new manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

When Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

That opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

News.title: Relentless Springboks give All Blacks 15 minutes of hell to lead series
News.content:
There will be no repeat of the All Blacks historic Test series victory in South Africa 30 years ago, after the home side ruthlessly ensured they will lead 2-1 going into the concluding weekend.

And the manner in which the Springboks blew away their fierce rivals in the last 15 minutes made Rassie Eramus’s men overwhelming favourites to finish the job in America next Saturday.

However, there were passages of this brutal battle that suggested that Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry could still produce a finale worthy of the billing if New Zealand can learn the lessons from this brutal encounter at the FNB Stadium in Johannesburg.

There was a late Kiwi try to give the scoreboard a humdinger hue but Erasmus’s side were well deserving of their second victory in as many Saturdays over their fierce rivals, and credit to the South Africa coach for outwitting counterpart Dave Rennie without needing to change his starting XV just before the kick-off, like he did seven days before.

Amazing what one can do with a simple but chilling game plan. The old scoundrel knew that if he slowed it down and let his scrum walk round the All Blacks scrum that his backs would have the precious space.

Yet, however it might feel away from Springbok turf, New Zealand will still fancy their chances of levelling it, especially after matching their opponents’ haul of four tries. Their fly-half, Ruben Love, missed five simple-enough points and until that last quarter it was an even contest. Yet, as it tends to, South Africa’s physical intensity and their almighty scrum eventually prevailed.

News.title: Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

News.title: ‘It’s just a useless gimmick’: Telegraph readers react to Dyson’s latest gadget
News.content:
Would you spend over £400 on a toothbrush? Telegraph readers aren’t convinced.

The new Dyson CameraJet has just launched, retailing for £419.99, which brushes, flosses and mouth-washes in one, with the help of a camera.

After Rebecca Astill gave her verdict on the gadget, we asked Telegraph readers for their views and whether Dyson can convince them to trade in their old faithfuls.

They share the toothbrushes they swear by, from manual to electric models, and whether they see any reason to upgrade. Here’s what they had to say.

Why readers are unconvinced

The majority of readers seem unconvinced by the CameraJet, with John arguing that a toothbrush and a smartphone “sounds like two accidents waiting to happen. Squirted in the eye with mouthwash as you drop the phone down the toilet”.

“It’s just a useless gimmick,” argues reader Donald Mckie, a retired NHS dentist. “The average patient wouldn’t have a clue what they would be looking at in their mouth on a phone screen,” he adds.

“Dyson as a brand is an aspiration for many but I don’t know how this appliance would improve anyone’s oral health.”

In his view, “the tank for the mouthwash at 12.5ml is far too small, the industry average will be somewhere near 250-300ml” to last long enough and successfully dislodge sticky plaque.

He also questions the picture quality of the camera with water spray, saliva, lips, facial hair and toothpaste in the way. “People nowadays will expect pin sharp detail, which I doubt this will deliver.”

News.title: DiCaprio’s Amazonian warrior queen
News.content:
It was while she was in hiding after recovering from the sixth attempt on her life, that the activist Juma Xipaia got a call asking if she would agree to be the subject of a documentary. The first female chief of the Middle Xingu region of the Brazilian Amazon, Xipaia was well known in Brazil for her passionate attempts to protect her indigenous community from the effects of deforestation, illegal gold-mining and – in particular – the catastrophic environmental consequences of the $11 billion Belo Monte hydroelectric dam project, a wildly ambitious and destructive endeavour that has affected livelihoods, fish stocks, ecosystems and biodiversity, with legal challenges still ongoing today.

Thirty-four-year-old Xipaia’s outspoken resistance and exposure of corruption relating to the dam’s construction led to the threats on her life. The last attempt was by poisoning, via a food delivery company, which resulted in her being on a ventilator with 70 per cent organ failure. She was on the verge of death, when, she says, she had a dream that she was given a choice – to take the easy path of dying, or the difficult path of coming back, and because she’s a fighter, that’s the one she chose. And a week later she walked out of the hospital.

Leonardo DiCaprio described the activist as one of the most incredible people he’d ever met Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

Like many activists representing indigenous communities she walked a tightrope between protecting the interests and traditions of her people, and not being perceived as standing in the way of progress in terms of the economic development that benefits Brazil as a whole, a paradox that was defined when President Lula da Silva regained power in 2023, and brought Xipaia into government.

Richard Ladkani, a film director who has made vibrant environmental documentaries such as The Ivory Game (about poaching) and Sea of Shadows (marine activists), was the man who called her. It was 2019, when Brazil was still under the brutal rule of Jair Bolsonaro and destruction of the Amazon was at its peak – an area of rainforest the size of Belgium was burned during his presidency, and thousands of illegal goldmines flourished, contaminating the forest, polluting the river with mercury (mercury is used to bind gold) and bringing crime and disruption to previously pristine areas.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“All summer long we had seen these dramatic apocalyptic images,” says Ladkani. “And I was posing for photos at the premiere of Sea of Shadows, with [executive producers] Leo DiCaprio and Jane Goodall, when Leo leaned over and whispered, ‘So Richard, what’s next?’

“And I said, 'We've got to do something about the Amazon.’”

DiCaprio came onboard as producer, and Goodall as an ambassador. Ladkani knew he had to find a powerful central figure to provide human and emotional context, someone who would be the voice of the Amazon. He drew up a list of possible candidates, until the Brazilian journalist Eliane Brum told him “do not make a decision until you have spoken to Juma Xipaia – when she speaks, the world listens. She can silence a whole room with her energy.”

‘For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one’

Right now, in a small restaurant in New York, Xipaia is not really in the mood to talk. It is February, and it’s snowing, and Ladkani, Xipaia and her husband, Hugo Loss, are here to publicise the resulting documentary, Yanuni – which took six years to make – at a screening attended by UN representatives and Brazilian diplomats. The recent news about Trump’s exploits in Venezuela has shaken them all and, more specifically, Juma has had a bad experience with American food which doesn’t really agree with her. She is a little reticent at first, but soon opens up with the help of an interpreter, and explains to me what it meant to be a cacique (chief), and how she was selected.

Indigenous leader Juma Xipaia and her husband Hugo Loss in the city of Aracaju, Brazil Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

“I never chose to be a cacique,” she says, “but I couldn’t stay quiet in the face of exploitation of my people – there was violence, and women being harassed and raped.” She is referring to the collateral damage that importing thousands of workers to build a dam inevitably brings. “Usually the role of cacique is given to the oldest male in the community – my dad and my uncles and my brother were all caciques, but the elders knew that they could trust me never to negotiate our rights with corporations or politicians, never to compromise. For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one. I accepted the position for two years, with the goal of strengthening on our territories and bringing sovereignty to our people.”

Xipaia was born in 1991 and had an idyllic childhood, she says, growing up in Tucumã, a small indigenous community along the Iriri River, about 250 miles west of the city of Altamira. They lived in wooden houses and ate fruit and nuts from the forest and fish from the river, and in 2006 she moved to Altamira for her education. But threats were encroaching her community, with land opened up for mining and farming, and in 2011, a licence was granted to construct the Belo Monte Dam, to stop up parts of the Xingu River, one of the most species-rich areas of the Amazon.

Aged just 21, Xipaia spoke out against the dam at a public hearing, but despite lawsuits, protest from indigenous people and large sections of society, construction went ahead. Xipaia attended law school in Altamira and studied plans put forward by Norte Energia, the company that built Belo Monte, helping to expose corruption that was going on within. In 2015, at the age of 24, she became a cacique, the first female leader of her people. Other communities had been bought off by Norte Energia with gifts of stoves, fridges, TVs.

In November 2019, she led a protest of angry Brazilian landowners and farmers to disrupt the Amazon: Center of the World international conference in Altamira. But by now she had become a target, and by the time Ladkani called her she had survived six attempts on her life, including her car being rammed with children in the back, and a threat to kidnap her son. She went into hiding for a year and she didn’t want to talk to anyone.

“She thought, the only way I’m going to survive is if I stop talking, because when I talk, people want to kill me,” Ladkani says. But she was finally convinced to take a call from him, and from the first moment, he says, he knew he had found the voice for his film. “Her poetry is the thing that stands out – the way she can describe emotions and feelings and put things into context, I felt it was unique. And when she told me the story of how she almost died because of the poisoning, I was in tears.

“I told her I wanted her to be the voice in the film and also offered her the role of producer. Because I knew nothing of indigenous life and I needed her to lead the way.”

An aerial view of the Belo Monte hydroelectric dam in Altamira Credit : CARLOS FABAL

It was a struggle from the word go. Xipaia was not happy about a translator being involved because of security reasons; she couldn’t trust anyone. So Ladkani, who is Austrian, took intensive lessons in Portuguese and within six months was fluent. “It was a key thing to show that I meant business and took her concerns very seriously,” he tells me.

The security budget for the film was huge, they needed the best, most experienced people: safe houses, secure drivers. And the arrangements had to extend for a year after filming was completed – a total of seven years. “Leo was extremely important here because he raised the first third of the budget, and this encouraged other philanthropists to be part of it.”

Filming began in 2020. There was no script and Ladkani didn’t know what he was going to get from it, just that he needed to tell the story of the pillaging of the Amazon via Xipaia’s voice.

And in the end it was a wild ride: it started with Xipaia leading protests against Bolsonaro, but after Lula was elected in 2023, he established a Ministry for Indigenous Rights, of which Xipaia was made state secretary, implementing a series of bills for the protection of the forest and employing lawyers, biologists and engineers to combat the destruction of the Amazon.

Juma Xipata and Leonardo DiCaprio at the Yanuni Premiere during the 2025 Tribeca Festival in New York City. Credit : John Nacion/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival

The film documents her move from her village to set up home in Brasilia with her son; getting together with her husband Hugo Loss, head of special operations for Ibama (the Brazilian Institute of Renewable and Natural Resources), an elite outfit conducting raids on illegal mines; and the birth of their first child, who was called Yanuni.

It was a lengthy, exciting journey, an improvisation which resulted in thousands of hours of film. “I just had to go with the unpredictable. The strength of any documentary is when unforeseen things happen, because a twist in direction is the greatest thing of any film structure.

“And we had that multiple times. I had chosen a woman to be the voice of the Amazon and two years later she became the second most powerful woman in the Indigenous Ministry – I get goosebumps now at the sheer luck. That was the first twist, and then Hugo enters her life, who happens to be this charismatic soldier of an elite force who would take me to the frontline of the Amazon resistance, and then Juma becomes pregnant and gives birth to Yanuni. Holy s**t. If I had written that as a script, everyone would have thrown it out as complete fiction.”

‘I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, “Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent”’

Leo DiCaprio was a producer on the film (rather than his usual role of executive producer), which meant he was far more involved. “He not only provided the money, but he gave me meaningful support throughout the production,” says Ladkani. In November 2021 DiCaprio attended Cop 26 in Glasgow, where he met Xipaia for the first time. “That meeting was spectacular – Leo posted a picture of the two of them together and said that she was one of the most incredible people he’d ever met.” The resulting attention helped to protect Xipaia, because a public profile is to some extent a safeguard. “There she is next to DiCaprio, so she’s not just a voiceless indigenous person from somewhere in the Amazon.”

There were many technical challenges. Because of security, Ladkani couldn’t film in the normal way, with lighting and a crew. “I had a second cinematographer, a brilliant guy from Brazil, called Fábio Nascimento, and I took him with me when I could – but that was only 30 per cent of the time. The rest I shot alone. I downsized my gear and basically shot the film with a DSLR, like a photo camera, so I looked like a tourist. To an outsider, I was just a white gringo taking pictures.” Xipaia had a hidden microphone beneath her shirt. If Ladkani was ever confronted, he claimed to be a YouTuber.

“Security demanded that we shot the film incognito, and that became its strength, because I was embedded within the family to the extent that they stopped noticing me,” says Ladkani.

An illegal gold-mining ship destroyed by Ibama in the Brazilian Amazon – it is dangerous work, with agents risking serious injury and even their lives Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Hugo Loss’s job involved protecting indigenous communities and flying over the forest and rivers of the Amazon routing out illegal goldmines, dredgers and excavators. His small team lands, arrests the miners and sets fire to all the expensive equipment, which is too bulky to confiscate. In the film we see massive plumes of thick black smoke rising above the forest. Penalties for environmental crime are insubstantial, but, says Loss, “It’s not for President Lula to change those things, it’s Congress, and it’s hard to change the law. But destroying the equipment is a real deterrent, because the machines are expensive, so it’s a risky investment.”

An illegal gold mine in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Loss and Xipaia met when her village was attacked in 2020 by illegal goldminers; she was in Altamira, a two-day boat ride away. She put out a cry for help on social media and Loss, who was also in Altamira, saw it and responded right away. He picked Xipaia up in a helicopter and asked her to take him to the exact location of the miners’ dredger. The attackers spotted them and ran, but Ibama were able to seize their boat and secure the area. “He saved her village and her people and her parents from an immediate attack and they fell in love and have been together ever since,” says Ladkani.

“I’m usually very shy about these things but from the first time I saw her in the helicopter I couldn’t stop thinking about her,” admits Loss. “Three months later I was doing an Ibama operation on land to remove some illegal loggers and I saw a hawk’s nest and I took a picture of it and sent it to her,” says Loss.

“It’s the bird whose feather I wear in my headdress,” interrupts Xipaia, shyly. She admits that she had first met Loss before the helicopter ride, at a meeting, but he was leaving as she arrived. “He shook my hand and I made eye contact with him and something told me – I can’t really explain what – that he was going to be my husband.”

Loss holds a Master’s degree in social anthropology from the University of Brasília and is one of Ibama’s most experienced field agents, yet he spent a good part of his career sidelined by Bolsonaro, who had no interest in protecting the environment. In February 2023, under Lula, he was appointed Ibama’s coordinator of enforcement.

Loss has taken part in hundreds of operations. His job is a dangerous one. We watch him flying helicopters over swathes of forest to spot mines, or patrolling the rivers looking for dredgers. Recently one of his team was killed in an ambush, another got burns over 60 per cent of his body.

Hugo Loss, Xipaia’s husband, on a mission to destroy illegal mining equipment for Ibama, Brazil’s government enforcement agency

Ladkani asked to accompany Loss on a raid. “Hugo told me, it's too dangerous, the risk of you dying is too high. It’s a small team, and you would be taking the place of a soldier on the helicopter so we would be down one security man, which means our job is much harder, and by the way, if we get into a gun fight, we are not your bodyguards, we are there to finish a job. You would have to save yourself.

“I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, ‘Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent.’ I laughed – and then I realised he wasn’t joking.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“Of course I had to think about that – I have a wife and two daughters. My wife and I discussed it. She grew up in a war zone in Beirut, so she understands threats, and how you can mitigate risks as well. She is also the producer of this film. We have had a long journey together – making conflict zone films like Sea of Shadows and The Ivory Game was no joke. But this one felt like a different level because of the 50 per cent quote.” He smiles.”‘I did hostile-environment training and we augmented the security to a degree where I felt it wasn’t 50 per cent any more.”

An illegal airbase in the Brazilian Amazon being destroyed Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

So Ladkani joined the team, and the resulting episode is terrifying: they are patrolling the river when they find a huge illegal dredger, used for gold mining. They board the dredger, its crew of illegal miners are put in a small boat and dispatched, and Loss’s team set fire to it. Attempting to get away, they realise their boat is still attached to the dredger by a chain, and they have only moments before an oxygen tank below the deck of the dredger explodes. Loss has to shoot the chain, but he has to hit it while it is taut, or the bullet would glance off. “The oxygen tank is steel and if it had exploded we would have been killed by the fragments if we were within 100 metres of that boat – and we were six metres away. It was Hugo who shot the chain – it took 50 shots at least. When Juma saw that footage she broke down and sobbed,” says Ladkani.

Do you like your job? I ask Loss.

He smiles. “Yes I do.”

Back in the 1970s, when two major roads were originally carved into the Amazon rainforest, of which 60 per cent is in Brazil, it opened it up for settlers to devastating effects – the population of the Brazilian Amazon quadrupled and millions of acres of trees were cut down for timber or land clearance and farming, and the rivers became polluted. Thousands of garimpeiros (prospectors) arrived, bringing disease, destruction and violence.

Indigenous people from the Mura tribe in a deforested area inside the Amazon rainforest near Humaita, Amazonas State, Brazil Credit : Ueslei Marcelino/REUTERS

Despite the protected reserves created by Lula during his first tenure (2003 to 2011), when Bolsonaro took over, he vowed that he would not demarcate a single millimetre of Indigenous land.

There was reason to be hopeful when Lula was re-elected in 2023, especially when he created the Ministry for Indigenous People. But it was an uphill struggle, and Xipaia left the post of State Secretary after about two years, and retired to her territory, where she still is. “She realised that it would be years, if not decades, before change could happen and she felt that her power was with activism from the front lines rather than being in an office in the city,” says Ladkani. “And what really hurt was her children having to grow up in the city and not having the connection to nature that she had.”

Smoke from illegal fires lit by farmers rises in Manaquiri, Amazonas state Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS

There has been a lot of progress, Juma says, compared to the Bolsonaro years “when it was genocide”. “It is hard to quantify all the changes because even though there was a change in the administration, it is important to understand that the government structure is very colonialist, no matter who is in power, and everything takes time. I entered the ministry when it was just being born.

“It was hard working in an office every day and not spending time with my children, and my son Tuppak [eight] told me that he wanted to go back to the forest, he was having a hard time at school in the city. I did not want to rob my son of that kind of childhood – being in the territory and getting his knowledge from the forest.”

I ask Loss and Xipaia if, with the way things are now, they are more inclined to hope or despair. “Most of the time I don’t think about the future,” says Loss. “I just focus on doing my work, one operation at a time.”

A wildfire consumes land deforested by cattle farmers near Novo Progresso, Para state, Brazil Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS/AFP via Getty Images

Xipaia thinks. “It depends where I am. When I’m in the forest with my family, there is immense fulfilment which is hard to explain; it gives me the hope and energy to keep wanting to protect it, and I want the whole world to get to know it.

“When I walk through the forest and harvest food there with my family and my people, it reminds me of what my ancestors were doing. The innocence of children, the idea of clean water, food without toxins – this gives me hope.”

“I don’t feel despair,” says Ladkani. “I feel like we’re in a war. There are plenty of good people fighting back, and that gives me hope. And there are lives on the line that we need to care about, which is the indigenous people, who are the frontline of our defence. They are defending nature for us so we need to make sure that they are heard and seen and respected. And we hope that the film puts a human face to that.

“We can’t pretend that destroying the biggest ecosystem on the planet is OK. If we lose the Amazon, we all lose.”

News.title: Alexander Isak starts to justify £125m price tag with double
News.content:
Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

News.title: Forced displacement in the West Bank could be ‘crime against humanity’, says UN report
News.content:
Israel’s forced displacement of more than 33,000 Palestinians in the West Bank could amount to a “crime against humanity” and involves “ethnic cleansing”, according to a report published by the UN.

A report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that Israeli actions in the area had sparked the “largest and longest displacement crisis in the West Bank since 1967” – the year in which Israel captured the territory.

The report said “large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from refugee camps … during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall [which] raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer”.

It added: “The documented use of airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations, to render entire camps uninhabitable, to force the displacement of their residents and to prevent their return, in the absence of imperative military necessity to justify such destruction and displacement, are not permissible under international law, appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

The 27-page report covers the period December 5, 2024 to January 31, 2026.

In January 2025, Israeli forces launched “Operation Iron Wall” in the northern West Bank in a bid to counter what they said were terrorist threats.

They destroyed hundreds of homes, cut off water and electricity, and barred humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Sham and Tulkarm refugee camps.

By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 percent in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged.

The three camps are among 19 in the West Bank established to shelter Palestinians after the 1948 Nakba, and are administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA).

Although still referred to as refugee camps, they are in fact now densely packed towns.

Sports.title: Watkins’ £51m Pro League move earns Exeter £2m windfall — but he was almost dumped on the scrapheap
Sports.content:
OLLIE WATKINS moving to the Saudi Pro League earns Exeter a tidy windfall.

The England striker joined Al-Hilal from Aston Villa for £51million on Sunday



And the League Two side pocket nearly £2m as part of the sell-on clause from his 2017 move to Brentford and subsequent Villa Park switch.

Yet Grecians boss Matt Taylor has revealed how close Watkins came to being dumped on football’s scrapheap.



He told SunSport: “It was in the balance of whether Ollie would have a football career, let alone one at League Two, Championship, Premier League and then international level.

“If he’d have been released at 18, 19 years of age, I don’t know if he’d have had a career. That’s how fine the margins are.”



The skinny teen struggled for an identity at St James Park and was shipped on loan to non-league Weston-super-Mare to learn the ropes.

Club coaches openly debated whether to send the youngster on another loan spell or cut him loose entirely before he broke through.

Taylor explained: “Ollie didn’t have a position on the pitch. He played in every position.

“He’d never been an out-and-out No9. There were times in that off-season where questions were being asked as to would it be another loan? Would he be released?

“What would it really look like for Ollie? He probably outperformed our expectations in that breakthrough season.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The turning point came when Watkins returned for pre-season completely transformed.

He packed on half a stone of lean muscle, giving him the athletic frame to start bullying defenders and catching the eye of the management.

Taylor said: “He came back like a thoroughbred horse.

It was incredible. All of a sudden, he’d out-jump and out-run defenders.

“Certainly when he was younger, Ollie relied a lot on confidence. Then he’d score in training or a pre-season game.

“And then the manager Paul Tisdale could see him leading the line as a centre-forward.”



Watkins caught fire against local rivals Plymouth and never looked back.

Taylor added: “It was that game where he announced himself on the first-team stage.

“Then for the next 12 months, he was almost unplayable. He became the main man.

“Once these young players get that prestige and responsibility, you can see them growing naturally.

“Suddenly he wasn’t a skinny 18-year-old anymore. He was a 20-year-old man who could outrun and outfight a lot of opponents and also had a fantastic skill set.”



Exeter’s model survives on producing elite professionals with the right mindset. Humility is essential.

Taylor stresses that while the Grecians operate in the lower divisions, the players they produce possess the hunger and drive required at the absolute top level.

He said: “I always go back to the biggest attribute of the players we’ve sold has been their mentality.



“Now, we might have been playing League Two and League One, but these were still elite professionals at that point, which is why they’ve gone on to be where they are in the pyramid.

“And that’s from their upbringing from their parents, first and foremost, their families, and then the support that the academy has been able to give them.

“We generally produce good people and good professionals as well as good players.

“But you have to be patient with young players. We usually hold on to them for longer than other clubs — and that’s exactly why Ollie was able to flourish.”

Taylor — who returned to take charge of Exeter for a second spell in March — knows the harsh realities of management after tough spells at Rotherham and Bristol Rovers.



He takes aim at top-heavy boardrooms that choke managers.

Taylor warned: “We’re not called managers anymore, we’re called head coaches. We’re not the most important people in the building.

“Unfortunately, there’s a director of football, a technical director, a head of recruitment, and various people at board level.

“You’ll have family members in the boardroom who think they’re football managers and will always jump to a rationale or a reason as to why they’re not getting success.”

Taylor kept Rotherham up in 2023 on the Championship’s lowest budget, only to be axed months later.



He feels managers are treated as disposable by owners chasing dreams.

The Exeter boss added: “I don’t understand why people don’t give managers or head coaches longer. It seems it’s easier to change the head coach than the players or the staff.

“They’re the ones who seem to be dispensable when it used to be the other way around.

“The truth of it is, in a league of 24, where your budget is, it’s probably pretty close to where you’re going to finish. So expectation as opposed to reality can be misguided.”

Exeter were relegated last season, forcing a complete reset as 13 senior players departed.



Most of Taylor’s squad are now academy products.

He said: “We won’t make you rich — but getting you the move upwards off the back of being with us will do. And with that there will be a financial reward.

“It’ll be a level up, or if not two levels up. If a player comes to Exeter and they’re not humble, they will not be successful.”

The fan-owned Grecians rely on smart coaching over big money.

Taylor concluded: “We have to be creative in terms of recruitment. We can’t compete financially.



“Steve Perryman used to say our pound’s got to be worth two. It means we’ve just got to go above and beyond and get the most out of each other as people.”

Sports.title: Russell Martin’s stubborn tactics are steering Leicester towards a total League One car crash
Sports.content:
THE definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again while expecting a different result.

If that is true, Russell Martin is writing the manual on footballing madness at the King Power Stadium.



Leicester’s 4-0 home loss against Oxford in League One was a new low for a club that famously won the Premier League against all odds just 10 years ago.

The Foxes are a club in desperate, agonising soul-searching mode.



After years of catastrophic mismanagement, soft dressing room cultures, and back-to-back collapses dragged them into the third tier, they needed a steadying hand.

When a house is on fire, you do not debate the aesthetics of the wallpaper — you put out the flames.

Instead, the board rolled the dice on Martin.

It was a staggering risk and right now it looks like a slow-motion car crash.

Martin is a fundamentalist. It is his way or the highway — but right now, his way looks like a direct route to footballing hell.

Yes, exciting, progressive, possession-based football looks magnificent.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Martin got Southampton promoted straight back to the Premier League through the play-offs after an incredible run following early pain a few years ago.

But he was hopelessly inflexible in the top flight. Trying to out-Pep Guardiola with inferior players meant it was always going to end in tears.

His stint at Rangers was a complete and utter disaster. He was chewed up, spat out, and dismissed within four months.

I doubt he will ever be able to walk into a pub on the Blue side of Glasgow again — though he might find a warm welcome with Celtic fans!

Now he is in the dog-eat-dog trenches of League One, managing a club where a losing culture has been baked in for two full seasons.



When a club forgets how to win, you do not ask them to play tippy-tappy roulette inside their own penalty box.

You build resilience, grind out results, and rediscover how to win matches by any means necessary.

Wherever Martin goes, he refuses to budge. Adaptability is completely foreign to him.

Good managers win football matches. They look at their squad, evaluate the division and find a pragmatic way to get three points.

Bad managers lose because they are stubborn one-trick ponies.



Martin – who has so many good qualities — is in serious danger of cementing his place in that second category.

His reputation is taking an absolute pounding. Having played under some proper, no-nonsense managers like Gordon Strachan, Paul Lambert, Darren Ferguson and Alex Neil, you would think he’d have learned the value of pragmatism.

It made zero sense for Leicester to appoint him after getting rid of Gary Rowett. Rowett would have been a steady pair of hands in the third tier.



They still have big earners like Wout Faes on the books on massive wages.

What is the point of paying his huge salary if you are not going to play him? Unless a Turkish or Saudi club are interested, they need to reintegrate him into the squad until the January window opens.

Leicester should be ripping up League One, but at this rate they will be in League Two next season!

It is utterly incredible how far the mighty have fallen.

If the Russell Martin experiment finally explodes, Leicester’s hierarchy must move heaven and earth to bring in Rob Edwards.



Look at Edwards’ record: two promotions, taking Forest Green into League One and guiding Luton into the Premier League.

He was flexible at Kenilworth Road and almost kept them in the top flight against all the odds.

I do not think the Hatters would have dropped to League One had they not bailed out on him mid-season back in the Championship.

Edwards did a good job with a Wolves team that looked hopelessly out of their depth when he came in.

Yet they bizarrely sacked him in the summer.



Crucially, Edwards is pragmatic, adaptable and knows how to win.

Right now, Leicester do not need an idealist. They need a winner before the unthinkable happens.

Sullivan upping his stake angers Hammers fans

WEST HAM fans are up in arms after divisive former chairman David Sullivan actually INCREASED his shareholding in the club.

Sullivan resigned from the board this summer following damning allegations of wrongdoing with young women in an explosive Panorama documentary — claims he has firmly denied.



Yet he triggered pre-emption rights alongside Daniel Kretinsky to block Amanda Staveley‘s consortium out.

Following the carve-up of Vanessa Gold’s 25 per cent stake, Kretinsky has increased his holding to 46 per cent.

Sullivan’s share is up to 40 per cent, while Tripp Smith holds 11 per cent.

Between them, Sullivan and Smith still command a 51 per cent majority voting block.

It is a terrible look that Sullivan has increased his power base when supporters so dearly want him gone altogether.



He is still attending matches, but when the big screens accidentally cut to him against Charlton, he was met by deafening boos.

The bizarre situation reached peak farce on Tuesday night against Wolves when Staveley and her husband were spotted queuing with fans at the main concourse entrance.

After the 4-2 win, fan bloggers filming outside realised they were accidentally blocking two people from leaving — Staveley and her husband standing patiently.

Staveley, though, will almost certainly try again. Perhaps she can now target buying out Sullivan and Tripp Smith’s remaining shares instead?

It does seem strange that Kretinsky doesn’t want full control of the club himself.



If the Czech billionaire goes to 51 per cent, he is legally obliged to launch a mandatory buyout for the rest of the shares.

Staveley, on the other hand, clearly wants complete control.

It will be fascinating to see if Staveley can eventually smoke the Czech out.

Yet the silver lining right now is that with Kretinsky as the largest shareholder, the club can finally focus purely on winning promotion without all the boardroom noise.

Sports.title: FIFA confirm Gianni Infantino WILL stand for another term as President – despite his plan to sell off the World Cup
Sports.content:
FIFA has been forced to confirm Gianni Infantino will stand for another term as President – despite his plan to sell off the World Cup

Infantino announced in April his intention to ask for a final four-year term as head of the global game.



But what appeared set to be little more than a coronation in Rabat, Morocco, in March, was thrown into disarray after the scheme to sell 20 per cent of the game’s crown jewels to a private US consortium emerged.

Infantino had already been on the back foot after intervening at the behest of US President Donald Trump to waive US striker Falorin Balogun’s red card ban.



But the leaking of the sell-off idea – dropped amid the worldwide condemnation – saw opponents, led by Uefa, gather their forces.

Uefa threatened to withdraw from all future Fifa tournaments unless Infantino quit – although that idea was pulled back last month after Fifa gave a commitment that there would be no return to the project.



Even so, Uefa, Asia and the North and Central American confederation Concacaf launched legal proceedings alleging Infantino’s effective £15bn valuation of the tournament would have amounted to fraud.

The three confederations want Swiss authorities to intervene but also lodged legal suits demanding “disclosure” of documents in three US states – New York, Florida and Colorado.

A number of national bodies, including the FA, have officially withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino, who has spent recent weeks travelling round the globe seeking to shore up his backers.

Asked on Saturday if he was sticking to his plans to stand again, while attending the opening weekend of the women’s under-20 World Cup in Poland, Infantino declined to answer.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But 24 hours later, a Fifa spokesman said: “The FIFA president announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027.

“Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election.”

Last week, Fifa hit back in the legal spat, branding the Uefa moves a “smear campaign” and suggesting it was little more than a fishing exercise.

Uefa, though, believes Infantino is struggling to hold on to his flagging authority, arguing that if there is nothing to hide, that will be clear from the disclosure of all relevant documentation.

As it stands, though, Infantino, 56, who has been in charge of Fifa since 2016, is the only candidate for the elections.



He is determined to stand, even though former Fifa governance committee head Miguel Maduro has insisted that having been elected three times previously, Infantino is ineligible to ask for a fourth term in power under the organisation’s statutes.

Uefa is ready to get behind Canada’s Victor Montagliani to be the “clean hands” candidate to take Infantino on.

So far, though, Montagliani has kept his counsel, with the deadline for nominations looming on November 18.

Even so, the fact that Fifa have ended up confirming that Infantino is sticking to his plans from five months ago suggests Zurich is starting to feel the global heat.

Sports.title: Taylor ecstatic with Croke Park swansong
Sports.content:
Katie Taylor acclaimed becoming a three-time undisputed world champion in her farewell fight at Croke Park as the most special moment of her decorated career.

Taylor outclassed Flora Pili in a unanimous points victory in front of a crowd of 80,000 to ensure her three decades as an amateur and professional boxer ended in fairytale fashion.

Wild celebrations followed the announcement that she had overwhelmed the previously unbeaten Pili 100-90 100-90 98-91 on the scorecards.

For Taylor the feeling of signing off in front of her fans bettered winning Olympic gold at London 2012, headlining Madison Square Garden and her trilogy against Amanda Serrano.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Katie Taylor shares her victory with her home crowd at Croke Park after beating Flora Pili

The 40-year-old said: "This was definitely the highlight of my whole career.

"I didn't think anything could get bigger than London 2012 and then MSG came along.

Image: Croke Park on Katie Taylor's final night

"I didn't think anything could get bigger than that first fight with Serrano and then here we are at Croke Park.

"I ended my career on top, like every athlete wants to do, on my terms, and I ended it as the undisputed champion.

"That's exactly how I wanted it to end. It was so important to me all along to end my career well."

Taylor thrilled Croke Park with a spine-tingling ring walk and also delivered in the ring by outclassing Pili across all 10 rounds.

She finished the fight by launching an all-out assault in the final 10 seconds that was roared on by the crowd and once the bell sounded, she smiled and hugged her opponent knowing she had thrown her final shots.

Taylor said: "This night was everything I expected and more. Thankfully I was able to hold my emotions together because I was getting emotional all week speaking about this event.

Image: Katie Taylor fights Flora Pili at Croke Park

"And over the last few months, the preparation for this has been so emotional. But the atmosphere was so special. It was beyond my wildest dreams. It was unbelievable.

"What an amazing night. Looking back on an amazing career, this was just a dream ending to a dream career for me. What a way to end.

"I don't think there's another country in the world that would sell 80,000 tickets for a female athlete. I'm convinced Ireland was the only country that would actually do that.

"What a way to end this amazing journey. I started off this career and I had the dream of becoming an Olympic champion.

"I achieved that, but then these last 10 years have been beyond my wildest dreams. It's been a remarkable 10 years.

Taylor is open to remaining in Irish boxing in some capacity, providing she can convince her husband Sean McCavanagh to relocate from Connecticut where they are based.

But wherever her path leads, the Bray Bomber's place in Irish sporting immortality is assured after the nation paid homage to a trailblazer in women's sport.

Image: Katie Taylor celebrates the final win of her career

"The whole country have seen my good times and also seen me during my devastation as well," Taylor said.

"I think people really resonate with your vulnerabilities as much as your successes. They saw me cope with the heartbreak of the Rio Olympics.

"They saw me cope with the heartbreak of the Chantelle Cameron loss. This country has seen my personal difficulties as well.

"My story is the story of everybody in this room, everybody in the whole country. We all have our good days, our bad days. Life is full of ups and downs.

"We all have seasons of trouble, seasons of success, but my disappointments and my struggles have always been in the limelight as well.

"I don't know why the adoration is there, but I'm just super grateful that it's there. I'm super grateful for this nation and for the dream for which we're here."

Hearn: Greatest Irish sportsperson of all time

Image: Katie Taylor celebrates her win over Flora Pili at Croke Park

Eddie Hearn speaking to DAZN:

"We went into this event and I said this will be the greatest atmosphere and greatest occasion boxing has ever seen and Croke Park, you did it tonight.

"There were 83,000 people in here tonight and they are still here. I wasn't supposed to do something we haven't done before. This is a woman who refused to take no as an answer and banged on every door. She's the greatest Irish sportsperson of all time.

"She made this happen. She made it happen because the entire nation supported her so proudly."

Sports.title: Daryz, Gstaad and Opera Ballo feature on stellar Arc Trials Day
Sports.content:
Daryz, Gstaad, Opera Ballo and Benvenuto Cellini all line up on an outstanding Arc Trials Day from ParisLongchamp on Sunday.

4.35 ParisLongchamp - Arc hero Daryz returns en route back to Arc

Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe hero Daryz returns to ParisLongchamp en route to his defence of Europe's most prestigious race, tackling the Prix Foy.

Francis-Henri Graffard's star returns having not being seen since his third in the Prince Of Wales's Stakes - where there were excuses for the run given his misbehaviour in the stables prior to the race. That run is the only blemish to an otherwise seamless four-year-old campaign to date, which has seen him win the Prix Ganay & Prix Aga Khan IV, showing a devastating turn of foot in both.

He was beaten at this meeting last term by Japanese raider Croix Du Nord in the Prix du Prince D'orange but bounced back with that famous victory a month later, seeing off Minnie Hauk in a pulsating renewal of the Arc.

Bay City Roller is currently 14-1 for the October showpiece and is a really interesting contender in both this and the Arc, having delivered his second Group 1 success when dispatching his rivals in the Coronation Cup at Epsom in June. He flourished in soft conditions that day and easing conditions combined with a return to a favoured track could see him go close.

Both the Antoine Griezmann-owned Uthred and Quest For Magic have an enormous amount to find on ratings and should be nowhere near the front two - although the latter did defeat Prix Vermeille contender Rabbit's Foot in Listed company last time out.

3.25 ParisLongchamp - Star Gstaad reopposes Opera Ballo and Ten Bob Tony

Star three-year-old Gstaad reopposes two of his rivals from the Sussex Stakes in Sunday's feature Qatar Prix du Moulin de Longchamp for a pot just shy of £400,000 to the winner.

Aidan O'Brien has been unlucky to bump into the brilliant Bow Echo on three of his four starts this year, going down to George Boughey's phenomenon in the 2000 Guineas, St James's Palace Stakes and Sussex Stakes by a cumulative three lengths. Clearly a star in his own right, Ryan Moore's mount cruised to an emphatic triumph in the Irish 2000 Guineas earlier in the campaign and with Bow Echo now retired, is arguably best of the European milers.

Image: Gstaad

Both Opera Ballo and Ten Bob Tony had to give Gstaad 8lbs the last day but that is reduced to 6lbs and both will hope that will be enough to close the deficit of just under three lengths.

Opera Ballo is a Group 1 winner this year, taking out the Jebel Hatta at Meydan in January before subsequently topping that up with an impressive weight-carrying display in the bet365 Mile at Sandown against some top rivals. He then was defeated in the Queen Anne by Ten Bob Tony, who bought up his sole Group 1 success with a dramatic finish - defying odds of 50/1. Kieran Shoemark's mount stayed on well after a bad start in the City Of York Stakes recently and could go even closer.

Erdenali represents the lethal duo of Francis-Henri Graffard and Mickael Barzalona and cannot be discounted. This gelded son of Caravaggio should have retained his unbeaten status in Group 3 company last time but was boxed in and only managed third when sent off the odds-on favourite.

2.50 ParisLongchamp - Sparan Nua and Sunly lock horns in competitive race

Sparan Nua and Sunly lock horns in a very competitive Group 1 Qatar Prix Vermeille.

Sparan Nua looked to relish the step up to a mile and half last time out in the Yorkshire Oaks, finishing with a late run but failing to displace King George winner Kalpana.

Sunly returned this year with big expectations, taking out a Group 3 at Saint-Cloud before running Aventure very close in the Group 2 Prix Corrida. This form has been boosted given the Wertheimer mare has since won the Group 1 Prix Jean et Louis Romanet. Sunly's run in behind Calandagan in the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud last time out was very eye-catching and she could be hard to beat here with Colin Keane booked.

Survie recently took out the Grade 1 Christophe Clement Turf Stakes at Saratoga and comes here with Ryan Moore in the saddle. George Boughey's charge - who is owned by the Coolmore powerhouse - did struggle with a previous yard around ParisLongchamp but seems to have been rejuvenated in Newmarket.

Tattycoram recently beat Tiffany at Headquarters, who has since boosted that form - winning a Group 1 in Germany.

Also at ParisLongchamp...

Arguably Europe's star two-year-old thus far in 2026, Avec Toi takes on four rivals in the Qatar Prix la Rochette at 12.58pm. Labelled a "machine" by trainer Christopher Head after a stunning success last time, all eyes will be on this daughter of No Nay Never - who takes on unbeaten contenders Vignelli and Imperial Strike.

Christopher Head could take out the first two Group contests on the card, given he saddles the promising Data in the Qatar Prix d'Aumale at 1.33pm. She was excellent in Group 3 company the last day and if she handles the step back up in trip and hike in class, she looks the one to beat. There is British representation in this race, with Ed Bethell fielding Rogue Passion.

Irish Derby winner Benvenuto Cellini is the star attraction in the 4pm Qatar Prix Niel for Aidan O'Brien. The Ballydoyle representative showed his brilliance at the Curragh following his controversial failed start in the Epsom equivalent, before running well in third in the King George. Francis-Henri Graffard fields Varandir in opposition, with Zaraki also a big contender for the Fabre team.

Elsewhere...

2.20 Fontwell - Royal Rhythm looks to defy 9lbs rise

2.55 Fontwell - Coastal Command returns for the King and Nicky Henderson

4.40 Fontwell - Jiar Madrik chases four-timer

11.00 Del Mar - five-runner Grade 1, with the winner often heading to the Breeders' Cup Juvenile

Sports.title: Osaka takes care of business while Jovic ends Eala Mania in US Open thriller
Sports.content:
Naomi Osaka stepped on court in another new look and eventually took care of business against Elise Mertens in a tense three-set victory to reach the fourth round of the US Open.

Osaka's 'business-chic' attire along with an all-out attacking game saw her come up clutch to land an impressive 6-3 3-6 7-5 win over 23rd seed Mertens on Louis Armstrong Stadium.

For her latest fashionable walk-on look, Osaka blended boardroom ​and locker-room aesthetics in a grey ‌checked blazer-hoodie and wide-leg pants, putting a tailored twist on traditional pre-match ​attire.

"Honestly, I can't believe I won this match," Osaka said, thanking the crowd ‌for the energy they provided.

"There was a certain point where I put my heart on the court and kept trying in every point. Thank you so much, but ‌honestly, I'm shocked I won. I'm not going to lie."

The 28-year-old, a two-time champion at Flushing Meadows, reeled off three games in succession to take a 4-1 ​lead in the first set, ⁠clinching it with a battling hold thanks to a string of booming serves.

Osaka ‌pushed the Belgian hard at the start of the next set with some heavy hitting from the ‌baseline before pouncing with a break in the third game, only to surrender the lead by dropping the next two games.

Mertens levelled the match and forced a decider, where ⁠she capitalised on several unforced errors by ​a frustrated Osaka to gain the ​upper hand, but there would be another momentum ​shift in the match after a medical timeout for ⁠the Japanese player.

Image: Osaka is a two-time champion at Flushing Meadows

After recovering a break late on, Osaka fired a huge ace to take a 6-5 lead and ⁠revved up her forehand in ​the following game to earn ​a meeting with second seed Elena Rybakina or Ukraine's Yuliia Starodubtseva.

"I didn't play amazing ​and it was getting me down, sorry about my ​behaviour, for the little kids watching," said Osaka, who threw her racket ​to the floor at one point.

"This is my favourite tournament. I wanted ⁠to play well in front of you. I'm just that glad I have the opportunity to play another match.

"I thought I was going to be ok, but clearly I was ⁠shaky."

Home hope Iva Jovic and ‌Alexandra Eala of the Philippines put their friendship aside for three hours before the 18-year-old American prevailed 7-5 3-6 7-5 on Arthur ​Ashe Stadium to reach the fourth round.

The two rising stars and close friends had already shared the ​court in New York during Fan Week when ‌they teamed up with their fathers for a light-hearted doubles hit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alex Eala shares what Filipino support means to her following her loss against Iva Jovic.

Jovic edged a tight opening set but Eala responded in the second as the 21-year-old ​raised her level to force a decider.

The final ⁠set again featured momentum swings, with ⁠Jovic trailing 4-2 before fighting back to close out the victory and extend her head-to-head record ‌against Eala to 3-0, with a win on each of the three surfaces.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alex Eala and Iva Jovic brought out their dads during ‘Stars of the Open’ US Open exhibition

"That felt like a marathon. I felt like I lost ‌my sanity five times over to win that match. But it's really worth it for this feeling," Jovic said on court.

"I'm usually not one that shows that many emotions. But this one really meant a ⁠lot to me. It's everything to have another ​match at the US Open."

Her victory sets up an all-American ​clash with Coco Gauff, who advanced earlier on Saturday by beating Spain's Cristina Bucsa.

Sports.title: Everton v Manchester United: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
1m ago 10.14 EDT 54 min Better from Everton, with a spell of possession and a shot from Johnson, well blocked by Shaw. The sparky George wins a corner off Dalot. Share

3m ago 10.13 EDT 53 min United advance, slowly and inconclusively. Their build-up was often too leisurely in the first half, but now it can afford to be. And there will be more gaps as Everton have to take a risk or two. Share

4m ago 10.11 EDT 50 min At one end, a neat turn by Barry yields less than it deserves. At the other, a neat cross from Rashford can’t find a taker. Share

6m ago 10.10 EDT 49 min That goal, which came out of nowhere, was United’s first on the road this season and the first time they’d taken the lead, home or away. Share

7m ago 10.09 EDT 47 min Mainoo, boosted by that assist, charges through the midfield, but Cunha’s lay-off can’t quite reach Rashford. Then Everton bounce back with a cross from the left that would be dangerous if anyone was on the end of it. Share

9m ago 10.07 EDT GOAL! Everton o-1 Man United (Mbeumo 47) That’s more like it! Mbeumo, found by Mainoo on the right, runs past three men and curls a left-foot shot into the far corner. View image in fullscreen Bryan Mbeumo of Manchester United scores. Photograph: Steve Flynn/Every Second Media/Shutterstock Share Updated at 10.14 EDT

10m ago 10.05 EDT 46 min No subs yet. United kick off and go sideways in midfield. Share

11m ago 10.04 EDT The players are out again, or at least United are. Everton wait in the tunnel as James Tarkowski lobbies John Brooks about something. Share

17m ago 09.58 EDT On xG, there’s not a lot to separate the teams. Everton 0.34-0.32 United. The United forward line has been the more imposing of the two, but James Garner, who captained their Under-21s before being brainlessly sold to Everton, has been the main man in midfield. And Jarrod Branthwaite, who was coveted by United a couple of summers ago, has been immense in defence. Share Updated at 09.59 EDT

20m ago 09.56 EDT And I’m late to an early spot from Justin Kavanagh. “Lovely footage from the tunnel,” he said, “of Lammens fixing up his captain’s tracksuit collar while standing behind Fernandes. Now that’s what you like to see in a keeper: an obsession with the little details and a fussiness for positioning and everything in its right place.” Share

21m ago 09.54 EDT Time for a glance at the post. “The chippy stall in your photo,” says Gary Naylor, “did some very good ones garnished with herbs and chillis a fortnight ago. Hard recomnend. “It might get some extra trade today as I understand that there may be a ‘Not a pound inside the ground’ boycott. Feels a bit performative that – but protests are.” Very true. Share

23m ago 09.52 EDT HALF-TIME! Everton 0-0 Man United No goals, no thrills, but an absorbing encounter. It ought to be 1-1: Cunha should have scored for United and Barry for Everton, only for both attempts to go over the bar when it looked easier to get them on target. Share

26m ago 09.50 EDT 45+3 min One last sortie from United. Cunha slips in Rashford, who is well marshalled by Branthwaite. Another shot from Fernandes, another block – and again it’s Branthwaite, who is quite clearly the man of the last three minutes. Share Updated at 09.52 EDT

28m ago 09.48 EDT 45+1 min Everton are finishing the half with some intensity. Mykolenko sends in a long throw, the ball falls to Branthwaite, whose low shot is on target – and well saved by Lammens, without much of a view. Share

29m ago 09.46 EDT 45 min Barry breaks free down the right, but never manages a cross. There will be three more minutes, thanks to that early knock for Maguire. Share

30m ago 09.45 EDT 44 min United have some possession and a few half-openings, but no shot. Share

32m ago 09.44 EDT 42 min The next bad ball comes from Fernandes. And then Everton have a proper chance! Johnson whips in a cross and Barry again gets his head to it. This header is far more confident … but over the bar. Share

33m ago 09.42 EDT 40 min United get forward, only for Mbeumo to play a loose pass to Cunha. At this rate, Sesko will be getting more than his usual 25 minutes. Share

34m ago 09.41 EDT 39 min Everton have a chance! Well, a quarter-chance. A free kick comes in and Barry rises to it, but his header is a bit woolly. View image in fullscreen Everton's Thierno Barry attempts a header at goal. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA Share Updated at 09.56 EDT

36m ago 09.39 EDT 38 min Will Unwin emailed again a few minutes ago. “Excitingly, half an hour in, Everton’s xG sits at an impressive 0.01, having managed one off-target shot and nothing else. Not a classic of the genre.” Ha. Share

37m ago 09.38 EDT 36 min Rashford beats one man, two men, but not the third man, Tarkowski, who puts the ball out for a corner. A better ball in from Fernandes leads to a brawl in the box and the ball squirts out for a goal kick. Share

40m ago 09.36 EDT 35 min Fernandes’ free kick is tame, Mbeumo’s follow-up cross is even worse, and both are easily headed away. Share

41m ago 09.35 EDT 33 min Cunha plays a one-two with Rashford, who sends him through – to win a free kick as Brennan Johnson brings him down. It’s just outside the area, almost on the byline. Share

42m ago 09.34 EDT 33 min We keep getting 30 seconds of action followed by two and a half minutes of lassitude. Maybe that’s football? Share

43m ago 09.32 EDT 31 min Lammens comes for a cross and fails to make it – but he does have Dewsbury-Hall, unnoticed by John Brooks, sticking an elbow in his throat. Share

45m ago 09.31 EDT 30 min Another cross from Rashford, whipped in hard and well defended by Branthwaite. Share

47m ago 09.29 EDT 28 min Everton knock the ball around in the sunshine. Garner plays two piercing passes, one down the left to Mykolenko, one towards the right to Armstrong, but it all ends in a goal kick. Share Updated at 09.29 EDT

48m ago 09.27 EDT 26 min Garner wins the ball well in midfield and Everton threaten something, which comes to nothing. They’ve had one shot so far to United’s six. Share

50m ago 09.26 EDT 24 min The game is opening up. United spring forward and again the old firm of Rashford and Shaw combine well, but Rashford’s curling cross finds no takers as Mbeumo seems not to see it coming. Sesko might have gobbled that up. Share

52m ago 09.23 EDT 21 min The first big chance! Rashford gets a good ball from Mbeumo and escapes down the left. His low cross is left by someone and received by Cunha, who can only hit it over the bar from near the spot. Share

54m ago 09.22 EDT 20 min Fernandes’ corner is headed away by Rohl. Dalot takes a volley and there’s another block – by Cunha. Share

55m ago 09.21 EDT 19 min Another shot for United, also a long one, and also tame – from Cunha this time. Everton are defending well in a doughty 4-5-1… But as I type that, Fernandes finds some space and he gets a better shot in – blocked by Branthwaite. Share

1h ago 09.19 EDT 18 min Shot from Tielemans, but he’s a long way out and Pickford has no trouble coping with a bouncing ball. Share

1h ago 09.18 EDT 16 min Everton do well down their left as Dewsbury-Hall’s toes begin to twinkle. But United drive them back and then slow things down. Share

1h ago 09.16 EDT 15 min Mainoo, usually so tidy in tight spaces, picks the wrong moment to play a backheel, but Maguire does the clearing up. Share

1h ago 09.14 EDT 13 min Now we do have the first yellow: Armstrong, for getting Fernandes in a rather random headlock. Share

1h ago 09.13 EDT 12 min Diogo Dalot goes in heavily on Tyrique George. Could be an early yellow but John Brooks opts for a lecture. Share

1h ago 09.12 EDT 11 min Rashford starts to sprint away on the counter, but he’s shepherded out. His last United goal was against Everton, and so was the second-last – he scored two in a 4-0 home win in Ruben Amorim’s rather short-lived honeymoon period. Share

1h ago 09.10 EDT 10 min And now Everton want a penalty! Barry goes down in the six-yard box as Martinez bears down on him. The ref waves away the appeals. View image in fullscreen Thierno Barry of Everton goes down in the penalty box. Photograph: Matt West/Shutterstock Share Updated at 09.36 EDT

1h ago 09.09 EDT 8 min Chance for United! They string together a lovely sequence, right to left, and Rashford releases Shaw on the overlap. His chipped cross brings a knock-down from Mbeumo and a volley from Fernandes … which hits the bar! Share

1h ago 09.08 EDT 6 min Brennan Johnson skims a cross in and Maguire manages a clearance. As Everton come again, Tielemans gets into trouble and his new mate Mainoo tidies up. Share

1h ago 09.06 EDT 5 min Senne Lammens goes long too – all the way to Pickford. Maguire returns. Share Updated at 09.06 EDT

1h ago 09.05 EDT 5 min Maguire is on his feet now, with a plug in one nostril and a bottle of water in one hand. He trots to the touchline for the obligatory minute off. Share

1h ago 09.04 EDT 4 min After lying on his side in worrying fashion, Maguire manages to sit up. A replay suggests it might be a broken nose – his face went into the back of Barry’s head. View image in fullscreen Manchester United's Harry Maguire receives treatment. Photograph: Lee Parker/CameraSport/Getty Images Share Updated at 09.35 EDT

1h ago 09.02 EDT 2 min Long ball from Pickford. Harry Maguire goes up for it with Thierno Barry and goes down in a heap. Leny Yoro starts limbering up. View image in fullscreen Manchester United's Harry Maguire clashes heads with Everton's Thierno Barry. Photograph: Lee Parker/CameraSport/Getty Images Share Updated at 09.34 EDT

1h ago 09.01 EDT 1 min Moyes and Carrick exchange fond smiles and Everton kick off. Share

1h ago 08.59 EDT The teams come out. Blue tracksuit tops and red ones. Jordan Pickford and Marcus Rashford. Kobbie Mainoo and James Garner. Harry Maguire and James Tarkowski. Bruno Fernandes and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. Share

1h ago 08.56 EDT “Looking forward to your top post-match analysis as much as your present...” says Paul Moody, generously enabling me to link to my free newsletter, United Writing. “Also looking ahead to tough games… City next Sunday... Hoping for 1-3 today and be very entertaining.” Share

1h ago 08.54 EDT “Selected scuttlebut,” says Ian Copestake, promisingly, “from Everton fans on the train from Birkenhead to the game is that the fans have been lied to. Promises made by the new owners (shiny new stadium not mentioned) have not been fulfilled. Mutiny is round the corner (probably at Sandhills).” Share

1h ago 08.52 EDT An unexpected proposal from John Stedman. “I like the new(ish) Dining Across the Divide series [in the Saturday magazine] and hereby propose a new feature: Drinking Across the Sporting Divide, which you can pitch to your taskmasters in Guardian Towers. “As a follower of LFC with no Liverpudlian antecedents, I suggest meeting you in a locale of your choice to debate in civilised tones the eternal recently manufactured enmity between your team and mine. The George and Dragon in Fordwich should be within The Guardian’s Blind Date budget.” John, I like where you’re coming from. Share

1h ago 08.48 EDT And here’s our correspondent at the ground, Will Unwin. “There is a subdued atmosphere at Hill Dickinson,” he reports, “as those in blue funnel into the ground, rightly concerned by the long term. Folarin Balogun’s failed move leaves them with only Thierno Barry as a recognised striker, although whether he can be prolific is unknown. “Michael Carrick is also short in certain positions and this is the start of a long season where playing twice a week could catch up with United. Left-back is the obvious problem position if Luke Shaw gets injured. He played every Premier League game last season, but that was without the rigours of European football in between. His fitness record includes plenty of blemishes, so everyone will keep a close eye on his performances and availability.” Share

2h ago 08.45 EDT David Moyes is talking to Sky, and of course he’s asked about the transfer window. “That’s all gone now, so we have to play football and that’s what we’ll do.” And what is he expecting from the fans? “Nothing different to usual. They’re always really good to us.” Share

2h ago 08.42 EDT It wouldn’t be an Everton game without a word from Mary Waltz. “Greetings from California,” she says, at what must be the break of dawn over there. “This season started so well. Points taken. Moyes at the helm. Of course we will add on deadline day.......... Or maybe not. Life as an Everton fan. Sigh.” Share

2h ago 08.09 EDT The first email comes in from Joshua Keeling. “United fan here,” he says. “Agree that all three results are possible. It’s never easy, going to Everton. Feels like United need to win today ahead of the derby next week.” Yes … they could probably only afford one defeat in this mini-season of five matches before the long international break, and they used it up at the first opportunity. Share

2h ago 08.06 EDT Teams in full Some eye-catching names on the benches. Everton have Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles, plus the 18-year-old Northern Irish striker Braiden Graham, the lesser-spotted Tyler Dibling and the elegant Hayden Hackney (mentored by Michael Carrick when they were both at Middlesbrough). United have Mason Mount back from injury, and he edges out Shea Lacey, so Bryan Mbeumo may have to put in a full shift on the right.
