The CDC-led coalition won the 2017 presidential election and subsequently governed Liberia from 2018 to 2024.

Koijee also questioned the political circumstances surrounding Mulbah’s statement, particularly his reported employment within the Office of Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung.

He said the relationship raises questions about the “independence, timing and motivation” of statements directed at opposition cooperation.

Koijee further criticized what he described as the NPP leadership’s weak response when its standard bearer and former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor faced criminal allegations and incarceration.

“At that defining moment, the statement attributed to the party leadership was, in our view, one of the weakest responses in the history of a party once renowned for its fighting spirit, political potency and revolutionary character,” he said.

The CDC Secretary-General maintained that his party would not allow what he described as political distractions and manufactured controversies to undermine cooperation among opposition forces.

“The mighty Congress for Democratic Change has no room for political distractions, manufactured controversies or attempts to fracture genuine opposition solidarity,” Koijee said.

He pledged that the CDC would remain “vigilant” and respond to what it considers efforts to undermine democratic cooperation among opposition groups.

Koijee concluded by thanking individuals and institutions that were formally invited to the roundtable and accepted the invitation, saying their participation demonstrated that the broader democratic conversation would continue.

“The democratic conversation continues, and no political grandstanding will derail it,” he said.

World.title: Co-Defendant Challenges Judge’s Ruling Granting Ex-VP Taylor House Arrest, Calls It Unlawful
World.content:
MONROVIA — A day after Criminal Court “C” ordered former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor moved from Monrovia Central Prison to guarded house detention on medical grounds, a co-defendant in the same narcotics case has formally challenged the ruling, arguing that Judge Ousman F. Feika had no legal authority to grant it and asking him to reverse himself.



In a filing captio ned “Exceptions to His Honor Ousman F. Feika’s Ruling in Granting Co-Defendant Jewel Howard Taylor Compassionate Release,” Garpue K. Wonlue takes issue with the September 4 order on six separate grounds, most of them turning on a single argument: that the law Judge Feika relied on does not apply to someone in Taylor’s position.



The Case So Far



Taylor, Liberia’s vice president from 2018 to 2024, was arrested at Roberts International Airport on August 19 in connection with what officials have described as a transnational narcotics trafficking investigation tied to a record cocaine seizure earlier this year.

She was formally charged over eight counts, including unlicensed importation, unlicensed sale and trading, and illicit trafficking of drugs, along with money laundering and abuse-of-office allegations.



Her lawyers spent the following weeks trying, without success, to keep her out of the general prison population.

A Monrovia City Court magistrate denied an initial request for compassionate detention, ruling that granting it fell within the authority of the Ministry of Justice rather than the judiciary the defense’s follow-up appeal to the Supreme Court challenging that denial did not stop Taylor from being remanded to Monrovia Central Prison. She entered custody on September 2.



The case then moved to Criminal Court “C,” the circuit with jurisdiction over major drug offenses, where Judge Feika ordered Taylor’s immediate transfer from prison to 24-hour guarded house detention at her residence, converting her pre-trial custody into house arrest pending the outcome of the criminal proceedings.

Feika was explicit that the order rested solely on medical grounds and carried no bearing on guilt, writing that the release “shall therefore not constitute dismissal, acquittal, pardon, immunity, or termination of the criminal proceedings.

The judge also noted that the State itself had not opposed the request.



The Challenge



Wonlue’s filing does not dispute that Taylor has a medical condition. Instead, it argues that the court used the wrong statute to address it — and in doing so, exceeded its authority. The exceptions raise six points:



1. Jurisdiction: The filing argues that Chapter 34, Section 34.20 of the Criminal Procedure Law — the provision Judge Feika relied on — applies only to people who have already been indicted, tried, convicted, sentenced and committed to prison. Taylor, still awaiting trial, doesn’t fit that description, the filing contends, and Wonlue asks the court to rescind the ruling and have her returned to custody at Monrovia Central Prison.



2. No such remedy exists: The Criminal Procedure Law provides for bail under Chapter 13 for the accused, and for commitment under Chapter 34 for the convicted, the filing says — but nothing in between for a pre-trial detainee seeking release on medical grounds. Granting “compassionate leave” from pre-trial detention, it argues, is a remedy the court created rather than one the statute authorizes.



3. Consent doesn’t create jurisdiction: The fact that the State did not oppose Taylor’s request doesn’t change the analysis, the filing argues — parties cannot agree to give a court power the statute doesn’t grant it.



4. Equal treatment. This is the filing’s broadest argument: that granting one high-profile, pre-trial detainee a form of release unavailable to others sets up a two-tier system, at odds with the fairness-in-administration standard in Section 1.2 of the Criminal Procedure Law and Article 11 of the 1986 Constitution. The filing points out that many pre-trial detainees at Monrovia Central Prison have untreated medical conditions of their own, and argues the proper remedy was to order the Bureau of Corrections to provide adequate care in custody — not to release one defendant from it.



5. The nature of the charges and the cost of enforcement: Given that Taylor faces serious felony charges — importation of controlled drugs, money laundering and abuse of office, as the filing describes them — Wonlue argues the release conditions impose an unfunded, unauthorized burden on the State, which must now provide round-the-clock security at her residence. Surrendering travel documents, the filing adds, doesn’t eliminate flight risk on its own.



6. The inquiry should have ended sooner: Once the court determined that Section 34.20 doesn’t apply to pre-trial detainees, the filing argues, that finding should have ended the motion rather than being followed by relief anyway. It maintains the appropriate avenue for a detainee with medical concerns is a bail motion under Chapter 13 — with bond, sureties and monitoring conditions — not compassionate leave.



What’s Being Asked



The filing asks Judge Feika to reverse course: to rule that Section 34.20 doesn’t apply to pre-trial detainees, to direct the Bureau of Corrections and Ministry of Health to provide Taylor medical treatment at JFK Medical Center or another approved facility while she remains in custody, and — if release is warranted at all — to take it up as a bail application under Chapter 13, with a substantial bond and formal sureties, rather than as compassionate leave.



Judge Feika has not yet ruled on the exceptions. Taylor remains under house arrest at her residence pending the outcome. All defendants in the case, including Taylor, are presumed innocent, and the charges against them remain allegations that have not been tested at trial.

World.title: Liberia Champions Key Discussions on Preventive Diplomacy and a Robust E10 Voice at the 9th E10 & I5 Annual Dialogue in Panama
World.content:
Panama – Liberia’s Political Coordinator to the United Nations Security Council, Cllr. Aloysius Jappah assumed an active role in the 9th E10 & I5 Annual Dialogue, hosted by the Republic of Panama in Panama City from 1 to 2 September 2026, delivering substantive interventions on preventive diplomacy, Council effectiveness, and the responsibilities that come with elected membership of the UN Security Council.

Since 2019, the Dialogue has convened annually to unite the ten elected members of the Council (the E10) with the five incoming members (the I5) to enhance institutional memory, coordinate priorities, and bolster the Council’s ability to uphold international peace and security.

This year’s event was inaugurated and concluded by Panama’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, H.E. Javier Eduardo Martínez-Acha Vásquez, and honored at its closing by former President H.E. Mireya Moscoso.

The current E10 for 2026 includes Bahrain, Colombia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Liberia, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia.

Starting on 1 January 2027, the newly elected I5 will consist of Austria, Kyrgyzstan, Portugal, Trinidad and Tobago, and Zimbabwe, replacing Denmark, Greece, Pakistan, Panama, and Somalia as their mandates end on 31 December 2026.

Speaking during the session on “Preventive Diplomacy in Action,” moderated with the support of the Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation and its presenters Sigrid and Henrik, Cllr. Jappah anchored Liberia’s contribution in the letter of the United Nations Charter — Chapter VI (Articles 33–38) on the pacific settlement of disputes, Chapter VIII (Article 52) on regional arrangements, and Article 99 on the Secretary-General’s early-warning authority.

“The best Council intervention is a crisis that diplomacy prevents,” Cllr. Jappah affirmed, adding that “the Charter calls on us to extinguish the spark of conflict before it becomes a blaze. When we subscribed to this organization, we pledged to fulfill that obligation.”

Commenting on the operational challenge of moving from early warning to early action, the Political Coordinator emphasized what he called the prevention paradox — that when preventive diplomacy succeeds, the crisis does not occur, and success is therefore less visible than failure.

He cautioned that sovereignty concerns and geopolitical divisions frequently delay Council action, resulting in inaction until violence erupts. He warned that “Early warning without early action,” he warned, “is only a forecast of failure.”

Drawing on Liberia’s own post-conflict experience, Cllr. Jappah stressed that peace agreements close a chapter but do not, by themselves, remove the grievances, institutional weaknesses, or local tensions that can reignite conflict.

He called for the sustained deployment of good offices, mediation support, regional engagement, inclusive dialogue, confidence-building measures, early-warning capacity, and local peace infrastructures — with the consent and ownership of the country concerned.

“Peace agreements close a chapter; preventive diplomacy helps keep the next chapter from reopening the war,” he said, noting that sustained international, regional, and national engagement has been decisive in consolidating and protecting Liberia’s hard-won peace.

Contributing to Session V on reinvigorating the Council’s role in preventive diplomacy, Cllr. Jappah observed that the Dialogue offered members a valuable opportunity to internalize how a hasty drawdown of peacekeeping operations can leave a country vulnerable.

He was speaking in response to interventions on how transnational organized crime — including transcontinental drug trafficking — can undermine governance in states just emerging from conflict, where institutions remain fragile.

On the question of how the E10 should engage the incoming Secretary-General, Cllr. Jappah urged elected members to first conduct an honest internal assessment and to invest deliberately in strengthening themselves as a caucus.

He proposed that the E10 build the discipline and coordination required to create what he described as a collective “veto,” together with the guardrails to use that leverage responsibly. He observed that, over a two-year tenure, “before an elected member really gets to understand the Council and its dynamics, it is time to exit,” and he called on the E10 to systematically leverage the institutional memory of what he termed the “Farewell Five” — the five outgoing members concluding their terms each year — so that hard-earned experience is transferred rather than lost.

He further cautioned that the Council too frequently holds briefings and open meetings at which statements are made that contain useful antidotes but are followed by no concrete action.

He urged that the traditional E10 luncheons move beyond merely setting the agenda for the Secretary-General’s luncheon with Permanent Representatives, and instead become a forum in which elected members act with one voice on decisive issues before the Council.

Cllr. Jappah welcomed the newly elected members—Austria, Kyrgyzstan, Portugal, Trinidad and Tobago, and Zimbabwe—emphasizing the importance of continuity in preventive practice, disciplined coordination among members, and adherence to the Charter as the Council’s composition changes.

“Prevention is not an abstract ideal,” he concluded. “It is the disciplined practice of acting before choices disappear.”

The E10 & I5 Annual Dialogue, established in 2019, gathers incoming, serving, and outgoing UN Security Council members to enhance institutional memory and align objectives. Panama, holding a non-permanent seat, hosted the 9th edition during its term, ending on December 31, 2026.

World.title: Liberia Elevates Diplomatic Standing as August E10 UN Security Council Coordinator
World.content:
NEW YORK — Liberia has successfully concluded its leadership as Coordinator of the Ten Elected Members (E10) of the United Nations Security Council for August 2026, marking a historic milestone in its global diplomatic resurgence.

Stepping into the helm of the E10 alongside Bahrain, Colombia, DRC, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Panama, Somalia, and Pakistan, Liberia strategically projected African leadership, unified non-permanent members, and shaped critical debate on pressing global peace and security files.

Key Achievements and Diplomatic Interventions

High-Level Security Council Diplomacy: Hosted UN Secretary-General António Guterres and E10 Ambassadors for a strategic luncheon centered on accelerating humanitarian interventions in Gaza and the West Bank.

Regional & Crisis Resolution:

Chaired the Political Coordinators’ Meeting to align consensus on the Libyan political process, security dynamics across West Africa and the Sahel, and the E10 Joint Statement on Security Council Working Methods.

International Judicial Oversight: Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary Lewis G. Brown II convened high-level negotiations with International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) President Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, driving resolution terms on judicial archives, institutional downsizing, and UN oversight sensitivities involving Rwanda and Tanzania.

🇹🇿 Humanitarian Advocacy & International Law: Spearheaded expert briefings on the Ukraine humanitarian crisis and led targeted press interventions demanding the immediate release of illegally detained UN and aid personnel in Yemen.

Council Reform & Strategic Alignment: Championed reform of Security Council Subsidiary Bodies to streamline operations and ensure unified diplomatic alignment between the E10 and the Permanent Five (P5).

A Lasting Legacy on the World Stage

Liberia’s month-long tenure as Coordinator demonstrated strategic leadership, robust policy alignment, and an elevated ability to forge consensus among diverse international partners. Upon concluding its leadership, the E10 alliance formally commended Liberia for its decisive steering of the Council’s thematic priorities throughout August.

Meanwhile, Pakistan has assumed the E10 Coordination role for September, while Liberia remains positioned as an influential, principled voice on the Security Council, committed to driving international peace, stability, and multilateral cooperation.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor to Receive Medical Care at Residence Under Restrictions as Drug Case Continues
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor is set to receive medical attention outside detention under strict conditions imposed by Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika amid ongoing concerns about her health.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The court’s decision comes after Howard-Taylor’s lawyers raised medical concerns and sought her release from detention to allow her to receive treatment.

Under the court’s directive, Howard-Taylor is required to surrender all travel documents, effectively restricting her ability to leave the country while the case remains pending.

The former vice president will also be subject to limitations on visitors at her residence, with access restricted to a family member and her physician or physician’s assistant.

Howard-Taylor remains entangled in an ongoing investigation and prosecution involving allegations connected to an alleged transnational cocaine-trafficking operation.

Her legal team has maintained that her medical condition requires appropriate care, while the case continues to attract public attention because of the seriousness of the allegations.

The court’s latest action provides for medical considerations while maintaining judicial controls over Howard-Taylor as proceedings continue.

World.title: Liberia: Judge Feika Grants Jewel Howard-Taylor Compassionate Release
World.content:
Monrovia — Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika has granted former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor’s request for compassionate release from detention on medical grounds.

The ruling follows concerns raised by Howard-Taylor’s legal team about her medical condition and their request that she be permitted to receive medical care outside detention.

Under the court’s ruling, Howard-Taylor is required to surrender all travel documents to the court as part of the conditions of her release.

The court also ordered that visits to her residence be limited to a family member and her physician or physician’s assistant.

Howard-Taylor is facing criminal charges in connection with an ongoing narcotics investigation. She has denied the allegations.

The court’s decision allows her to leave detention while the legal proceedings continue.

This is a developing story.

World.title: Liberia: LIS Officer Thomas Kesselly Reportedly Shot in Foya
World.content:
MONROVIA — Thomas Kesselly, a member of the Liberia Immigration Service (LIS), was reportedly shot on Thursday, September 3, 2026, with conflicting accounts emerging over the incident.

Kesselley was reportedly shot at the LIS Academy in Foya.

While initial reports said Kesselly was shot, another account claims he shot himself.

However, family sources have expressed doubts about the self-inflicted shooting claim and are seeking clarity on what happened.

Kesselly’s condition and the circumstances surrounding the incident remain unclear as authorities have yet to provide a definitive account.

World.title: Liberia: Witness Alleges Howard-Taylor Link to Cocaine Trafficking Investigation and Political Plot
World.content:
Monrovia — A police investigator has testified in court about an alleged cocaine-trafficking operation in Liberia, telling the court that former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor was allegedly approached over a proposed protection arrangement and that discussions also involved an alleged plan targeting the administration of former President George Weah.

The testimony was given by Raphael Wilson, Acting Commissioner of Police for the Crimes Services Division, who said he supervised the investigative team that conducted the probe.

Wilson told the court that investigators traced the alleged network to meetings involving Liberians and foreign nationals in Dubai and Liberia, beginning around 2021.

According to his testimony, a Liberian identified as Sheikh Bashir Kanti met individuals in Dubai who expressed interest in returning to Liberia to resume business activities.

Wilson alleged that the individuals later disclosed plans to establish a cocaine-trafficking operation, with Liberia allegedly intended to serve as a transit point.

The witness further testified that the foreign nationals sought protection from a senior government official to facilitate their activities in Liberia.

According to Wilson, meetings were subsequently arranged in Liberia involving Bashir, the foreign nationals and individuals identified in the investigation as Tony and Maga.

He said investigators secretly recorded at least one of the meetings using cameras and written notes as part of their investigation.

Wilson testified that cocaine trafficking and the use of Liberia as a transit route were discussed during the meeting.

The witness further alleged that participants wanted assurances that their activities would receive protection from influential government officials.

According to Wilson, Jewel Howard-Taylor agreed to provide the requested protection but indicated that she would first return to Liberia and discuss the matter with her superior.

The testimony forms part of the prosecution’s effort to establish Howard-Taylor’s alleged connection to the broader investigation.

Alleged Political Plot

Wilson also testified about discussions that, according to the prosecution, involved an alleged plan directed against the government of former President George Weah.

The witness said the discussions surrounding the alleged protection arrangement were connected to a broader political plan involving senior political figures and an alleged attempt to undermine or overthrow the government.

However, Wilson’s testimony did not establish in court who allegedly initiated the plan, the specific actions contemplated or the precise role Howard-Taylor allegedly played.

Those matters remain subject to further evidence and examination by both the prosecution and defense.

Wilson said the alleged operation continued during the Weah administration and that investigators expanded their inquiry after some of the individuals involved returned to the region.

Foundation Mentioned in Testimony

The court also heard testimony concerning an alleged connection between some of the individuals under investigation and the Jewel Starfish Foundation, an organization associated with Howard-Taylor.

Wilson said one of the participants mentioned that Howard-Taylor operated the foundation.

The witness further testified that an individual identified as Nicholas expressed willingness to assist with the foundation.

The prosecution is presenting the alleged connection as part of the broader relationship it says existed between political figures and individuals under investigation.

US$45,000 Allegedly Delivered

Wilson also testified about an alleged cash delivery during one of the meetings.

According to the witness, a shopping bag was handed over during the meeting, and investigators later received information that approximately US$45,000 had been placed inside the bag.

The circumstances surrounding the alleged payment, including its intended recipient, purpose and connection to the alleged drug-trafficking operation, remain issues for the court to determine.

Investigation Continued After Weah Presidency

Wilson told the court that the investigation continued after the conclusion of the Weah administration in 2024.

He said investigators later determined that some of the individuals under investigation had returned to the region in 2025, prompting further investigative activity.

According to the witness, intelligence officers subsequently identified additional individuals allegedly connected to the investigation.

Wilson maintained that the investigation relied on intelligence gathering, recorded meetings and information obtained during the probe.

The testimony places several issues before the court, including the alleged cocaine-trafficking operation, claims of political protection, financial transactions and an alleged plan targeting the former Weah administration.

However, the allegations remain matters to be tested through evidence and cross-examination.

Howard-Taylor’s alleged involvement has not been established merely by Wilson’s testimony. She remains entitled to the presumption of innocence unless and until a competent court determines otherwise.

The defense is expected to challenge aspects of the investigation, including the credibility and interpretation of the witness’s account, the alleged recordings, meetings, financial transactions and claims concerning the political plan.

The court will ultimately determine whether the prosecution has produced sufficient admissible and credible evidence to establish the charges against Howard-Taylor and the other defendants.

World.title: Kabimba is on point, President Hichilema must appoint Action-Oriented Cabinet!
World.content:
Economic Front President Wynter Kabimba has appealed to President Hakainde Hichilema to consider assembling a more action-oriented cabinet as he begins his second term in office.

Speaking to Phoenix News ahead of President Hichilema’s official announcement of his cabinet, Kabimba said he expected the President to appoint a team of ministers who would perform better than those in his previous administration.

The Economic Front strongman is definitely on point. As a matter of fact, this measure shouldn’t just stop at Cabinet level. It should be extended Permanent Secretaries and District Commissioners.

In his previous administration, we had a number of officials who either priotised private jobs or had a laissez faire approach towards work. They never bothered venturing into the field to investigate whether government policies were being implemented accordingly.

As Kabimba has rightly observed, the President deserves a stronger team to help him fulfil the commitments he made to the Zambian people during his campaigns.

The President needs to assemble a team of the likes of ZNS commander Lt. Gen. Maliti Solochi. The man is action-oriented…..he has hands on approach towards work. Whenever there’s an assignment to be undertaken within his jurisdiction, he doesn’t leave the responsibility at the mercy of his juniors. You’ll find him ‘pa ground’ supervising the work himself or getting soiled.

Some PSs and DCs are not even known by the masses as they are always closed-up in their deluxe offices enjoying tea with cookies! Only a few such as the likes of Elvis Nkandu and Thabo Kawana easily stand out as their work speak for themselves.

With more challenges expected in the years to come such as youth unemployment, the El Nino factor or food shortages, we expect the President to take his time to identify individuals who are easily going to align themselves with his vision for the country. As for you job seekers, a little patience would definitely do😊

We submit…..

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Political/Social Analyst

Zambezi

World.title: SADC Troika Considers Zambia’s Post-Electoral Crisis
World.content:
SADC Troika Considers Zambia’s Post-Electoral Crisis

The Southern African Development Community’s security organ is preparing to take up Zambia’s post-election crisis, after receiving a preliminary report from its election observer mission.

King Mswati III of Eswatini, who took over the chairmanship of the SADC Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation Troika last month, is expected to convene member states to consider the situation. Zambia’s main opposition leader remains in jail, and a former Cabinet minister is dead following a military raid conducted during the vote count.

Zambia held its general election on August 13. Voting passed off peacefully, but the aftermath brought allegations of vote manipulation and result tampering, including claims that the Zambia Army was deployed inside counting centres and that results were altered under military supervision.

On August 14, a military raid on the Lusaka home of opposition leader Brian Mundubile left former Minister of Transport and Communications Mutotwe Kafwaya dead. Several of Mundubile’s colleagues were arrested in the same operation, among them UNIP president and former Botswana bishop Trevor Mwamba, and former Law Association of Zambia president George Chisanga.

Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, took refuge inside the United Nations building in Lusaka after the raid. UN Secretary-General António Guterres sent a Special Envoy from New York to negotiate a resolution.

The UN sought safe passage for the two men, or their transfer to a third-party embassy in Lusaka. President Hakainde Hichilema rejected both options, demanding they surrender to police, who were investigating alleged security breaches and claims that the opposition had formed a militia.

Five days after the raid, Secretary to Cabinet Patrick Kangwa confirmed Kafwaya’s death. He said Mundubile had formed a militia intending to seize power illegally.

Mundubile and Zulu were handed over on August 27 to the Eight Church Mother Bodies at the Anglican Cathedral of the Holy Cross in Lusaka, who surrendered them to police. Both now face treason charges and are held at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility in Kabwe, roughly 200km from Lusaka, awaiting trial.

Soldiers sealed Zambia’s courts during the constitutional window for filing election challenges, blocking Mundubile and civil society groups from lodging a petition through normal channels.

Chief Justice Mumba Malila later disclosed that a petition had reached him regardless, filed by private mail. He named former Law Association of Zambia president Linda Kasonde and civil society leader Brebner Changala as the petitioners. Malila said the filing method was unusual but that he would use his constitutional powers to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court.

The Constitution requires election challenges to be resolved before a new president is inaugurated. Government proceeded with the inauguration regardless. Hichilema was sworn in for a second term on September 1 at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka, with the Kasonde-Changala petition still before the Constitutional Court.

World.title: From Civil Servant to Stateless: Mukandila’s Citizenship Ordeal
World.content:
A man does not need to lose his freedom and his nationality on the same day, yet that is precisely the position in which incarcerated Lusaka lawyer Celestine Mukandila now finds himself, after the state moved to cancel his National Registration Card and passport while he remains in custody, effectively declaring him stateless at the very moment he is least able to contest it in the ordinary course of civic life.

Mukandila, secretary general of the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance, says he is a Zambian citizen by descent and has challenged the cancellation of his documents, arguing that citizenship cannot be revoked through administrative action without following the law.

His position rests on a specific constitutional provision. Mukandila says he acquired Zambian citizenship at birth through his mother, who was a Zambian citizen at the time of his birth in 1990 in Lubumbashi, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. He explained that his mother was Ushi by origin, from Matanda Village in Mansa, Luapula Province, and that his maternal family had deep roots in the province.

Being born outside Zambia did not, in his account, make him a foreigner, because Article 36 of the Constitution provides for citizenship by descent where, at the time of birth, at least one parent was a Zambian citizen by birth or descent.

“My position is therefore straightforward: I acquired Zambian citizenship by descent at birth through my Zambian mother. I did not apply to become Zambian as an adult, nor did I obtain my citizenship through naturalisation,” Mukandila said.

He said he was approximately 16 years old when he became eligible for national registration, and therefore could not be personally held responsible for any alleged irregularities surrounding the acquisition of his NRC, since he was still a minor navigating a process his family, not he alone, would have managed.

“If the State alleges that fraud was committed in the acquisition of my NRC, then it must identify the alleged fraudulent representation, identify who made it, and establish who had the legal responsibility for making the relevant declarations at the time,” Mukandila said.

He said his family returned to Zambia in 1999, although his mother continued spending periods in the DRC because of her employment. Mukandila also questioned why his nationality was only being challenged now, when he had previously served as a civil servant and had undergone State verification processes without issue.

“The National Registration authorities themselves have previously recognised me and issued me with national documentation,” he said.

He has also demanded that authorities explain the legal basis for cancelling his NRC and passport, including identifying the alleged fraud, the authority that made the decision, and the procedure followed before the cancellation was carried out.

Mukandila said a Gazette notice could not substitute the law, arguing that public officers must exercise statutory power within the limits prescribed by law.

He said the matter was bigger than him personally, because citizenship should not be used as a political weapon against citizens holding views different from those in government.

“I demand only what every citizen is entitled to demand. Let the law be followed. Let the evidence be produced. Let due process be respected. And let the rule of law prevail over political expediency,” Mukandila said.

The case adds to a growing list of disputes in which opposition-aligned figures have found their legal standing, whether through citizenship, bail, or access to counsel, challenged through administrative or security channels rather than tested first through ordinary judicial process, a pattern that has drawn concern from legal commentators and civil society figures in the weeks following the general election.

World.title: UPND Alliance Spars UN Human Rights Report
World.content:
A government publicly disputing the findings of a United Nations human rights mandate holder is not, in ordinary circumstances, a routine political exchange. It is a moment in which a state stakes its own credibility against that of an international system built specifically to scrutinise governments during periods of political stress. That is precisely the position Zambia now occupies.

United Party for National Development Alliance spokesperson Edmond Miti has rejected a statement issued by UN Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and association, Gina Romero, calling it hasty, inaccurate and one-sided. Romero had called on Zambian authorities to release political detainees and restore democratic accountability, a statement made against the backdrop of events that have already claimed one life and placed a former presidential candidate and his running mate in detention on treason-related charges.

What is actually being disputed

Miti’s rebuttal is not a minor clarification. He accused Romero of presenting unverified allegations as settled fact, and of containing significant errors of law. His central argument rests on a distinction he insists must hold regardless of political rank: “Being an opposition leader or a political figure does not place anyone above the law, nor does it transform a criminal suspect into a political detainee,” he said.

That distinction, however, sits at the heart of why UN Special Procedures exist in the first place. Special Rapporteurs are appointed precisely because national governments, when accused of political persecution, are not considered neutral arbiters of whether their own conduct amounts to persecution or legitimate law enforcement. Miti’s insistence that allegations of treason must be tested by independent courts is, in the abstract, unremarkable. What makes it significant here is the context in which it is being asserted: a former Cabinet minister and sitting MP is dead following a raid conducted during live vote counting, his death denied by the state for five days until a habeas corpus filing forced disclosure, and the two men now facing treason charges were present at that raid.

The government’s defence

Miti sought to reframe the UPND administration’s record affirmatively, describing it as a law-abiding government that has elevated respect for human rights to unprecedented levels. He pointed to the abolition of the death penalty and changes to public order practices as evidence that reform in Zambia is substantive rather than rhetorical, and cautioned the international community against confusing legitimate criminal investigations with political witch-hunts.

He drew a deliberate contrast between Romero’s approach and that of a separate UN figure, the Secretary-General’s own Special Envoy, who Miti said engaged constructively on the ground in Zambia rather than issuing judgment from a distance. According to Miti, it was this envoy who facilitated the handover of opposition leaders to security agencies, operating on explicit assurances that their fundamental rights would be respected, a commitment he said the Zambian government continues to honour.

That claim of continued protection sits uneasily alongside separate, corroborated reporting that the detained opposition figures have faced severe restrictions on legal and family access at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility, and reports that they have twice refused prison-supplied food amid unresolved concerns over their safety. Whether those restrictions are consistent with the assurances Miti describes is a question his statement does not address.

Sovereignty versus scrutiny

Miti’s legal argument leans heavily on the principle of non-interference. “Under international law, the mandate of UN Special Procedures requires strict adherence to objectivity, impartiality and non-interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states,” he said, arguing that Romero failed to meet this standard by operating from a distance without thorough local verification and without adequately incorporating input from Zambian authorities.

This is a genuine and long-standing tension within international human rights law: sovereign states retain the right to conduct their own criminal justice processes, while UN mandate holders retain the right, indeed the obligation, to scrutinise those processes when credible concerns arise about politically motivated detention. Neither principle automatically overrides the other, and disputes of exactly this kind, a state insisting on non-interference, a rapporteur insisting on independent scrutiny, have historically been resolved only through sustained international pressure, further investigation or, in some cases, neither, leaving the underlying facts contested indefinitely.

Why this matters beyond the statement itself

Miti closed by describing Zambia as a committed constitutional democracy, open to fair scrutiny but grounded in mutual respect and national sovereignty. That description will now be tested against events that are, for the most part, no longer in serious factual dispute: a sitting MP died from gunshot wounds during a state security operation; his death was not acknowledged for five days; two senior opposition figures remain detained on charges connected to that same raid; and questions about their access to legal counsel, family visits and safe food remain unresolved more than a week into their detention.

The dispute between the UPND Alliance and the UN Special Rapporteur is, in that sense, not merely a disagreement over wording or diplomatic tone. It is a contest over which account of these events, the government’s or the international community’s, will shape how Zambia’s post-election period is remembered and how accountable its institutions are ultimately held to be.

World.title: Death of Constitutionalism — How August 13 Marked a Turning Point for Zambia’s Democracy
World.content:
Death of Constitutionalism — How August 13 Marked a Turning Point for Zambia’s Democracy

By Oscar Mike Chops

For five days, the Zambian state told the public, implicitly and explicitly, that former Cabinet minister and sitting Member of Parliament Mutotwe Kafwaya could not be found. For five days, his family did not know whether he was alive. When the truth finally emerged, it came not from a government statement volunteered in good faith, but because a court had been asked to compel one.

The sequence of events, now established through official confirmation, opposition accounts and a court filing, has been described by commentators as marking a decisive rupture in Zambia’s constitutional order rather than a gradual decline. What happened in the 48 hours after polls closed on August 13, and in the five days of silence that followed, has become the defining controversy of President Hakainde Hichilema’s second-term inauguration.

The raid

On the evening of August 14, as live vote tabulation was still under way across the country, a heavily armed Joint Task Force entered the private Kabulonga residence of Tonse Pact presidential candidate Brian Mundubile. The unit was made up of elite personnel drawn from the Zambia Army, the Drug Enforcement Commission and the Zambia Police Service.

During the operation, state security personnel opened fire inside the residence. Among those present was Mutotwe Kafwaya, former transport minister and Member of Parliament for Lunte, who sustained multiple gunshot wounds. Eleven other individuals, including opposition political staff, were forcibly apprehended and detained at the scene.

Kafwaya did not survive his injuries.

Five days of silence

What followed was not an immediate acknowledgement of a death in state custody, but an extended period in which senior government representatives explicitly rejected reports of Kafwaya’s death or critical condition.

When Mundubile’s running mate, Makebi Zulu, publicly stated that Kafwaya had been taken to a military health facility with severe chest wounds, officials at the Ministry of Defence dismissed the claim outright, insisting that no record of Kafwaya existed at their facilities.

The blackout held for nearly five days. It was broken only when Kafwaya’s wife, Dinis Ng’andu Kafwaya, filed an urgent habeas corpus application in the High Court of Zambia, a legal instrument that compels the state to produce a detained person before a judge or account for their whereabouts. It is a measure of how completely ordinary channels of accountability had broken down that it took a widow’s court filing, rather than a government press briefing, to force disclosure.

Faced with mandatory judicial scrutiny, Inspector General of Police Graphel Musamba issued an official statement on August 19, finally confirming that Kafwaya had died from gunshot wounds inflicted during the August 14 operation.

Competing narratives

To justify the use of lethal force during a raid conducted while votes were still being counted, state security organs have pointed to an alleged “insurgency plot,” citing the recovery of cash and weapons at the scene.

Mundubile and Zulu have firmly rejected this characterisation. They argue the narrative was constructed to achieve three specific outcomes: to rebrand what they describe as an extrajudicial killing as a response to armed confrontation; to justify non-bailable charges of treason, sedition and espionage against senior opposition figures; and to force principal opposition contenders into hiding or legal detention during the narrow statutory window in which election petitions must be filed.

Whichever account proves accurate through further judicial process, the underlying facts are no longer in dispute. A sitting Member of Parliament died from gunshot wounds during a state security operation conducted at a presidential candidate’s private residence while the country’s votes were still being tallied. His death was denied by the state for five days. It was confirmed only after his widow sought judicial intervention.

A nation left to grieve in silence

The human cost of these events has rippled well beyond the courtroom. Kafwaya was a son of Northern Province, and his killing has become deeply entwined with the region’s collective mourning. The Bemba Royal Establishment, in an unprecedented decision reached during an urgent meeting on Friday night, cancelled the 2026 Ukusefya pa Ng’wena traditional ceremony, one of Zambia’s largest cultural gatherings, citing the region’s grief and the continued detention of prominent political figures from the area.

Former Northern Province minister Chungu Bwalya described the ceremony’s cancellation as entirely justified, noting that holding festivities while a son of the region lay dead and others from the province remained in detention would have signalled indifference to real suffering.

Constitutional stakes

Commentators tracing the sequence of events argue that what collapsed on August 13 and in the days after was not merely a political dispute but a structural safeguard: the presumption that state power, however forcefully exercised, remains answerable to judicial oversight in real time, not five days and a court order later.

Zambia now carries this into its second Hichilema term. Opposition figures Mundubile and Makebi Zulu remain in detention on treason-related charges connected to the same events, their case now moving through the ordinary channels of the courts. Kafwaya’s widow has secured, through legal action, the disclosure the state initially withheld. What remains unresolved is accountability for the raid itself, and for the five days during which the truth was denied.

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi on Hunger Strike?
World.content:
Uncertainty over what is happening inside Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility has deepened after reports emerged that detained opposition figures Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu have stopped eating food supplied by the institution, with their own legal team unable to fully explain why.

Defence counsel Sakwiba Sikota, part of the team representing both men, stopped short of confirming the hunger strike outright, but his account painted a picture of a legal team locked out of the very access it needs to know what is happening to its clients.

“I haven’t been to them today or yesterday, but we will be going there,” Sikota said, describing a pattern of restricted visits that has left even the lawyers uncertain about conditions inside the facility.

He traced the immediate concern back to the question of food safety. According to Sikota, Mundubile and Zulu have specifically asked for meals to be brought to them from outside the correctional facility rather than eating what is prepared internally, a request that prison authorities have repeatedly turned down.

“You see how they refuse the food being provided by the facility… So they have opted not to take food from the facility,” he said, describing the decision as a direct response to that refusal rather than an unprompted protest.

Behind the food dispute lies a broader breakdown in trust, Sikota suggested. He linked the difficulty in visiting the two men to what he called an unhelpful posture from officials at the facility, saying restricted access has made it impossible for the legal team to independently verify what the two detainees are being given to eat.

“There is a real need for them to be wary of the fact that they cannot be sure of what they are being given by the authorities, because the attitude of the authorities has shown no interest in that of goodwill,” he said.

Asked directly whether fears of poisoning were behind the men’s refusal to eat, Sikota declined to confirm this, saying he was not in a position to state it as fact. His caution reflects the wider information gap surrounding the case, in which claims and counter-claims have circulated without official confirmation from correctional authorities.

Sources close to the matter say the current standoff is not the first of its kind. This, according to those sources, is the second occasion since their detention began that Mundubile and Zulu have refused prison meals, suggesting a recurring pattern of distrust rather than an isolated incident.

Additional claims have surfaced regarding who is actually guarding the pair. Sources allege that Zambia Army commandos, rather than the ordinary correctional officers typically assigned to Mukobeko, have been posted around the two detainees, a security arrangement described as unusual and, by some accounts, without precedent in recent Zambian correctional practice.

Compounding the concern is the reported difficulty faced by friends and relatives attempting to visit the two men. Multiple sources say access for family members has been tightly restricted since the detention began, limiting independent channels through which the public could otherwise verify the detainees’ condition.

Taken together, the restricted legal access, the reported presence of military personnel and the refusal to eat facility-prepared food have combined to raise serious questions about the treatment of Mundubile and Zulu more than a week into their detention on treason-related charges.

Correctional authorities and government officials had not, by the time of publication, issued any public response confirming or denying the reports of a hunger strike, the restrictions on visitors, or the presence of military guards at the facility. The silence has left the matter unresolved, with Mundubile and Zulu’s legal team indicating it intends to press for renewed access in the coming days.

World.title: Release Mundubile, Makebi, Demands Kalaba
World.content:
A widening rift between political rhetoric and judicial practice has drawn sharp criticism from Citizens First president Harry Kalaba, who says Zambia’s courts are being used selectively depending on whose electoral fortunes are at stake.

Kalaba has demanded the unconditional release of Tonse Alliance presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and lawyer Makebi Zulu, arguing that their continued detention reflects a broader climate of political intolerance rather than a genuine legal process.

His statement did not stop at the two men. Kalaba called for every political detainee currently held in the country to be released, describing this as a necessary precondition for dialogue, national reconciliation and healing after a bruising election season.

At the heart of his argument is a contradiction he believes exposes the government’s true priorities. Courts were closed to any challenge of the presidential election outcome, he noted, yet those same courts remain open and active for challenges brought against duly elected parliamentary candidates.

“It is deeply concerning that while the UPND leadership denied the people of Zambia an opportunity to validate the presidential electoral outcome by closing the courts of law, it has now turned to those same courts to challenge duly elected parliamentary candidates,” Kalaba said.

He described this as “a troubling pattern of expediency over principle,” warning that it risks eroding public confidence in the justice system altogether.

Detention practices came under equally pointed criticism. Kalaba said he had received reports of opposition supporters being held for as long as 14 days without appearing before a court, a practice he labelled an abuse of the justice system.

“Such actions amount to an abuse of the justice system and point to a dangerous trend of its weaponisation. This must come to an immediate end,” he said.

A further, more urgent concern surfaced in his remarks: alleged plans to abduct Mafinga South Member of Parliament Faith Munthali. Kalaba called on authorities to investigate the claims and guarantee her safety without delay.

He tied these domestic developments to international scrutiny, saying recent events lend weight to warnings already issued by United Nations Special Rapporteurs about a shrinking democratic space in Zambia.

Rather than direct his appeal solely at government, Kalaba turned to the country’s institutions of conscience. He urged civil society organisations, faith-based bodies and the clergy to speak out in defence of constitutional democracy, justice and national unity, cautioning that silence in the face of injustice only deepens the crisis.

Citizens First, he stressed, remains committed to non-violence, equity, justice and respect for the rule of law. His closing appeal was aimed squarely at the ruling party: an end to what he termed “hypocrisy in the application of the law,” and a single, uniform standard of justice for every citizen.

World.title: Power lose  Champions League opener
World.content:
Zambian champions Power Dynamos have launched their CAF Champions League campaign with a 1-0 loss to Sudanese club Al Merrikh at the Amahoro Stadium on Saturday night.

‎

‎Abubakar Bangora’s 37th minute penalty was the difference in the first leg tie of the first preliminary round.

‎

‎The penalty was awarded to the home team after Power defender Dominic Chanda was adjudged to have made a foul in the box.

‎

‎Bangora stepped forward and beat Lawrence Mulenga in the Power goal to give Al Merrikh the lead.

‎

‎Power coach Oswald Mutapa said the tie will be decided in the return leg next week, and lamented his side’s slow start.

‎

‎“It is bad we have lost but I feel yes we didn’t start well. I think the first fifteen to twenty minutes we didn’t play our game,” Mutapa said.

‎

‎The coach also questioned the penalty decision.

‎

‎“The time we played our game we conceded through a penalty, which I don’t think was because I feel our player kicked the ball before he touched the opponent,”_ he said.

‎

‎Mutapa noted improvement in the second half.

‎

‎“Much better in the second half, I guess they were comfortable with a 1-0 score-line and trying to play on the counter attack. We tried to play but we didn’t create as many opportunities as we would have loved. At the end of the day, first half we are down 1-0 we have to play the second half at home,” he added.

‎

‎The return leg is set for Saturday, 12 September at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola.

‎

‎The winners on aggregate will advance to the Second Preliminary Round scheduled for 16-18 October and 23-25 October.

‎

‎The 16 winners from that round will progress to the group stage at the end of November.

World.title: Africa: The Continent Has the Capital - It Needs the Alignment.
World.content:
Africa's industrial moment is not waiting for more money. It is waiting for the right kind — structured correctly, sequenced intelligently, and aimed at the right stage of a project's life. Afreximbank's Oluranti Doherty on why the continent's financing problem is really a coordination problem.

Why this series exists

Our new editorial initiative seeks to unearth an answer to a question that most development institutions have debated but few have answered: why does a continent that grows the world's finest cotton wear clothes made somewhere else — and what would it actually take to change that?

The answer is not, as it is so often presented, a story about roads or ports or missing technology. For centuries, the processing of Africa's raw materials into finished goods happened elsewhere by design — and the wealth that process generated remained elsewhere by consequence. That is the inheritance this generation of African industrialists, financiers, and policymakers is trying to overturn. Our programme is the journalistic record of whether they are succeeding.

The initiative is built on a straightforward premise. Africa's industrial potential is not poorly understood because the facts are unavailable. It is poorly understood because the right stories are not being told, to the right audiences, in the right register. A $40 million commodity export that could be an $800 million manufacturing industry is not, primarily, a financing problem. It is a narrative problem — and a narrative problem is one that journalism, data, and sustained institutional distribution can address.

The programme is anchored in cotton and textiles because the value chain is visible, traceable, and human — from the smallholder farmer harvesting seed cotton by hand to the factory floor where garments leave for European retailers. But it is not, ultimately, a story about cotton. It is a story about whether Africa can manufacture, add value, and compete globally — and what the continent's own financial institutions, entrepreneurs, and policymakers are doing to make that happen.

We distribute our journalism through the institutional wire network that reaches the fund managers, analysts, trade ministers, and development finance executives who price African risk every day. The argument is simple: the story Africa tells about itself is not the story its industrial performance warrants.

To begin that work, our editorial team sat with Ms. Oluranti Doherty — Managing Director for Export Development at Afreximbank — to understand what two decades inside the actual mechanics of African industrial finance looks like from the inside. The conversation ranged from the mathematics of a cotton boll to the architecture of a $70 billion African capital coalition, from the five-year ramp-up period of a new factory to the $4.2 billion annual cost of a bad story.

The math behind the optimism

The numbers, when she lays them out, are startling less for the size of the loss than for the size of the opportunity still sitting on the table. Raw Beninese cotton, from farm to port, sells for $1,500 to $2,000 a metric tonne. Transformed into garments, the same fibre is worth $16,000 to $20,000 a tonne — a value increase of ten to fifteen times. Scale that across 40,000 tonnes of annual production, and a $40 million commodity export becomes an $800 million manufacturing industry.

"Africa produces and exports cotton lint," Doherty says, "but much of the value generated in the cotton, textile and garment value chain occurs through spinning, weaving, dyeing, finishing, garment manufacturing, branding and retailing" — steps that have historically happened somewhere else. Benin's industrial zone, known as Glo-Djigbé, was built specifically to bring those steps home.

« What we need to prove more is that it can be replicated programmatically in every cotton-producing country. »

Not as a copy-paste template, she is careful to say, but adapted to the politics, infrastructure and ambitions of each place that tries it.

A different theory of the challenge

For years, the general explanation for why more African countries haven't replicated that success has been simple: not enough financing. Doherty, whose job is quite literally to arrange that financing, disagrees. And her disagreement is, oddly enough, the most encouraging line in the whole conversation, because it points to a solvable problem rather than an intractable one.

"It is relevant," she says of financing, "but what you need is a combination of financing solutions" tailored to each stage of a project's life — patient equity for the earliest, riskiest years; long-term project debt once a factory is built; working capital structured around the actual rhythm of the business, whether that trade cycle runs 60 days or 360. The failures she has seen tend to come from mismatches — a seven-year project financed with three-year money — rather than from an absence of capital altogether.

Afreximbank The value at stake in AfricaÂs cotton-to-cloth chain, summarised in four key figures

« Having financiers who can understand that this is the reality of industrial and manufacturing projects is very important — and increasingly, I believe, they do. »

That is a fixable problem, and Afreximbank has spent the past several years building the tools to fix it: a dedicated project-preparation facility to help entrepreneurs get their first plans investment-ready, and FEDA, a Rwanda-based equity fund built specifically to supply the patient capital that traditional lending cannot.

Closing the coordination gap

When Doherty steps back from individual transactions to describe the larger architecture of African industrial finance, her diagnosis shifts from frustration to something closer to strategic clarity. The continent does not lack capital. It does not lack viable projects. What it has lacked — until recently — is the mechanism for connecting the two.

« Africa has capital. Africa has viable projects. What has been missing is not resources — but alignment »

"Africa has development institutions, commercial banks, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds," Doherty says. What has been missing is a problem she calls "systemic fragmentation," in which capable institutions work in silos rather than in partnership.

The Alliance for African Multilateral Financial Institutions (AAMFI), a coalition Afreximbank helped launch, has brought together African-owned lenders with a combined balance sheet of $70 billion — capital that can now move behind large industrial projects in a coordinated way rather than depending on any single institution to shoulder a deal alone.

Rewriting the risk premium

Researchers have estimated that negative media narratives about the continent add up to $4.2 billion a year in inflated sovereign borrowing costs; Doherty believes the true figure, once corporate financing is included, is considerably higher.

« We are not asking for favorable risk assessment as Africans. We are simply requesting an accurate one. »

An accurate assessment, she argues, is one that weighs a young, fast-urbanising, increasingly educated population and proven projects like Glo-Djigbé alongside the risks that any market carries, rather than pricing an entire continent off a single, outdated story.

"I would like the fund manager to look at projects such as the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone as evidence that African cotton can be processed sustainably in Africa into exportable garments at industrial scale," she said — proof that the story is already changing, one factory at a time.

A continent coming into alignment

The continent's most ambitious trade project, the African Continental Free Trade Area, drew a hopeful assessment. Its architecture, Doherty said, is "directionally aligned" with what a West African textile manufacturer needs — tariff schedules, rules of origin, and Afreximbank's own cross-border payment system, PAPSS, are all pointed the right way.

The destination she describes is a striking one — cotton grown in one African country, spun and woven in a second, sold in a third, with predictable rules and frictionless payments throughout. It does not yet exist at scale. But in this conversation, it did not feel like aspiration. It felt like a schedule.

Benin's twenty thousand new jobs, its rising share of processed cotton, its garments now hanging in European stores — these are not yet the full story of African industrialisation. But they are, Doherty insists, the proof that the story is real, that it is replicable, and that the only question that remains is speed.

About Ms. Oluranti Doherty

Ms. Oluranti Doherty is Managing Director for Export Development at Afreximbank, where she oversees export financing across manufacturing, agro-processing, extractives, and industrial parks and special economic zones. She brings more than twenty years in project finance, credit analysis and industrial policy advisory. Recent transactions include a $1 billion project-preparation facility with Shelter Afrique and a $15 million SME finance facility for Zimbabwean export value chains. She is a Fellow of ICAN, and studied at IMD Lausanne, the University of Leicester and Olabisi Onabanjo University.

World.title: Africa: Loza Maléombho Is Building An Industry From African Stories
World.content:
Internationally recognised after Beyoncé wore her designs, Ivorian designer Loza Maléombho is now looking beyond fashion. Through Pokou, she is combining Baoulé history, local craftsmanship and artificial intelligence to build an African-owned creative universe spanning clothing, film, art, architecture and digital experiences.

On the fourth floor of a building in Treichville, one of Abidjan’s busiest commercial and cultural districts, the world of Ivorian designer Loza Maléombho is expanding beyond the clothes hanging in her workshop.

Maléombho is developing Pokou, a creative universe inspired by Queen Abla Pokou, the legendary founder of the Baoulé people, and reimagined through science fiction, fashion and digital technology.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to tradition, Queen Pokou led her people from the Ashanti Kingdom towards present-day Côte d’Ivoire. When they were unable to cross the Comoé River, Pokou sacrificed her only son to save her people. The story, which symbolises courage, selflessness and communal survival, is also associated with the origin of the name Baoulé, often translated as “the child is dead.”

“It is a story that everyone knows in Côte d’Ivoire so people can identify with it. But it is also a story about sacrifice, and I think that is something any audience can relate to in family, work, and life in general,” she said.

Maléombho drew on this story for her YouTube Pokou series, which launched in June 2026.

Developed using generative artificial intelligence alongside Maléombho’s own research and design work, Pokou is intended to promote the clothing label while opening routes into film, art, architecture, craftsmanship and digital experiences.

The project represents the designer’s attempt to turn African stories into commercially valuable, African-owned intellectual property.

Maléombho is not starting from obscurity. Her international breakthrough came when singer Beyoncé wore pieces from her Spring/Summer 2016 collection in the “ Formation ” music video. She later created a custom outfit for Beyoncé’s 2020 visual album, Black Is King . The appearances introduced her work to a global audience and strengthened her reputation for combining contemporary silhouettes with West African materials and imagery.

Now she wants to take the label beyond celebrity recognition and luxury clothing.

“The idea today is not that we want to dissociate ourselves, but that we are evolving more toward a multicultural creative studio and toward cultural intellectual property,” Maléombho said.

“We are no longer focused solely on producing products for sale, but more on creating a universe as such. There are characters, there are clothes, there are art objects, there are interactive experiences, there are architectural concepts.”

The shift is partly a response to the limitations confronting fashion businesses based in African markets. A conventional label must design collections, source materials, maintain consistent production, organise distribution and find buyers. Maléombho says African brands often have to do this without the supply chains, finance and logistics available to established international companies.

Her own business has encountered difficulties sourcing raw materials, finding specialised workers, maintaining consistent quality, accepting online payments, securing finance and transporting finished products.

Côte d’Ivoire’s cotton industry illustrates one of these structural gaps. The country is a significant West African producer, with output forecast at 590,000 bales of cotton lint in the 2026/27 marketing year. However, only a small proportion is processed by domestic spinning and weaving businesses; most fibre is exported to textile-producing markets in Asia.

That disconnect helps explain why Maléombho can work extensively with Ivorian artisans while still importing some of the cotton used in her collections.

Rather than relying only on selling larger volumes of clothing, she wants to create several commercial entry points into the same cultural universe.

“It is creativity, it is cultural ownership, it is our cultural stories,” she said. Pokou could encompass clothing, art objects, interiors and architectural concepts, while enabling collaborations and licensing agreements with companies in other sectors.

Artificial intelligence has allowed Maléombho to visualise parts of this universe more quickly, but she rejects the suggestion that it is the author of the work.

“What is very important to specify is that I do not give creativity to artificial intelligence,” she said. “People tend to think that AI designs everything, and then creativity is lost. But artificial intelligence makes a huge number of mistakes in terms of storytelling or even mythology in our African traditions.”

The digital ideas eventually become physical objects in the Treichville workshop. Maléombho works with artisans to test fabrics, dyes, embellishments and accessories. Bronze workers make buttons and a signature gold-plated buckle inspired by a Baoulé mask.

Jute, ordinarily used in sacks for packaging and exporting cocoa, is transformed through dyeing, appliqué, beadwork and printing. Raffia, Baoulé cloth, Kita cloth and hand-dyed cotton also form part of the brand’s visual language.

Baoulé is a traditional Ivorian cotton fabric, handwoven in distinctive patterns and colours and often worn at ceremonies, while Kita is a West African textile handwoven in narrow strips of cotton and silk.

For Norou Sow, a leather craftsman and artisan who has worked with Maléombho for more than ten years, the collaboration has changed both his methods of work and his livelihood.

“She taught me to work in a group. She also taught me to develop my experience,” Sow said. “Many things changed in my life when I started working with her.”

The company employs 10 people directly and works with more than 50 artisans in Côte d’Ivoire. Maléombho says 90% of its inputs or production are local, while some cotton and some manufacturing are sourced internationally.

The label sells through outlets or concept stores in Côte d’Ivoire, the United States, Nigeria, South Africa, the United Kingdom and Tanzania.

Côte d’Ivoire-based fashion and tourism specialist Dorine Negou sees the larger challenge as persuading African brands and consumers to recognise the commercial value of their own cultural identities.

“I think the difficulty is that we Africans want to adopt European models too much,” she said. “We have so many things that can enhance our value and attract more attention to us. It is up to us to rely on our brands, on our nature, on where we come from, and know how to showcase what we have.”

Yapo Patrick is a visual and installation artist who has taught colour and textile techniques for more than 20 years at the Centre Technique des Arts Appliqués (CTAA), or Technical Centre for Applied Arts, in Bingerville, Côte d’Ivoire.

Patrick said Maléombho’s journey demonstrates how formal training must be combined with personal commitment and a willingness to take risks: “There will always be limitations and difficulties, but creators have to commit themselves personally. They have to dare and decide to act despite those difficulties.”

However, turning the success of individual designers into a stronger domestic fashion industry will require broader investment in skills and local production. Although Côte d’Ivoire is a major cotton producer, only a limited share of its raw material is transformed locally into finished textiles and clothing.

Patrick believes vocational training for designers, pattern makers and tailors could help expand production and encourage Ivorians to buy locally made fabric and clothing.

“We need more information, more initiatives and more people investing in professional training,” he said. “If Ivorians can produce and consume Ivorian products, including fabrics, that will generate revenue and encourage both the state and the private sector to develop an ecosystem in which the fashion industry can grow.”

Close 

Maléombho believes that Africa possesses a vast narrative and cultural inheritance but captures too little of its commercial value. The opportunity, in her view, is to turn stories, materials and craft traditions into products that retain a distinct identity while meeting international standards.

Her clothing label provides the initial commercial foundation. Its luxury pieces target customers drawn to the house’s craftsmanship and cultural references, while shoes, belts, jewellery and other accessories offer less expensive entry points.

Pokou would extend that model. A consumer might first encounter a garment in a film or digital world. A character could lead into a collection, while an imagined building might inspire furniture or another designed object. The story itself could be licensed or used in collaborations across different industries.

Over the next three to five years, Maléombho hopes to complete the transition from a fashion label into a cultural studio built around intellectual property. She believes the model could create jobs in traditional crafts, film, digital production and artificial intelligence.

“It is not just a clothing brand,” she said. “It is truly a multicultural studio that is in tune with the times and also knows how to innovate while keeping its roots in its history.”

From its base in Treichville, Pokou is attempting to bring Baoulé history into dialogue with artificial intelligence, craftsmanship with cinema, and clothing with architecture.

Maléombho believes the constraints facing African creative businesses can themselves produce innovation.

“The legacy I would like to leave would really be to show that, first of all, with very little, we can create much more value,” she said. “It is even within the constraints that we have the opportunity to innovate.”

World.title: 8 everyday things that would quit working without data centers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Data centers are the largely unseen infrastructure behind modern life, powering everything from the apps on your phone and shows you stream to online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence.

Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Most Americans may never see one, but they rely on them constantly, often without realizing it.

"Data centers have been around for as long as technology has been around," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you’re touching technology and using everything from social media to your email, all of that information, all of the data is being processed in a data center."

As more of the economy moves online, data centers have become far more than a niche piece of the tech industry. They are increasingly essential infrastructure for everyday American life. The U.S. is home to roughly 4,000 operational facilities, with thousands more planned or under construction as demand for cloud computing and AI accelerates.

Here are eight ways data centers quietly power the services Americans rely on every day.

1. They make your favorite apps work

From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind the services people use every day. When you open an app, upload a photo, refresh your feed or send a message, your phone is connected to servers that retrieve and deliver that information in seconds.

The apps may live on a screen in your hand, but much of the work happens far away inside a physical facility filled with computers running continuously.

2. They keep your streaming and gaming smooth

Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and other streaming platforms rely on massive computing infrastructure to deliver movies, videos and music to millions of users at once. Data centers help store enormous libraries of content and move it quickly enough to prevent the pauses and buffering that frustrate viewers.

ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM

Online games also rely on data centers to connect players, synchronize what is happening in a match and reduce the lag that can make a game unplayable. The more people stream, game and use data-heavy services, the more computing power those platforms need behind the scenes.

3. They store your photos and files

Your iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups do not just float around in cyberspace. They are stored on physical servers inside data centers, often with copies kept in multiple locations to help prevent data loss.

That means a lost phone or broken laptop does not necessarily mean lost memories or work file — but it also means the cloud depends on vast amounts of real-world hardware.

4. They help Google answer your questions instantly

Search engines rely on data centers to sort through enormous amounts of information and return results in fractions of a second. Every query triggers systems that locate relevant webpages, images, maps, videos and other information before sending the results back to your device.

What feels like a simple Google search is actually a complex exchange between your device and powerful servers processing requests at an enormous scale.

5. They make online shopping possible

When you order something online, data centers help manage inventory, process payments, make product recommendations and track packages to your door. They also allow retailers to update product availability and pricing quickly as demand changes.

ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI

During major shopping events such as Black Friday, those systems have to handle a surge of shoppers and transactions without crashing.

6. They keep GPS and navigation running

Google Maps, Waze and other navigation services depend on computing infrastructure to process traffic patterns, routes and location data in real time. They combine information from roads, users, businesses and mapping systems to estimate travel times and suggest alternate routes.

Without the data centers behind them, navigation apps would not be able to react as quickly to accidents, congestion or changing road conditions.

7. They make remote work possible

Video calls, cloud-based software, shared documents and workplace messaging all rely heavily on data-center infrastructure. Every Zoom meeting, Slack message and live edit to a shared file depends on servers that keep information synced between people working from different locations.

THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS

For many companies, data centers have become as essential to day-to-day operations as office space, phones and electricity.

8. They power the next generation of technology

Every time someone asks an AI chatbot a question, generates an image or uses an AI-powered search feature, data centers provide the computing power working behind the screen. Those requests require far more processing than a basic web search because the systems must analyze information and generate a response in real time.

That is a major reason the technology industry is racing to build bigger and more powerful data centers, often equipped with specialized chips designed for AI workloads.
