World.title: From the archive: To friend or not to friend other expats in Mexico?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a humorous look at the often thorny issue of friendships among expats.

Any foreigners who’ve been in Mexico for more than two minutes know this truth: expat relationships are complicated.

I read with interest Louisa Rogers’ article on expat relationships, and found myself nodding along to much of it. Feeling threatened by large numbers of new foreigners moving to my area? Check! Hyper awareness of my ratio of Mexican-to-foreign-born friends? Check! Complaining about “those other gringos” who are messing up some designated “elsewhere”? Oh my goodness, please don’t make me look in the mirror.

Friends unless proven otherwise

My policy these days is to keep a very light grip on everything from my friendships to my own ideological musings. I pre-like everyone now, purposefully rather than by default. I haven’t met you, but I am sure you are a friend, until and unless you prove otherwise.

And I would really appreciate it if you wouldn’t prove otherwise.

But this attitude was hard-won, not discovered in a sudden stroke of coolness. It’s been over 20 years — uh-oh, am I bragging? — and it’s taken a long time to make peace with my identity both as an individual and as part of the greater foreigner-in-Mexico population. I don’t know if it’s my time here or just my age. Maybe it was a really good mushroom trip. But I just refuse to get worked up: if you want to be friends, we’re friends. I’ll try to help you if you need help. If you don’t like me, then, oh well. I guess we’re not friends.

The comment section of this humor piece I wrote made the “not friends” column abundantly clear; self-sorting, even.

And it got me thinking: is online communication among us all helping or hurting? After all, no one would be as nasty to people’s faces as we might be online. Online, we’re anonymous; we could be anyone; and we can’t get punched in the face for being rude as hell.

A polarized society, at home and abroad

Perhaps it’s a reflection as well of the general polarity we find in the United States. I’m certainly not immune from self-sorting, of course: finding common ground with friends who are openly enthusiastic about a felon president is not always easy. In any case, everyone has strong opinions either way.

Yes, we foreigners are a varied bunch, each of us as unique as a snowflake. Complicating matters is the fact that the average U.S. or Canadian citizen is not someone who would voluntarily move to Mexico. Right off the bat, then, you’re dealing with someone whose type you might not be too familiar with.

Overall, the most even-keeled people I’ve met have been retirees, though this isn’t a hard and fast rule. You can be a weirdo at any age!

People closer to my own age are a bit of a mixed bag, though, and I’ve had a few relationships with other paisanos end abruptly at this point. This has only happened once with a Mexican friend, a neighbor who blocked me after I friended her husband, who I thought was also my friend, on Facebook. Given the demographics, I’d say the number of times it’s happened with those from my own culture makes it conspicuously likely.

Abrupt endings to friendships

The first cut off was by a couple from the U.S. who wanted help translating and getting paperwork done upon arrival. We’d had some great conversations online beforehand, but in real life, our chemistry was pretty tense and weird. No matter; they were paying me for my help, and I was going to do whatever I could to make it worth it. Mostly, it was fine.

But then there was a misunderstanding about what exactly was being charged, and I suddenly found myself buried under some very intense, urgent messages. I gifted them some extra live interpretation time as a sign of goodwill and thought we were fine. Later, though, when I wanted to send a message to see how their house hunting had gone, I realized I’d been blocked on WhatsApp and Facebook.

Since then, I’ve found I’m not the only person to have received that treatment. A clear picture of kookiness has emerged, so I guess it’s not just me. The experience did convince me, however, that I definitely did not want to make a career of helping people settle down here.

Another cut-off came from someone who’d been a friend and mentor to me for over 20 years. That one was completely unexpected, and it hurt. I’d excused myself from what I saw as a minor favor, an action which my friend apparently interpreted as a sign of deep disrespect. I was oblivious that he was upset with me, and only learned that he was months later from another friend. By the time I wrote him to apologize, that was it. I never heard from him again.

The last incident was quite recent, with a friend of three years. I thought we were really close, but when I unwisely hounded her about getting her dog fixed so it wouldn’t get all the dogs in the neighborhood pregnant, that was it, too. I was asked to leave her house immediately, even though home was over three hours away.

Keeping an open mind on other expats

What is with these gringos and abruptly cutting people off? Mexicans may have a reputation for being dramatic, but my relationships with them have gone through rocky patches and come out just fine. Only my own paisanos have been so mad that they banished me from their lives. Is it something about North Americans, or is it just something about North Americans who live in Mexico? I will probably never know.

But I have not sworn off other U.S. Americans. Currently, we have a small breakfast group of foreigners in Xalapa that meets once a month. We share a nice meal and chat. We wouldn’t all necessarily be best friends were we in the U.S.

But this is different. When you’re in a foreign country without family, it’s nice to know people who know your culture and language on a native level. Real friendships, I still believe and have proven, are possible.

But for people who I know will definitely still be my friend even if I berate them about their unsterilized pets, I’m sticking with Mexicans.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum delivers her second-year report as trade tensions simmer
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 31, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report, reflecting on the state of the nation as her second year in office draws to a close. She touted falling homicides and a stable economy, only to face a pointed rebuttal from opposition leaders who accused her administration of manipulating crime statistics and shielding officials tied to drug trafficking.

Mexico continues to grapple with security challenges on a variety of fronts, a fact underscored by a car bomb in Zacatecas Sunday night — the state’s third such attack in four days. But Mexico’s security forces remain active and on Monday claimed a high-profile target: Soldiers and marines killed Luis Enrique Barragán, alias “R5,” the accused leader of extortion against Michoacán’s avocado growers, in a shootout in Tocumbo.

Trade friction with Washington ran through much of the week. A dispute over cheese naming rights is complicating already-strained talks over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Mexico continues to push back against the threat of U.S. tariffs, and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 gathering Wednesday to press Mexico’s case against tariffs on steel, aluminum and cars.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum’s second-year report meets a sharp opposition response

President Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report Tuesday, a 67-minute address touting a 51% reduction in homicides since taking office, record foreign direct investment and a stable economy. She said her administration’s relationship with Washington “has had its challenges” but reiterated that “sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared.”

Opposition senators offered a starkly different account. PAN’s Ricardo Anaya disputed the government’s homicide figures, arguing that reclassified deaths obscure a rising toll, while PRI’s Alejandro Moreno accused the administration of an unspoken “pact” with organized crime, pointing to the unresolved U.S. extradition request for Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. Sheinbaum has said her administration won’t shield anyone who has committed a crime.

The president also used Wednesday’s press conference to accuse the Trump administration of trying to “create divisions” within her cabinet ahead of November’s U.S. midterms, calling it part of a long-standing U.S. pattern of pressuring “independent governments.” Her approval rating stood at 68% heading into the report, among the highest of any Mexican president at this point in a term, according to polling firm El Financiero. Along with the high approval rating, the newest results of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ found an almost 10-point increase in the president’s performance.

Security: Zacatecas car bomb and a cartel leader’s death

Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente — the third explosives attack in Zacatecas in four days. Authorities are investigating whether the blast was retaliation for the Saturday capture of an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) sicario. The explosion damaged 30 properties and 13 vehicles; classes were suspended and army troops deployed to the municipality.

The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The singing frog that came to symbolize midcentury Mexico
World.content:
While it may be a fine place to avoid New Orleans’ sweltering heat, Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library serves a much larger purpose as a repository of Mexico travel and tourism ephemera, including magazines, hotel brochures and highway maps.

Together, the collection offers a unique look at how the United States’ southern neighbors were constructed as attractive vacation destinations throughout the midcentury.

Mexico especially loomed large in the imagination of U.S. tourists. It was a period when, as historian Mauricio Tenorio notes, Mexico was understood as a “Brown Atlantis” — where revolutionary thought fermented, and the Pan-American Highway promised access to exotic adventures. Everyone wanted to meet Frida Kahlo and visit Teotihuacán, all while dreaming up global politics anew.

Two brochures found in the Mexican ephemera collection tell how Mexico feted itself for an international community, including the crooning amphibian that would become the country’s unofficial mascot during the time.

The singing frogs of Taxco

First is a trifold brochure from arguably Mexico’s most famous nightclub during the second half of the 20th century — Cantarranas. However, the site didn’t always host the international glitterati.

Located in the silver-mining town of Taxco, roughly 2.5 hours outside of Mexico City, the estate was initially conceived in 1538 by Hernán Cortés, who ordered its construction so that he could extract the region’s precious materials.

Dubbed Hacienda Cantarranas, – literally “singing frogs” due to the loud chorus of frogs living in the nearby area – Cortés’ son Martín de Cortés oversaw its construction, which featured large stones along a hillside. Over the years, the infrastructure took its toll on the unstable land it was built on and was ultimately abandoned in favor of a new locale.

For the next four centuries, the site was nothing more than a derelict ghost of Mexico’s colonial past. That is, until one entrepreneur saw an opportunity.

Antonio “Tony” Reyes Ramírez, who would later become Taxco’s minister of tourism, officially opened Cantarranas in 1957. Eager to capitalize on its history, Reyes Ramírez kept the name and leaned on its playful imagery in his marketing materials.

Cantarranas quickly developed a global reputation as a lively hangout throughout the 1960s and 70s, and even featured prominently in a popular television show of the time.

The brochure for Catarranas promises tourists a night of “flamenco dancing by Estela Calderón,” “Carl Brice directly from Nassau, Bahamas,” “Primitive African Drums by the owner and Manager of Cantarranas Tony Reyes,” and “The Latin American Rhythms of the great pianist Juan García Esquivel.”

The nightclub also housed several distinct spaces, including the “Twilight Room,” the “Patio,” the “Flamenco Room” and the “Mulata Room.” Newspapers of the time reported that, inside Cantarranas, “the audience moves en masse from room to room as each show finishes.”

During that same decade, the brochure from Tulane notes that Cantarranas was chosen as the backdrop for an episode of the NBC series, “I Spy,” entitled “Return to Glory,” which aired Feb. 23, 1966.

In it, Alexander Scott – played by Bill Cosby – is tipped off by U.S. intelligence to visit Cantarranas, where he rendezvouses with the wife of a deposed president of an unnamed Latin American country. Famed Mexican actress Dolores del Río plays the part of the wife, as Cosby and costar Robert Culp try to negotiate the democratic leader’s return to his home nation.

Cantarranas’ popularity continued to grow throughout the early- to mid-1970s.

A newspaper article from 1974 lists several of the club’s attractions, including “Flying Indian Men,” a discotheque called “The Psychedelic Cave,” bullfighting lessons, a piñata party, and calypso songs by Carl Brice.

However, as a new decade dawned, Cantarranas was beginning to lose its luster.

An article from 1978 reported that “Cantarranas is a little rough around the edges.” Two years later, the club was described as “the kind of place that you wouldn’t miss if you missed it. But worth it if you’re utterly bored.”

Unable to sustain itself any longer, in 1983, the Mexican state of Guerrero acquired the property and converted it into a culinary school and arts center. In 1992, it changed hands once again, this time to the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México as a school for foreign nationals.

Despite its short life, Cantarranas heralded Mexico’s midcentury miracle as its nascent legacy was beginning to be forged.

The birth of Señor Frogs

Twelve years after Cantarranas opened, another Mexican restaurateur, Carlos Anderson, was cooking up a similar concept that would come to define the Mexican resort experience well into the 21st century – Señor Frog’s.

First opened in Mazatlan in 1969, Señor Frog’s capitalized on that same midcentury swagger, with waiters slinging tequila shots and cajoling spontaneous conga lines in a neon cave. It’s unclear why Señor Frog’s succeeded where Cantarranas ultimately failed, but it did.

It wasn’t just the nightclub scene, either. The Tulane collection includes another brochure with a singing frog on it — this one from Pemex or Petróleos Mexicanos, the company formed in 1938 by the Mexican government to sell the nation’s significant oil supply.

The brochure includes maps of Mexican highways and invites travelers to explore the best routes. There is no mention of Cantarranas, or Taxco, or even nightclubs. However, at this point the singing frog had become emblematic of Mexico’s exotic sights, electric nights and cultural spectacle.

From Hacienda Cantarranas to Tony Reyes’ “Singing Frogs” bar, through a national oil company and today’s Señor Frog’s franchises, the brochure in Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library chronicles the birth of a national symbol, while documenting how tourists were meant to imagine the delights of midcentury Mexico – strange, inviting and culturally savvy, not unlike a crooning amphibian.

Kevin M. Anzzolin earned a PhD in Romance Languages and Literatures from the University of Chicago. He is the author of “Guardians of Discourse: Literature and Journalism in Porfirian Mexico,” published by the University of Nebraska Press (2024), which received an Honorable Mention from LASA-Mexico for Best Book in the Humanities in 2025. He currently teaches language and literature courses at Christopher Newport University (Virginia, USA). He also publishes in more public fora.

World.title: Is Mexican-made kombucha underrated?
World.content:
There are few drinks in history with an eccentrically bubbly origin story like kombucha.

The fermented probiotic can be traced back to China around 221 B.C. during the Qin Dynasty, when it was consumed as a “remedy for immortality” by those who considered the yeasty, naturally carbonated black tea a source of long-lasting health and vitality.

The long history of kombucha

In 414 B.C., the Smithsonian reports, the cloudy beverage was imported to Japan by a Korean doctor named Kombu, in order to treat Emperor Inkyo. To further complicate its history, Japan already had its own form of kombucha, made from kombu (brown seaweed) and cha (tea).

According to Forbes, kombucha began to spread during the global trade expansion of the 20th century, when the fermented Chinese tea variety migrated into Europe, with Russia and Germany having adopted it as “kambucha” and “kombuchaschwamm,” respectively.

In 1955, Italian piano prodigy Renato Carosone delivered a hit single, “Stu Fungo Cinese!” (translated as “The Chinese Fungus!”), which was rooted in a Chinese mushroom infusion similar to kombucha.

The drink gained mainstream popularity in China during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s, with homebrews known as “Stomach Treasure” touted as digestive tonics.

Finally, in the 1990s, kombucha entered the North American market, largely thanks to major U.S. brands like GT’s Kombucha.

In the past decade, kombucha’s ubiquity — and value — has skyrocketed as one of the fastest-growing beverage markets on the continent. Now a mainstream supermarket item, North American kombucha sales generated revenue of US $2.1 billion in 2025, with revenues expected to top US $4 billion by 2033.

Of course, the United States accounts for much of the lion’s share. But a market study revealed that Mexico is predicted to have the continent’s largest compound annual growth rate for kombucha in the coming years.

So what has taken kombucha so long to work its magic in Mexico?

Mexico as a country of many beverages — except kombucha, until recently

In my personal recollection, the Eurasian style of kombucha was never plentiful in Mexico. As a child, I could get all sorts of aguas frescas, carbonated sodas and any flavored drinks imaginable. As I grew older, that evolved into other forms of consumption (micheladas, carajillos, etc.). But I have no memory of ever seeing kombucha on a restaurant menu, at a cafe or in mercados.

Here’s my theory: With all of the other beverages that are made in, and often native to, Mexico — including tepache, a naturally fermented pineapple drink — the craft of Asian and Western kombuchas couldn’t get a foothold. In a country where you can easily get tequila, mezcal, pulque, sugar cane aguardiente, rum, atole, arroz con leche and so much more on practically every corner in any pueblo (often made by someone in the neighborhood with generations of family knowledge, ancestral practices and native ingredients at their disposal), kombucha didn’t necessarily have much demand. I’ve watched señoras prepare natural tea remedies from flowers they’ve handpicked from their gardens. But getting offered kombucha inside someone’s home? Never.

It wasn’t until the mid-to-late 2010s that I started to notice kombucha — commercially and independently bottled — as a relatively more common option around Mexico.

Kombucha in Veracruz and other states in Mexico

Near my home in downtown Xalapa (a region known for its rich and deeply rooted coffee history), all of the new-school cafes now offer kombucha, with a noticeable amount of homebrewed and locally made brands available. While recently enjoying my neighborhood on foot, I popped into a few nearby cafes — touted for their espressos, flat whites and other caffeinated brews — and was excited to see artisanal kombucha on nearly every menu. I asked the owner of Marcelo whether she has noticed a rise in kombucha’s popularity and consumption; she confirmed that within the past five years (by her estimation) kombucha has exploded with trendiness across Mexico. She even started to experiment with brewing her own batches, but after failed attempts, opted to get her supply from LindaSol Fermentería, a micro-kombuchería located a few miles from her cafe in Xalapa.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by the pickle (@thepickleofbrighton)

My personal go-to is Agua Brava, made by the chef at Bravo Pizza, a small pizzeria that opened in Xalapa two years ago. Their kombucha flavors rotate weekly and are made in-house and bottled on-site. Among other favorites that I’ve found in Veracruz are Komboocha Puerto (from the port city of Veracruz), Dominga Kombucha (from Cholula, Puebla) and Naran Fermentos (from Xalapa). Mexico City, Guadalajara, San José del Cabo and other cities are no different, offering their own unique brands like Cali Kombucha in Baja California Sur. Data and testimonials suggest that kombucha first infiltrated Mexico’s market roughly a decade ago, when Mexican-owned brands like the aforementioned Cali Kombucha and Brew Lab from Oaxaca launched their brands around 2015 and 2016, respectively.

To highlight the Mexicanization of kombucha since then, “kombucherías” are now a thing in Mexico — as evidenced in the social media reel above, made by a British tourist tasting Oaxacan kombucha in Mazunte. Spoiler: It’s “banging.”

Kombucha a la mexicana: Basil jamaica, pineapple coconut, and more

Though you won’t casually walk past a kombuchería on every corner, you’re likely to encounter a local kombucha brewer in your neighborhood, who might directly sell unmarked jugs or labeled microbatches of their SCOBY-made (Symbiotic Culture Of Bacteria and Yeast) concoctions. You’ll also find it in most grocery markets with a cosmopolitan clientele, or in small businesses that are dedicated to holistic living and organic products.

Often, the flavors have a tropical Mexican vibe: maracuyá, tamarindo, coconut, mango. Some brands add additional ingredients like ancho chile peppers, jalapeño, honey or kiwi for an extra kick of spice, sweetness or tang. Puebla’s Domingo Kombucha has a killer guayaba option — subtly effervescent, fruity and mellow. Mexico City’s Umani offers canned options including orange turmeric, Mexican pepperleaf and fig. Bruja Sana from Yucatán emphasizes herbally minty options with green, earthy additions like romero and hierba buena.

Many of Mexico’s leading kombucha brands are independent, and offer or encourage other lifestyle supplements like yoga and Pilates classes, SCOBY workshops and more. It’s far from commercial profit and mass-made consumer-targeted sales; instead, kombucha offers a doorway into a wider range of health-centered practices and mindful consumption with regional flavor.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: New episode: ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast tackles expat money habits and mistakes
World.content:
Money affects everyone living in or traveling to Mexico. It is with that in mind that Mexico News Daily has launched a new weekly series called “Mexico and My Money.” You can read about the thinking behind the series here: Mexico and My Money: A new series MND on personal finance.

Our team recently conducted a survey of over 700 expats living in 25 states throughout Mexico about how they handle money while living in the country. The results were striking: Despite wariness of Mexican banks, 71% of respondents own a home in Mexico and nearly eight in 10 have made some kind of investment here — in real estate, a business, stocks or bonds. Nearly one in five respondents said they’d been victimized by a financial crime, with stories ranging from a landlord who kept a deposit “without cause” to a household employee who stole from a family over eight years. You can see the full results here: Mexico and My Money: What you told us about your personal finance habits and hang-ups.

In this week’s episode of “Confidently Wrong,” George and I dig into those results. We talk about banking in Mexico, cash and credit cards, the money mistakes expats wish they’d avoided. You will learn what are others doing differently and about best practices for money in Mexico. Check it out!

Confidently wrong about Mexico and my money: Episode 7 - Season 3

Watch this video on YouTube

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Hepatitis A Cases More Than Double in 2026
World.content:
COSTA RICA · HEALTHCARE

Key Facts — What happened Costa Rica has confirmed 772 hepatitis A cases in 2026, more than double last year’s total of 373.

— How big San José province alone accounts for 562 of those cases, about 73% of the nationwide total.

— What it means Health officials blame gaps in the water supply, since hepatitis A spreads through contaminated water and food.

— The catch Most patients are working-age adults aged 20 to 64, making up 601 of the 772 total cases.

— What comes next Health officials have stepped up surveillance in schools and food businesses while urging safer water use.

Hepatitis A cases in Costa Rica have more than doubled this year, with San José hit hardest.

San José, Costa Rica, where officials say gaps in the water supply are driving this year’s hepatitis A outbreak. Photo: “National Theatre of Costa Rica.jpg” by Richie Diesterheft derivative work: MrPanyGoff, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Costa Rica has confirmed 772 hepatitis A cases so far in 2026. That is more than double the 373 cases reported for all of last year, according to Infobae.

Health officials say most cases are clustered in the San José area. The capital province accounts for 562 of the total, or 73% of all cases nationwide.

San José at the Center of the Outbreak

San José is Costa Rica’s capital province, the country’s most populous region. Investigators say gaps in the local water supply are helping the virus spread there.

Health inspectors detected contamination in part of the water system in August. That finding supported the outbreak’s link to unsafe water, officials said.

The outbreak has touched several communities within San José province. Health teams have investigated cases across the capital area since August.

Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by a virus. It spreads mainly through contaminated water and food.

Costa Rica’s Ministry of Health has been tracking the outbreak since early 2026. The ministry updates its case count regularly as new tests confirm infections.

A similar outbreak in July 2023 involved just 13 confirmed cases at the time. This year’s total is many times larger already, health data show.

Working-Age Adults Make Up Most Cases

Most patients are working-age adults between 20 and 64 years old. That group makes up 601 of the 772 confirmed cases, health data show.

Health officials counted 111 cases among people aged 10 to 20. Just 26 cases involved children younger than 10, records show.

Older adults over 65 accounted for 31 cases. Just three infants under age one were affected, records show.

Common symptoms include fever, tiredness and stomach pain.

Jaundice is a yellowing of the skin and eyes. It can show up in more severe cases of the infection.

Teenagers and young adults face a higher risk of severe symptoms, officials say. Jaundice and other complications are more common in that age group.

How Health Officials Are Responding

Costa Rica’s health ministry is urging residents to boil water before drinking it. It also recommends washing hands often with soap and water.

Officials are also asking people to handle food carefully and clean surfaces regularly. Both steps can help stop the virus from spreading further.

The ministry has stepped up surveillance in schools across the province. It is also watching food businesses more closely for signs of contamination.

A vaccine against hepatitis A exists and is considered highly effective. It usually takes a few weeks to build full protection.

Public health experts say outbreaks like this one are preventable. Continued investment in clean water systems could stop future flare-ups, they say.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is causing Costa Rica’s hepatitis A outbreak?

Health officials point to gaps in the water supply in the San José area. Hepatitis A spreads mainly through contaminated water and food.

How many hepatitis A cases has Costa Rica reported in 2026?

Costa Rica has confirmed 772 cases so far in 2026. That is more than double the 373 cases reported for all of last year.

Who is most affected by the outbreak?

Most patients are working-age adults between 20 and 64 years old. That age group makes up 601 of the 772 confirmed cases.

Sources: Infobae, La Nación (Costa Rica), The Tico Times, Outbreak News Today, Delfino.cr, Costa Rica’s Ministry of Health (Ministerio de Salud), and The Rio Times Online.

World.title: Mexico Fines Elektra Over Celaya Carbon Monoxide Leak
World.content:
MEXICO · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Officials fined Mexican retailer Elektra 11,731 pesos (about US$690) after a July carbon monoxide leak.

— The scale A diesel generator running with no safety measures leaked gas inside one Celaya store, endangering customers and staff.

— What it means Local civil protection officers in Celaya penalized Elektra for running that generator without proper precautions.

— The catch Officials had warned of fines above 46,000 pesos (about US$2,700), but the final penalty came in far smaller.

— Where The store sits on Calle Morelos in Celaya, a manufacturing city in Guanajuato state, Mexico.

A leaking generator briefly shut down an Elektra store in Celaya, and the retailer has now paid a modest price.

An Elektra store front in Mexico, similar to the Celaya location fined over a safety lapse. Photo: “Torres corporativas Grupo Elektra.jpg” by Werther mx, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Elektra is a major Mexican retailer and consumer lender, part of Ricardo Salinas Pliego’s Grupo Salinas conglomerate. One of its stores sits on Calle Morelos, a busy commercial street in Celaya, a mid-sized manufacturing city in Guanajuato state.

On July 12, a diesel-powered generator at that store began leaking dangerous carbon monoxide gas. Local civil protection officers temporarily shut the store down until the danger was fully resolved.

A Generator Leak Forced a Temporary Closure

A customer visiting the store that Sunday reported the danger to local authorities, according to La Silla Rota. Civil protection officers arrived and found the generator running with no safety measures in place.

Both customers and employees were still inside the store when officials arrived on the scene. They said carbon monoxide levels inside had grown severe enough to cause serious harm.

The store’s manager initially refused to switch the generator off, saying he lacked the authority to do so. Civil protection staff disconnected the machine themselves and ordered everyone to evacuate.

Celaya had already seen a similar tragedy that year. An employee died in March after carbon monoxide poisoning tied to a generator at another downtown store, La Silla Rota reported.

The Elektra store reopened just days after the closure, according to the local newspaper Periódico Correo. It first had to meet civil protection’s safety requirements before resuming normal business.

A Small Fine, but Fresh Scrutiny

Celaya’s civil protection agency has now fined Elektra 11,731 pesos (about US$690) for the July safety lapse. Officials said the store had run its generator without the required precautions in place.

That penalty is far smaller than the fine officials floated back in July. They had warned at the time that violations like these could bring fines above 46,000 pesos (about US$2,700).

Even the larger figure would be a rounding error for a company the size of Grupo Salinas. Still, the case adds fresh scrutiny to Elektra’s workplace safety record in Mexico this year.

Grupo Elektra’s retail and financial service points now number more than 7,700 across Mexico and several neighboring countries in Latin America. Its retail arm sells appliances, electronics, furniture and phones to millions of shoppers.

Grupo Salinas also owns Banco Azteca, a lender that mostly serves middle- and lower-income customers. Neither Elektra nor Grupo Salinas has publicly commented on the Celaya fine so far.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened at Elektra’s store in Celaya?

A diesel generator at the store leaked dangerous carbon monoxide gas on July 12. Local officials shut the store temporarily until the danger passed.

How much was Elektra fined, and how does that compare to the warning?

Celaya’s civil protection agency fined Elektra 11,731 pesos (about US$690). Officials had earlier warned that fines could exceed 46,000 pesos (about US$2,700).

Is the Celaya store still closed?

No, the store reopened just days after the July shutdown. It resumed normal business once officials confirmed the danger was resolved.

Sources: Periódico Correo, La Silla Rota, El Sol del Bajío, Grupo Elektra (company reports), The Rio Times.

World.title: Chinese Automakers Reshape Chile’s Car Market
World.content:
CHILE · MARKETS

Key Facts — What happened Sport-utility vehicles (SUVs) made up 54.7% of new car sales in Chile through August this year.

— How big Chinese automaker BYD shipped 1,918 battery-electric and hybrid vehicles into Chile’s Port of San Antonio in one delivery.

— What it means Chinese brands have grabbed roughly a third of Chile’s car market this year, up sharply from a few years ago.

— The catch Despite that surge, plug-in electric vehicles still make up only about 6.5% of Chile’s total car market.

— What comes next Toyota remains Chile’s top-selling brand with 17,444 vehicles sold, and BYD alone expects over 10,000 more by year’s end.

SUVs, Chinese brands and new electric vehicles are reshaping Chile’s car market fast.

Sport-utility vehicles — SUVs — now dominate car lots across Chile. They made up 54.7% of new sales through August, Chile’s National Automotive Association (ANAC) says.

Chinese automaker BYD is riding the same wave. It shipped 1,918 battery-electric and hybrid vehicles into the Port of San Antonio in one August delivery.

Toyota Holds On as SUVs Take Over

Toyota remains Chile’s best-selling brand overall. It sold 17,444 vehicles between January and August this year.

The Toyota Hilux pickup truck is Chile’s top-selling single model, according to industry rankings. SUVs and trucks like it now make up more than half of all new car sales.

Chile’s overall new car market has been growing this year, industry tallies show. That growth has helped push SUV sales past half of the total.

SUV growth is not limited to compact crossovers. Bigger pickup trucks and mid-size crossovers are also part of the trend.

BYD’s Record Shipment Signals a Chinese Wave

BYD’s August delivery was one of the largest of its kind ever recorded in Chile. Diario Financiero called it the country’s biggest single shipment of electric and hybrid vehicles.

The vehicles arrived aboard the BYD Changzhou, a giant car-carrier making its first-ever call at a Chilean port. Diario Financiero and other outlets called the delivery a milestone for Chile’s car trade.

BYD expects to bring in more than 10,000 electric and hybrid vehicles by the end of this year. That would make it one of the fastest-growing brands in the country.

Chinese brands overall have captured roughly a third of Chile’s car market this year, The Rio Times has reported. That is a sharp jump from just a few years ago.

Industry rankings published this year show nine of Chile’s 20 best-selling car brands are now Chinese. That marks a sharp change from just a few years ago, according to the rankings.

Great Wall Motor — known as GWM — has broken into Chile’s top six automakers by sales. It now leads all Chinese brands in the country, rankings show.

Tesla’s growing presence is intensifying the competition too. Buyers now have more models, battery ranges and price points to choose from than before.

Electric Cars Still Have Room to Grow

Plug-in electric vehicles still make up only about 6.5% of Chile’s total car market. That leaves plenty of room to grow, industry watchers say.

ANAC’s newly published annual report confirms the pattern. It says electrification is accelerating quickly across Chile.

Plug-in models still remain a small slice of the market, it adds.

High prices remain the biggest barrier for many Chilean buyers. Limited government incentives make electric models a harder sell for many families.

Chile does offer some tax breaks for electric and hybrid buyers. Industry groups say those breaks are still too small to offset high sticker prices.

A still-small charging network adds to the challenge. Closing that gap will decide how fast electric cars spread across the country, analysts say.

Chile’s government has pledged to expand the charging network in the coming years. How quickly that happens will shape how fast electric cars catch on.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are SUVs so popular in Chile right now?

SUVs made up 54.7% of new car sales through August this year. Toyota’s Hilux pickup remains the country’s top-selling single model.

How much of Chile’s car market do Chinese brands control?

Chinese automakers have captured roughly a third of Chile’s car market this year. BYD alone shipped 1,918 vehicles into the Port of San Antonio in one August delivery.

Are electric cars catching on in Chile?

Plug-in electric vehicles still make up only about 6.5% of Chile’s car market. BYD expects to import more than 10,000 electric and hybrid vehicles by the end of this year.

What is holding back faster electric car adoption in Chile?

High prices, limited government incentives and a still-small charging network remain the biggest barriers. Closing those gaps will decide how quickly electric cars spread nationwide.

Sources: Chile’s National Automotive Association (ANAC), Diario Financiero, Publimicro, RutaMotor, Chile’s Ministry of Energy, The Rio Times.

World.title: Record Copper Prices Reshape Chile’s 2027 Budget
World.content:
CHILE · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Copper prices touched about US$6.60 a pound this week, a record rarely seen before now.

— The scale Mine troubles in Chile, Indonesia and Congo plus heavy stockpiling in the United States are tightening world supply.

— What it means Chile’s new 2027 budget still assumes a cautious average price of just US$5.37 a pound.

— The catch Despite record prices, state copper giant Codelco’s rising costs and falling output leave little spending room.

— Where it’s felt Every one-cent shift in copper’s yearly average price moves Chile’s government revenue by about US$60 million.

— What comes next Chile must submit its full 2027 budget by September 30, with spending growth capped at 1 percent.

A historic copper price rally is testing how much Chile’s government is willing to spend.

Codelco’s Chuquicamata mine in northern Chile, where record copper prices are reshaping the country’s budget math. Photo: “Mina de Chuquicamata, Calama, Chile, 2016-02-01, DD 121.JPG” by Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Copper prices touched about US$6.60 per pound this week, a level Chile has rarely seen before. For the world’s top copper producer, that record is reshaping budget talks in Santiago.

Chile’s government is not betting that today’s high prices will last. Its new 2027 budget assumes copper will average just US$5.37 per pound, a far more cautious estimate.

Chile mines more copper than any other country on Earth. Every big swing in the metal’s price ripples straight through the national budget.

Why Copper Keeps Climbing

Several mines have run into trouble this year, tightening world supply. Heavy rain shut down part of Chile’s Los Pelambres mine for weeks.

Escondida is the world’s largest copper mine. It is now pulling ore that holds less metal than before.

Mines in Indonesia and Congo have been slow to recover from accidents of their own. Those outages have squeezed global supply even further.

This year’s average copper price has run near US$6.00 per pound. That is up nearly 40 percent from a year earlier.

Not every demand signal points the same way. Chinese vehicle sales are a major source of copper demand worldwide.

Those sales fell more than 20 percent in July from a year earlier. That drop shows demand can soften even as supply stays tight.

In the United States, buyers have been stockpiling copper ahead of possible new import taxes. That extra buying has pushed prices even higher on top of the real shortage elsewhere.

A weaker US dollar has added fuel too. Softer inflation data has made copper cheaper for foreign buyers to purchase.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is adding to the squeeze too. Data centers built for AI use huge amounts of copper wiring for power and cooling.

A recent industry report says AI data centers could use about 400,000 tons of copper a year over the next decade. That demand could peak near 572,000 tons in 2028, the report found.

A Cautious Budget Despite the Windfall

Chile’s Budget Directorate sets a reference copper price each year to guide government spending. For 2027 it chose US$5.37 per pound, well below this week’s market price.

That is still higher than the US$4.38 per pound Chile used for its 2026 budget. Every one-cent shift in the yearly average price moves revenue by about US$60 million, mining group Núcleo Minero says.

A government advisory panel of economists helps set that reference price every year. They average forecasts spanning roughly a decade, smoothing out short bursts like this week’s rally.

Deputy Marco Antonio Sulantay says any extra money should first fix the state’s existing cash problems.

Chile has long saved part of its copper income for leaner years. That money sits in the Economic and Social Stabilization Fund, built during earlier copper booms.

Officials tap that fund when copper prices fall, instead of raising taxes or cutting programs. That saving habit is part of why officials are urging restraint now.

Economist Jaime Abedrepo says the extra money should patch budget gaps, not fund new programs. He argues there is little room to boost spending right now.

Not everyone in Santiago agrees with that caution. Some lawmakers want more of the copper windfall spent right away.

The Finance Ministry keeps resisting those calls.

Codelco Faces Four Difficult Years

Part of the caution comes from Codelco, Chile’s state-owned copper company. Its chairman says the company faces four difficult years ahead.

Production has fallen 16 percent over four years. Costs per ton have jumped 82 percent in that same time.

Codelco’s debt has also grown, up 50 percent over that period. That debt makes it hard to fund a planned US$34 billion investment program.

That investment plan is meant to open new ore deposits and replace aging mines. Without it, Codelco’s output could keep sliding even as demand for copper grows.

Investors are watching closely to see whether Codelco can deliver on that plan. A shortfall there would only add to the world’s copper squeeze.

What Chile Does Next

Chile must submit its full 2027 budget by September 30. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz has said spending growth will be capped at 1 percent.

The copper rally has already strengthened Chile’s peso against the US dollar. A firmer peso helps cool imported inflation, giving policymakers a little extra comfort.

The record copper price gives officials some breathing room either way. Leaders are choosing caution over a spending spree, at least for now.

Global demand for copper is unlikely to fade soon. Electric grids, data centers and factories all need more of the metal worldwide.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did copper prices reach a historic high?

Mine disruptions in Chile, Indonesia and Congo have tightened global supply. Fear of new United States import taxes is fueling heavy stockpiling, pushing prices even higher worldwide.

Why does Chile’s 2027 budget assume a lower copper price than the market?

Chile’s Budget Directorate always sets a cautious long-term price rather than today’s market price. For 2027 it chose US$5.37 per pound, well below this week’s roughly US$6.60 price.

Why does Codelco’s financial health matter for Chile’s budget?

Codelco is Chile’s state-owned copper company and the world’s largest copper producer. Its chairman says four straight years of falling output and rising costs leave little room for new spending.

How is artificial intelligence affecting copper demand?

A recent industry report says AI data centers could use about 400,000 tons of copper a year over the next decade. That demand could peak near 572,000 tons in 2028, the report found.

What happens next for Chile’s 2027 budget?

Chile must submit its full 2027 budget to Congress by September 30, 2026. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz has said spending growth will be capped at 1 percent.

Sources: Radio Maray, Chile’s Budget Directorate (Dipres), Núcleo Minero, Portal Innova, CNBC, Carbon Credits, The Rio Times.

World.title: Callao Armors Buses Against Extortion Attacks in Peru
World.content:
PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Bus company Corredor Rosado in Callao, next to Lima, is fitting steel cabins and bulletproof glass onto its buses.

— The scale Peru recorded 214 attacks on transport workers from August 2024 to May 2026, killing 152 people.

— The catch The armor project covers just one Callao bus route; extortion attacks keep killing drivers elsewhere in Peru.

— Who it affects Peru’s Public Ministry recorded 25 attacks on Callao transport workers between August 2024 and July 2026, killing nine drivers.

— What comes next Callao aims to armor all 50 buses by the end of 2026, split evenly between the city and bus consortium.

Callao is fitting city buses with steel cabins and bulletproof glass as extortion gangs keep killing transport workers across Peru.

A city bus like those on Callao’s Corredor Rosado route, now being fitted with armor. Photo: “E.T. Unidos Chama S.A., Lima, Peru. DOC-784.jpg” by KK70088, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Bus company Corredor Rosado is bolting steel cabins onto its fleet in Callao, next to Lima. The upgrade adds 21-millimeter glass that can stop bullets, La República reported.

Callao’s city government and the bus consortium are splitting the cost evenly. They aim to armor all 50 buses on this route by the end of 2026.

Steel Cabins and Bulletproof Glass

The steel cabins wrap around the driver’s seat for extra protection. Reinforced glass panels are built to survive gunfire at close range.

Some municipalities are negotiating lower “social cost” prices with armor companies. Officials say that discount could let more bus corridors afford similar upgrades.

Peru’s transit authority ATU (the Urban Transport Authority) launched Corredor Rosado to link Callao with Lima. Commuters use it daily to reach jobs and schools across both cities.

The corridor rolled out a new fleet of natural-gas buses in April 2026. The armor upgrade adds fresh protection to that same fleet, months later.

The buses will also carry satellite-tracked security cameras. Those cameras feed live video straight to Callao’s monitoring center.

City officials say that real-time link should speed up emergency response. Faster alerts could help police reach an attack scene sooner.

A Deadly Pattern Behind the Upgrade

Infobae reported 214 attacks on Peru’s transport workers from August 2024 to May 2026. Those attacks left 152 people dead and 131 injured nationwide.

Seventy-two of those deaths came in 2026 alone, Infobae reported. The toll has kept climbing even as some operators armor their fleets.

Peru’s Public Ministry handles criminal prosecutions nationwide. It recorded 25 attacks on Callao transport workers between August 2024 and July 2026.

Nine drivers or fare collectors died in those attacks. Prosecutors tied the killings to extortion gangs operating on the route.

Callao Mayor César Pérez said some bus companies now refuse to keep paying extortionists. “We need to give drivers peace of mind,” he told La República.

Transport unions have staged nationwide strikes more than once in 2026 over rising extortion demands. Drivers say gangs demand so-called “cupos” — cash payments to let buses keep running.

Peru’s government has repeatedly renewed a state of emergency across Lima and Callao this year. The latest 60-day extension began in late August to help police fight organized crime.

Other Lima Companies Arm Up Too

Other Lima bus operators aren’t waiting for city help. VIPUSA has armored about 70% of its fleet on its own, Infobae reported.

The company spends up to S/3,000 (about US$892) per bus. VIPUSA has absorbed that cost so far without raising fares.

Company officials have not ruled out a fare increase later, Infobae reported. One driver told Infobae that “our lives hang by a thread” in public transport.

VIPUSA began armoring buses after gunmen shot at one of its vehicles in Lima’s Puente Piedra district in April 2026. The attack killed a passenger and wounded others, La República reported.

Some VIPUSA drivers have said they are considering leaving Peru for Spain after death threats from extortionists. Infobae reported those threats in March 2026.

What Happens Next

Callao’s model splits the cost between city hall and the bus consortium. If cheaper “social cost” pricing spreads, more corridors could copy the approach.

For now, the 50-bus Callao fleet remains a pilot project. Peru’s wider extortion crisis against transport workers is far from solved.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Callao buses getting steel cabins and bulletproof glass?

Extortion gangs have repeatedly attacked drivers on the Corredor Rosado route. Callao’s government and the bus consortium are armoring buses to protect their crews.

How many buses will be armored, and by when?

Corredor Rosado plans to armor all 50 buses on its route. Callao’s government and the bus consortium aim to finish by the end of 2026.

How many transport workers have been attacked in Peru?

Infobae reported 214 attacks on Peru’s transport workers from August 2024 to May 2026. Those attacks killed 152 people and injured 131 others.

Are other bus companies in Lima also armoring their fleets?

Yes. Bus company VIPUSA has armored about 70% of its fleet on its own, spending up to S/3,000 (about US$892) per bus.

Sources: La República, Infobae Perú, El Comercio Perú.

World.title: Peru Funds Pope Leo XIV’s Homecoming Visit
World.content:
PERU · GOVERNMENT

Key Facts — What happened: Peru’s government transferred S/63.2 million (about US$18.8 million) to the Foreign Ministry to fund Pope Leo XIV’s visit.

— How big: He is scheduled to visit Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa from November 11 to 16, 2026.

— What it means: Leo XIV, the first American pope ever, also holds Peruvian citizenship and once led Chiclayo’s diocese.

— The catch: The decree limits the money to “goods and services” for the visit, barring any other use.

— Who it affects: The Chiclayo-area Mass alone is expected to draw more than one million pilgrims, regional officials say.

Peru is spending nearly US$19 million to welcome home the first American pope, who once served as bishop of Chiclayo.

Pope Leo XIV, born Robert Prevost, spent eight years as bishop of Chiclayo before his election as pope. Photo: “Pope Leo XIV 1.png” by ⁠Edgar Beltrán, The Pillar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Peru’s government has transferred S/63.2 million (about US$18.8 million) to the Foreign Ministry. The money will help pay for Pope Leo XIV’s first visit home to Peru.

Leo XIV is the first American pope in history. He also holds Peruvian citizenship and once served as bishop of Chiclayo.

A Bishop Peru Calls Its Own

He is scheduled to visit Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa. The trip runs from November 11 to 16, 2026.

Locals call him “the Peruvian pope” after two decades of pastoral work there. He spent eight of those years leading the Chiclayo diocese.

Leo XIV was born Robert Prevost in Chicago, in the United States. He later joined the Augustinian order and worked as a missionary in Peru.

Gulf News reported that many residents in Chiclayo still remember him fondly. They recall his years of pastoral work before he became pope.

The last pope to visit Peru was Francis, back in January 2018. Leo XIV’s return carries deep personal meaning for him.

The Vatican announced the trip on August 5, 2026. It forms part of a wider tour that also includes Uruguay and Argentina.

Lima Funds a Homecoming

The transfer was authorized under Supreme Decree 176-2026-EF, published in Peru’s official gazette. President Keiko Fujimori and Finance Minister Elmer Cuba signed the order.

It draws on the Finance Ministry’s contingency reserve, money set aside for unplanned costs. The decree limits spending to “goods and services” for the visit.

It bars officials from spending the money on anything else. The Foreign Ministry now has five days to detail the breakdown.

This follows an August decree naming the visit a matter of “national interest.” That order set up a high-level commission to coordinate security and transport.

The Foreign Ministry chairs the commission and also acts as its technical secretariat. It expedited customs clearance for equipment needed for the visit.

Officials estimate the visit could generate S/150 million (about US$44.7 million) in economic activity. That includes spending on hotels, restaurants, transport and local crafts.

Peru’s Catholic Church has also launched a national collection. It hopes to help cover the visit’s organizing costs.

Chiclayo Braces for a Record Crowd

The centerpiece Mass will be held outside Chiclayo, at Las Pampas de Pimentel. Regional officials expect more than one million pilgrims to attend.

Chiclayo’s diocese has scheduled the Mass for November 13 and 14. El Tiempo reported that authorities are deploying a special security plan for the crowds.

The Mass will center on the Cross of Motupe, a cross venerated across northern Peru. Devotees consider it one of the region’s most sacred images.

Francis drew large crowds during his 2018 visit to Lima and Puerto Maldonado. Organizers expect Leo XIV’s turnout to be even larger.

A closing Mass is planned for Lima before the pope returns to Rome. That service will close out his six days in the country.

Peru hopes the visit leaves a lasting legacy for religious tourism. Officials want Chiclayo to become an international pilgrimage destination, drawing on Leo XIV’s ties there.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much money did Peru allocate for Pope Leo XIV’s visit?

Peru’s government transferred S/63.2 million (about US$18.8 million) to the Foreign Ministry to fund the visit.

When is Pope Leo XIV visiting Peru, and which cities will he see?

He is scheduled to visit Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa from November 11 to 16, 2026.

Why is Chiclayo significant for Pope Leo XIV?

He served eight years as bishop of Chiclayo before his election as pope. Locals there call him “the Peruvian pope.”

What can Peru’s funds be spent on for the visit?

The decree limits the money to “goods and services” for organizing the visit. It bars officials from spending the funds on anything else.

Sources: Agencia Andina, El Comercio Perú, Infobae Perú, RPP Noticias, El Tiempo, CNN.

World.title: Colombia Risk Premium to Keep Falling, Skandia Says
World.content:
COLOMBIA · MARKETS

Key Facts — What happened: Skandia’s Manuel García says Colombia’s investor risk premium should keep falling in the coming months.

— How big: The cost of insuring Colombia’s bonds against default fell to about 141 points by mid-July, down from 232 in March.

— What it means: García credits the government’s new fiscal plan for restoring confidence and cutting borrowing costs nationwide.

— The catch: Even after that sharp drop, Colombia still costs more than Brazil to insure its debt against default.

— What comes next: Government bond yields near 12% to 13% should fall further and ease costs for borrowers.

A Skandia executive says Colombia’s shrinking risk premium points to cheaper borrowing for the government and private business alike.

Bogotá’s financial district, where analysts track the country’s borrowing costs. Photo: “Skyline downtown Bogota.jpg” by Tijs Zwinkels, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

A financial group in Colombia expects the country’s investor risk premium to keep falling in the months ahead. Manuel García leads wealth management at Skandia and made the call this week.

A risk premium is the extra return investors demand to hold a country’s debt. A lower premium usually means cheaper loans for governments and companies alike.

García credited the government’s fiscal plan for the falling risk premium. He said a credible plan lowers borrowing costs and draws in more private investment.

Colombia’s borrowing costs used to track Mexico’s and sit well below Brazil’s, García said. That pattern reversed recently, making Colombia look riskier than Brazil for a while.

Why the Risk Premium Keeps Falling

Colombia’s government debt equals about 60% of the size of its economy, García noted. Even so, he said the government’s shift toward market-friendly policy is reassuring investors.

The cost of insuring Colombia’s bonds against default fell to about 141 points by mid-July. That is down from a peak of 232 points in March, according to La República.

The decline picked up speed after Colombia’s first-round presidential vote on May 31. Analysts credited hopes for a market-friendly government, La República reported.

García said high government borrowing is also squeezing out loans for private companies. He said that effect matters more than the central bank’s interest rate.

Banco de Bogotá’s chief economist linked the rally to hopes for fiscal discipline. Markets wanted proof the new government would follow through on its promises.

Colombia Still Costs More Than Its Neighbors

Colombia’s borrowing costs remain the highest among major Latin American economies, Portafolio reported. The gap between Colombia and Brazil narrowed from 86 points in March to just 16 points by mid-July.

Analyst Diego Montañez said financial markets still see Colombia as comparatively risky today. He said Colombia’s risk score remains historically high, even after this year’s improvement.

Credit rater S&P (Standard & Poor’s) puts Colombia’s debt at BB-, just below its safest tier. Moody’s rates Colombia higher, with a stable outlook from both agencies.

David Cubides of Banco de Occidente said Colombia’s risk premium had been unusually high. Munir Jali of BTG Pactual urged the government to pursue cheaper loans from multilateral lenders.

García pointed to car makers as one sign private investment is returning. He said multinational automakers are again discussing plans to assemble cars in Colombia.

García expects Colombia’s bond yields to keep falling from today’s 12% to 13% range. Lower yields would help the government and private borrowers pay less to raise money.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a risk premium?

It is the extra return investors demand to hold a country’s debt instead of safer options. A lower premium usually lowers borrowing costs for governments and companies alike.

Why does Manuel García expect Colombia’s risk premium to keep falling?

García of Skandia says the government’s credible fiscal plan keeps winning over investors. He expects that confidence to keep pushing bond yields and borrowing costs down.

How does Colombia’s risk premium compare with Brazil’s?

Colombia has long paid more than Brazil to insure its debt against default. That gap has narrowed sharply in 2026, with Colombia still pricier than Brazil.

Sources: Valora Analitik, La República, Portafolio, S&P Global Ratings, Moody’s Investors Service.

World.title: Colombia Scraps Special Mining Districts to Lure Investors
World.content:
COLOMBIA · MINING

Key Facts — What happened: Colombia’s mining ministry eliminated all ten special mining districts created under the previous government since 2024.

— How big: The special districts had blanketed about 10% of Colombia’s national territory across 119 municipalities before this repeal.

— What it means: Foreign mining investment fell from US$1.5 billion in 2022 to just US$178 million by 2025.

— The catch: The repeal does not cancel any existing mining titles or mining applications already submitted for review.

— What comes next: Minister Arboleda says her ministry will cut red tape and move fast to show results.

Colombia scrapped all ten special mining districts set up in 2024, saying the zones drove investors away instead of protecting land.

An open-pit mine in La Guajira, one of Colombia’s biggest mining regions. Photo: “Cerrejón 3.jpg” by Tanenhaus, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Colombia’s mining ministry eliminated all ten special mining districts across the country earlier this month. The previous government had created the zones back in 2024 to manage mining nationwide under stricter environmental rules.

Mining Minister María Nohemí Arboleda announced the repeal on September 3 at Colombia’s National Mining Congress in Cartagena. She said the special districts scared off investors nationwide instead of protecting local land and mining communities.

Mining plays a major role in Colombia’s export economy and overall national income today. The country ranks among Latin America’s top coal and gold producers, with sizable nickel and emerald output too.

Investment Fell Sharply Under the Old Rules

The special districts once covered about 10% of Colombia’s national territory before this month’s repeal. They stretched across 119 municipalities in several regions nationwide, according to the mining ministry.

Arboleda said foreign mining investment collapsed sharply under the old system of special mining districts. It fell from US$1.5 billion in 2022 to just US$178 million by 2025, a drop of almost 88%.

Mining royalties also dropped 34% over that same three-year period from 2022 to 2025, the ministry said. Mining exports fell by about US$4 billion across those same three years, officials said.

Arboleda said the special districts were poorly designed from the very beginning, she told the congress. She said the rules ended up discouraging both small miners and large foreign investors alike.

No Existing Titles Are Being Cancelled

Arboleda stressed the repeal does not touch anyone’s existing mining rights anywhere in the country. No current mining titles or pending applications will be cancelled over this change, she said.

She said nobody in the mining sector should worry about this new decision. Nothing had actually been built inside the special districts before the repeal, she noted.

The mining ministry says the review took several months of technical study before this decision. It concluded the zones brought delays without adding real protection for local mining communities nationwide.

Ministry Vows Faster, Simpler Rules

Arboleda said her ministry will now cut back on regulatory paperwork across the mining sector. She told the mining congress she wants faster results without delay.

The head of Colombia’s Mining Association expects new investment of up to US$4 billion by 2030. That forecast depends on investors regaining confidence after years of falling mining investment nationwide.

President Gustavo Petro’s government first launched the special districts to shield local mining communities from unregulated activity. Critics said the rules instead pushed away the very investment those communities needed most for jobs and growth.

The mining ministry says further regulatory changes could follow in the coming months as it reviews the sector. It wants Colombia to compete better for global mining investment in the years ahead.
