World.title: The annual Delhi Yamuna flood threat- why September matters?
World.content:
A year after the Yamuna inundated large parts of Delhi, the river is again flowing above the danger mark. The immediate threat may be lower this time, but heavy rain in the upper catchment could quickly change the picture, exposing how vulnerable the cityâs floodplain still remains.

That vulnerability is built into Delhiâs geography. Every monsoon, as September sets in, the city watches the Yamuna closely because even a sharp rise in the river or a sudden surge in upstream discharge can quickly put thousands living and working along the floodplains at risk.

The danger mark at the Old Iron Railway Bridge is 205.33 metres, while evacuation of vulnerable residents begins when the river reaches around 206 metres.

On September 6, the Yamuna was flowing at 205.59 metres, already slightly above the danger mark.

And it is not just the people living along the river who feel the impact. When the Yamuna rises sharply, critical roads and infrastructure can also be affected. The Loha Pul, a vital link between Central Delhi (including Kashmere Gate and Old Delhi Railway Station) and East Delhi, is among the key crossings vulnerable to rising waters during severe floods.





2025: When the Yamuna broke its banks

Last year, the warning turned into a full-blown crisis.

The Yamuna crossed the danger mark and rose above 207 metres, inundating several low-lying parts of the Capital and forcing more than 10,000 people to evacuate vulnerable areas.

The warning numbers you should know

The impact extended well beyond flooded homes. Roads and public infrastructure were affected, electricity supplies were disrupted and houses were left covered in mud and silt after the water receded.

Thousands whose livelihoods depended on the floodplain also took a hit.

Floodwaters reached the Ring Road and Outer Ring Road, disrupting traffic between Majnu ka Tilla and the Salimgarh bypass. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi stopped cremations at Nigambodh Ghat and the Geeta Colony ground because of flooding. Water-treatment infrastructure was also affected.

A major factor was the enormous volume of water released from the Hathnikund Barrage in Haryana after intense rainfall in the upper Yamuna catchment.

2026: Is Delhi facing another repeat?

A year later, attention is once again turning to the Yamuna.

The monsoon remains active, with heavy rain reported in parts of Delhi and northern India. The immediate concern is not simply the riverâs current level, but how much water is being released upstream and whether intense rainfall in the catchment pushes those levels sharply higher.

The Yamuna has remained comparatively stable this year, despite crossing the danger mark.

2025 vs 2026 of Yamuna flood threat

Dr Shiv Singh Rawat, water expert and convener of the WalkForYamuna Campaign, said the difference becomes clearer when the upstream discharge is examined. âThis yearâs situation needs to be understood in its proper hydrological context. The maximum discharge released from Hathnikund Barrage during this year was around 64,000 cusecs, which is significantly below an extreme flood situation. That helps explain why Delhi experienced a much less severe river-flood situation than in 2025.

â

But that relative stability offers no guarantee.

The India Meteorological Department has warned of isolated heavy rainfall over Haryana, Chandigarh and Delhi from September 10-12.

Fairly widespread rain, accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning, is also likely over Uttarakhand from September 6-12, while rainfall disturbances are expected over Himachal Pradesh.

For Delhi, what happens upstream can matter as much as what happens within the Capital itself.

A spell of intense rainfall in the upper catchment can send a surge downstream, leaving communities along the floodplain with limited time to respond.

The flood threat does not end with the water level

The relatively stable Yamuna this year may have given Delhi a temporary reprieve, but the underlying vulnerability remains.

The floodplain is not simply vacant land beside the river.

It acts as a natural buffer during floods, helps recharge groundwater and performs an important ecological function.

Know how a Yamuna flood unfolds in Delhi

âThe 2-km-stretch on both sides of Yamuna acts as a buffer for floods, restores groundwater balance and acts as an organic filter. However, excess rain will create flooding in Delhi, and sanitation is not adequate to handle floods in the Capital,â says environmentalist Kavita Ashok.

Rawat warns that the greater danger could emerge gradually through construction and development. âThe concern is that areas outside the most restrictive floodplain zones could gradually become corridors for permanent construction, infrastructure and commercial riverfront activity,â he says.

âThat would undermine the very floodplain functions that protect the city.â

The question, therefore, is not only whether the Yamuna will rise this September. It is whether Delhi is becoming more or less vulnerable when it does.

Living with the Yamuna

For families living along Delhiâs floodplain, the monsoon is not simply a season of heavy rain. It is a recurring threat of displacement.

When the river rises, families may have to move their belongings, livestock and essentials to higher ground with little warning.

Delhi Yamuna Floodplain (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

The granddaughter of Ramu Sahni, who lives with his family near the Yamuna floodplain, told TOI that residents donât receive any advance warning.

âWe receive no warning on time. We see the rise in the water level of Yamuna and ourselves decide to shift to the roads with all our belongings. The authorities then notice the crowd on the roads and help us with tents.â

Sahni, who came to Delhi from Bihar in search of employment many years ago, says the relief arrangements have also changed.

âEarlier, they used to provide us with some ration and water in tents but now the situation has changed,â he says. âI donât live here for free, I pay rent.â

Houses built around Delhi Yamuna Floodplain (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

For many residents, simply relocating permanently is not an easy option.

Their lives are tied to the floodplain through work, transport, markets and social networks. When the water recedes, they return.

âWe return back here when the water recedes after 2 months. This is all we have. I run a rickshaw, we are mostly ragpickers. Where will we go?â

That cycle of evacuation, waiting, returning and rebuilding has become part of life for many families.

Animals: The overlooked victims

For families with livestock, evacuation is even more complicated.

Leaving home is one thing. Moving buffaloes, cattle, calves and other animals to safety is another. Stray animals are even more vulnerable, particularly when rising water cuts off their escape routes.

Buffaloes in the river | Fencing installed (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

Sahni says livestock is not simply property for floodplain families, it is their livelihood. âPeople usually take their buffaloes with them on the roads.

How will they earn? Now they have installed fencing around a small Yamuna pond here. How will buffaloes go there? They need to be there for survival. If a flood comes right now, there is no way we can rescue them immediately as there is only a small route to travel.â

When asked who rescues stray animals during floods, he had no clear answer.

PETA India told TOI that animals stranded during floods can face exhaustion, dehydration, hunger, injury and drowning, making rapid rescue and access to food, clean water and veterinary care critical.

âThe biggest challenge when trying to reach animals in emergency situations is getting to them in the first place. Access may be cut off by rising water, for instance,â said Sachin Bangera of PETA India.

During last yearâs floods, PETA Indiaâs Rapid Response Team arranged a boat to rescue dogs stranded in flooded areas and at risk of drowning.

âAnimals who are left chained are the most vulnerable because they cannot escape, or they become exhausted and drown,â Bangera said.

Aditi Bakshi, Animal Welfare Advocate and Specialist - Government and Public Policy at Mercy For Animals, says the problem goes deeper than rescue.

âMany people are forced into an impossible choice by a system that gives them no option. Rescue boats and relief camps do not take animals. When the administration tells a family to evacuate and will not let them bring their cow, their pigs, or their two goats, the family has to choose between their childrenâs safety and the animalâs life.â

She argues that flood preparedness must explicitly include animals.

According to Bakshi, Delhi lacks a comprehensive operational framework covering animal evacuation, including a nodal officer, mapped animal shelters, pre-monsoon fodder stocks, evacuation protocols for large animals and regular drills. âA plan that has never been drilled is not a plan; it is a document,â she says.

Delhiâs real test: Preparing before the next flood

For Delhiâs floodplain residents, the Yamuna may rise for only a few days.

The disruption can last months.

That makes flood preparedness about far more than issuing warnings once the river begins to rise.

âRelief must be immediate, but rehabilitation must be humane and sustainable. People should not have to repeatedly rebuild their lives every monsoon,â says Dr Heera Lal Patel, IAS.

During a flood emergency, he says, authorities need to provide clear information, accessible evacuation routes, transport and safe shelters.

Vulnerable families cannot be expected to organise an evacuation on their own.

Rawat argues that Delhi needs scientifically determined, risk-based floodplain zoning.

âThe real measures of success are: how many people are taken out of high-risk locations, flood-storage capacity restored and new encroachment prevented.â

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

For companion-animal guardians, PETA India recommends identifying safe locations where pets will be accepted, keeping an emergency kit ready, and ensuring animals are microchipped or wear collars with updated contact details.

But the larger challenge is institutional.

The Yamunaâs rise is predictable. The exact scale and timing of a flood may not be.

For communities living beside the river, that distinction can mean the difference between having time to evacuate and scrambling for safety as the water arrives.

And every September, Delhi faces the same question: when the Yamuna rises again, will the city be better prepared, or will thousands once again be forced to leave their lives behind?

World.title: 'We eradicated Naxalism, will eliminate narcotics': Amit Shah on drug-free India by 2029
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday said the Narendra Modi government has prepared a roadmap to make India drug-free by 2029, calling the fight against narcotics a national security priority.

Addressing the media, Shah stated that the fight against narcotics has moved beyond isolated actions to become a coordinated national campaign.

Shah said it was PM Modiâs objective that âdrug-free youth powerâ would lead India towards Viksit Bharat by 2047. He said the government was committed to tackling narcotics with the same approach it used against Naxalism and terrorism.

âBefore 2014, the fight against narcotics was largely conducted in small units and isolation,â Shah said, adding that agencies had often focused on catching small-time accused.

The government, he said, had now made the anti-narcotics fight a national security priority.

Detailing the approach Shah stated that the government has strengthened its anti-narcotics drive through NCORD, state anti-narcotics task forces and joint coordination between agencies, along with the MANAS helpline and a revamped NCB. It also created the NIDAN database of narcotics offenders and a nationwide data-driven map of drug hotspots and trafficking patterns.





The government now uses a âbottom-to-topâ and âtop-to-bottomâ reverse investigation model, tracing small drug seizures back to their source and large consignments forward to their intended users to uncover the wider network.

Shah also highlighted the governmentâs claims on internal security, saying terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir was declining and the sentiment of separatism had weakened since the abrogation of Article 370.

He said those who had envisioned a Maoist âred corridorâ from Tirupati to Pashupati had laid down arms and joined the mainstream, while more than 10,000 youths in the northeast had also surrendered their arms.

Shah said Naxalism, which had persisted for five decades, had become a thing of the past. âWe have eradicated Naxalism and will deal with menace of narcotics in the same manner,â he asserted.

World.title: ‘Every student’s life is precious’: Rahul Gandhi flags student housing crisis after deadly Delhi collapse
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress leader

on Sunday expressed grief over the building collapse in Delhiâs Satya Niketan, urging the NDRF, Delhi Fire Service and other rescue teams to make every possible effort to reach those trapped under the debris.

One person has died, two are in critical condition and several others are feared trapped following the collapse, officials said.

Rahul Gandhi, in a post on X, said: " The news of the building collapse in Satya Niketan, Delhi, is extremely heartbreaking and alarming. Reports indicate that several people are trapped under the debris, including many students from Delhi University. My appeal is that NDRF, Delhi Fire Service, and all rescue teams reach every single student by making every possible effort, ensuring that the injured receive the best possible immediate treatment, so that no effort is spared in saving anyone.

"

"Congress and NSUI workers are present at the scene and are ready to provide every possible assistance. In this hour of difficulty, we all stand with the victims and their families. Students' lives were already filled with strugglesânow the situation has turned life-threatening. Due to the lack of good hostels in colleges or universities, students are forced to live in PG accommodations, 40-40 at a time under one roof, in inhumane conditions.





Every student's life is precious, and their protection must be ensured under all circumstances," Rahul added.

A five-storey building being used as a boys' paying guest accommodation collapsed in the Satya Niketan area of South-West Delhi at around 1.30 pm on Sunday, triggering a major search and rescue operation in the densely populated neighbourhood near Delhi University's South Campus.

Officials said one person was killed in the collapse, while two others were critically injured.

Several people were initially feared trapped beneath the rubble as rescue personnel searched through the debris.

JCB machines were deployed at the site to clear the collapsed structure and assist emergency teams in reaching those who may have been trapped.

Delhi Police said the exact number of people trapped or injured was not immediately known. Multiple people were rescued and shifted to hospitals as the search operation continued.

The building, located in an area lined with student accommodations, paying guest facilities and eateries, collapsed along narrow and densely populated lanes, making rescue operations challenging.

Building was being used as PG

According to Delhi Police, a local enquiry found that the structure was around 40 to 50 years old and comprised a basement and five upper floors. It was being used as a PG accommodation.

"From the local enquiry, it came to knowledge that this was a 40â50-year-old building, comprising a basement and five upper floors, and it was used as a PG accommodation.

Repair work was underway in the basement when the incident occurred," the Delhi Police stated.

The Delhi Fire Department received an alert about the collapse at around 1.30 pm, following which emergency personnel and rescue teams were rushed to the site.

The rescue operation remained underway as teams continued to remove debris and search for survivors.

Congress demands immediate action

Congress leader Abhishek Dutt described the incident as deeply distressing and called for immediate assistance to the victims and their families.

âThe issue far more significant than the election itself is the manner in which children are losing their lives here and how buildings in Delhi keep collapsing like this,â Dutt told ANI.

He described the loss of lives as âdeeply tragicâ and called on the government to support the victims' families and take steps to prevent similar incidents.

âRight now, the focus must be on helping the children and their families,â he said.

Kejriwal calls collapse alarming

AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal also described the incident as "extremely tragic and alarming" and urged the Delhi government to take large-scale measures to improve public safety.

"The incident of the building collapse in Satya Niketan, Delhi, is extremely tragic and alarming. I pray to God that the people trapped in the debris are rescued safely and quickly. Due to the government's negligence in Delhi, many such accidents have already occurred.

The government must wake up from its slumber. There is a need to take large-scale action to ensure the safety of citizens."

AAP MP Atishi demanded urgent relief operations and a high-level inquiry into the collapse.

"The news of the building collapse at Satya Niketan in Delhi's Moti Bagh is extremely heartbreaking and alarming. The apprehension that several people, including students, are trapped under the debris is deeply distressing.

We appeal to the administration to carry out relief and rescue operations with utmost promptness and to safely extricate all those trapped under the rubble."

She added, "The government must conduct a high-level investigation into this incident and ensure strict action against those responsible for negligence, so that such painful tragedies can be prevented in the future."

AAP leader Saurabh Bharadwaj alleged that unchecked illegal construction and corruption had contributed to repeated building-related incidents in Delhi.

"Just a few days ago, you saw a four-story building collapse in Saket. It took the government and the MCD a whole week to admit it was a four-story building. Initially, they kept claiming it had only two floors... I am telling you about this case here as well. An illegal PG facility was operating in a four-story building... A basement was being illegally excavated there during the monsoon season," Bharadwaj told ANI.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

He further alleged lapses involving multiple departments, saying, "Unless you go beyond the 'small fish' and target the 'big crocodiles'âthe DC, the Commissioner, the one who was walking his dog in the stadium- this will keep happening...

Previously, only the MCD was taking bribes. But for the past year, the MCD, the Fire Department, and the SDM/DM departments have all been taking bribes."

AAP leader and former Delhi mayor Shelly Oberoi also criticised the Delhi government and the BJP-ruled Municipal Corporation of Delhi over alleged safety violations.

"Sometimes buildings are collapsing, sometimes fire incidents are shaking Delhi. The tragic accident in Satya Niketan is yet another proof of the BJP's dilapidated governance system and the failure of the BJP-ruled MCD. No action against illegal constructions, no adherence to safety rules, and no accountability either. Why should the people of Delhi pay the price for these accidents with their lives?"

World.content:
A five-storey building collapsed in Delhiâs Satya Niketan, killing one person and injuring three. Six people were rescued as several students were feared trapped under the debris.

Singapore minister K Shanmugam condemned racist online comments targeting Indians amid discussions over Nepal floods , calling them âshameful, nasty, totally unacceptableâ.

Here are the top news stories of the day:

Delhi building collapse leaves students feared trapped, rescue operation underway

A five-storey building collapsed near Shiv Mandir in Delhiâs Satya Niketan on Sunday afternoon, killing one person and critically injuring three others.

Six people have been rescued and taken to AIIMS Trauma Centre.

Several students living in PG accommodation are feared trapped. Delhi Fire Services, NDRF, police and other agencies are conducting rescue operations at the site.

Singapore minister condemns racist comments targeting Indians amid Nepal disaster

Singapore senior minister K Shanmugam condemned racist and xenophobic online comments targeting India amid discussions surrounding the Nepal disaster. He said police were investigating the comments and that Singaporeâs digital development ministry would approach social media platforms to remove posts violating their guidelines.

Shanmugam called the remarks âshameful, nasty, totally unacceptableâ.

How Iranian money still reaches US banks despite sanctions

A Wall Street Journal investigation found that about $9 billion in Iranian funds passed through US banks in 2024 despite sanctions. Iranian money can reach American lenders indirectly through foreign banks, shell companies and currency exchanges. Iran also uses oil transfers, Chinese yuan, cryptocurrency and financial networks in Hong Kong and Dubai to keep trade and payments flowing.

India backs UN map resolution while objecting to J&K depiction

India voted in favour of a UN General Assembly resolution promoting equal-area world map projections but clarified that it does not endorse any specific map. The MEA said Indiaâs sovereign territory, including Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted according to its official map. India said any inaccurate or misleading depiction of its territory is unacceptable.

Ganga crosses record flood level in Patna as Bihar flood impact widens

World.title: What does the law say about inheritance? Know your rights
World.content:
What can a daughter, wife, widow or mother legally claim?

Inheritance rights

Hindu women: Daughter has equal coparcenary rights

Vineeta Sharma

v Rakesh Sharma

Muslim women: Share depends on the family structure

Christian women: Sons and daughters inherit equally

Parsi women: Daughter does not lose out to son

What happens when there is no will

Inheritance rights of women in India.

What if there is a will â but the daughter gets nothing

Legal steps to challenge a will

How can one challenge an unfair will

What if a woman is denied her share in property

What if the family says she has already given up her share

stridhan

So, what is a womanâs share in family property

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

For generations, inheritance in India has been shaped by family relationships, religious personal laws and the nature of the property being inherited.A daughter may have an equal right with her brother in one situation, but not necessarily in another. A widow may be entitled to a share in her husband's estate, while a woman may also own property in her own right through inheritance, gifts or other means.The biggest question often arises when a person dies without leaving a will. In such cases, known as intestate succession, the applicable law determines who inherits and in what proportion. The rules differ across religious communities.The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, governs succession among Hindus and also applies to Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, subject to its provisions. Muslims are generally governed by Muslim personal law on intestate succession, while Christians and Parsis are principally covered by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.So what can a woman legally claim?One of the biggest changes in women's inheritance rights came with the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which made a daughter a coparcener by birth in a Hindu joint family governed by Mitakshara law, with the same rights and liabilities as a son.The Supreme Court's 2020 judgment inclarified that this right is by birth and does not depend on the father being alive when the 2005 amendment came into force.Marriage also does not take away a daughter's coparcenary rights.But an important distinction must be made between coparcenary property and a parent's self-acquired property.If a Hindu father dies intestate leaving behind his wife, son and daughter and the property is his self-acquired property, all children and the widow are Class I heirs. In a simple example involving Rs 1 crore, the wife, son and daughter would each receive about Rs 33.33 lakh.Advocate Rupali Jain explains why the calculation can be very different for coparcenary property. If the Rs 1 crore is Mitakshara coparcenary property, the father's notional share is first calculated. His share is then distributed among the relevant Class I heirs.On that calculation, Jain says, "wife receives about Rs 11.11 lakh and each child Rs 44.44 lakh."The example highlights an important point: a daughter is not automatically entitled to "half" the property simply because she is a daughter. The nature of the property must first be established.Another common misconception is that every property owned by a parent is ancestral property in which children have a birthright. That is not necessarily so.Muslim inheritance in India operates under Muslim personal law, which does not follow the same joint-family property model.Islamic inheritance rules identify different categories of heirs and prescribe shares depending on which relatives survive the deceased. The applicable school of Muslim law can also matter.The daughter will generally receive half the son's share but the actual calculation depends on all the surviving heirs.A widow's share also depends on whether the deceased leaves descendants. Broadly, under commonly applied Sunni rules, a widow receives one-eighth where there are children or certain descendants and one-fourth where there are none."The share of a Muslim woman therefore has to be calculated based on the complete family structure," said advocate Pritish Sunil Teckchandani.Muslim testamentary succession is also different. Generally, a Muslim's power to make a will is restricted to one-third of the estate without the consent of the heirs, subject to applicable personal-law rules.For Christians, intestate succession is primarily governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.Where a Christian man dies without a will leaving a widow and children, the widow receives one-third of the estate, while the remaining two-thirds goes equally to the children.For example, if a Christian man dies leaving a wife, one son and one daughter and an estate worth Rs 90 lakh, each would ordinarily receive Rs 30 lakh. "The widow and each child would ordinarily receive one-third each," said Teckchandani.The position changes depending on which relatives survive the deceased, but there is no distinction between sons and daughters in the straightforward situation described above.Unlike Hindu law, Christian succession has no equivalent concept of coparcenary rights by birth. A Christian daughter does not become a co-owner of her father's property merely because she is his daughter; her inheritance generally arises upon succession.Parsi intestate succession is governed by special provisions in Part V of the Indian Succession Act. The exact entitlement depends on the relatives who survive the deceased.Thus, where a Parsi man dies intestate leaving a widow, son and daughter, the son and daughter inherit on an equal footing under the applicable rules.The calculation can change where there are more children, a predeceased child, grandchildren or other specified relatives.When a person dies without a valid will, the property does not automatically go to the eldest son or the closest male relative. The applicable succession law determines who inherits.For Hindus, the Hindu Succession Act lays down a hierarchy of heirs. A widow, son, daughter and mother are among the Class I heirs of a Hindu man who dies intestate.For Muslims, inheritance is calculated under applicable Muslim personal-law rules rather than a Class I heir system.For Christians and Parsis, the relevant provisions of the Indian Succession Act apply.This is why there is no single formula for a woman's inheritance in India. Her share can depend on her religion, relationship to the deceased, the relatives who survive, the nature of the property and whether there is a valid will.âFor self-acquired property, a Hindu father can generally leave the entire property to his son and exclude his daughter through a valid Will. A daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter,â said Tekchandani.This is where the nature of the property becomes particularly important.A person can generally make a will determining how property that they legally own and can dispose of should be distributed. Therefore, a Hindu father can ordinarily leave his entire self-acquired property to his son and exclude his daughter."The daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter," said Teckchandani.But a will cannot simply wipe out another person's existing coparcenary interest. A daughter who already has a coparceny share cannot be deprived of that existing interest merely through her father's will."An unfair will is not necessarily an invalid will," explained Teckchandani. However, a woman can challenge a will if there are grounds to question its validity. These can include forgery, lack of testamentary capacity, coercion, undue influence, improper execution or other suspicious circumstances.Jain said courts may examine factors such as whether the testator was elderly, ill or dependent on the beneficiary, whether the beneficiary isolated the testator from other family members, whether there was a sudden departure from an earlier will, or whether the beneficiary was involved in preparing or executing the document."The person alleging coercion must produce credible evidence; mere suspicion or the fact that one child received substantially more property is generally insufficient," said Jain.Medical records, previous wills, messages, bank documents and testimony from doctors, neighbours, lawyers and attesting witnesses may become important evidence.The first step is to establish what the will says and what property it covers.A woman challenging a will should obtain the will, death certificate and relevant property documents. If probate or letters of administration proceedings are pending, she can enter the proceedings and raise objections."If probate proceedings are filed, enter appearance/file objections or a caveat, after which the proceeding becomes contentious," explained Jain.If no such proceedings are pending, the appropriate civil remedy will depend on the circumstances.The court can examine whether the will was properly executed and attested, whether the deceased had testamentary capacity and whether there was fraud, coercion, undue influence or another circumstance affecting its validity.The first step is to establish the property's ownership and character. Sale deeds, title documents, mutation records, partition deeds, gift or settlement deeds, wills and other records can help determine what a woman is actually entitled to.Depending on the dispute, a woman may approach a civil court seeking remedies such as partition and separate possession, declaration of rights, cancellation of an invalid document or an injunction.One of the biggest risks comes when family members ask a daughter to sign a release deed, relinquishment deed, family settlement, partition document or NOC without fully understanding its consequences."The biggest mistake is giving up legal rights informally in the name of maintaining family relations, without understanding the property's character or documenting the settlement," said Jain.A woman should determine whether the property is self-acquired, inherited or coparcenary, establish her legal share and obtain independent advice before signing away any interest.A daughter may be told that she has no claim because she is married, that her brother "needs the property", or that her share was already given to her through wedding expenses orWhether a woman has actually relinquished a property right depends on the applicable law and whether there is a legally valid document or transaction establishing that relinquishment."Family pressure can make people sign documents simply to avoid conflict, but such documents can have significant and sometimes irreversible consequences," said Teckchandani. A verbal family understanding and a legally valid relinquishment or settlement document are not necessarily the same thing.Well, there is no single answer to this question.For a Hindu woman, a daughter can have equal coparcenary rights with a son, while inheritance of self-acquired property after an intestate death follows a different calculation.For a Muslim woman, the share depends on the applicable personal law and the complete family structure. For Christian and Parsi women, succession is principally governed by the Indian Succession Act, with sons and daughters generally treated equally in the relevant intestate situations.A will can also change the outcome, particularly when it concerns property that the testator was free to dispose of. But a will that is unequal is not automatically invalid, nor can it simply extinguish an existing legal interest such as a coparcenary share.For women facing an inheritance dispute, the key questions are therefore: What personal law applies? Who survived the deceased? What kind of property is involved? Was there a valid will? Was the property already transferred or partitioned? And has the woman actually and legally relinquished her share?Knowing the answers to those questions is often the difference between walking away from property and successfully asserting a legal claim.

World.title: Police officer suspended for mishandling case to favour accused in Keralam’s Thiruvananthapuram
World.content:
A civil police officer attached to the Pettah police station in Thiruvananthapuram was placed under suspension on Sunday for allegedly mishandling a case relating to the assault of minor children at a city restaurant in order to allegedly favour the accused persons.

The suspended officer, identified as Zulfiqar, was found not to have issued arrest intimations to the relatives of the accused in the case that involved the assault of four minor children.

The incident reportedly took place on August 27 at a hotel where the students ordered a half ‘mandhi’. After being allegedly told by the restaurant staff that rice was available without limit, the children asked for a second serving. The request allegedly led to an altercation, following which the restaurant owner and employees allegedly assaulted the children.

Based on a complaint filed by the children’s parents, the police had taken the restaurant owner and two other employees into custody. However, the accused persons were granted bail on the same day owing to alleged procedural lapses in the arrest. As a result, the accused were able to avoid being remanded in custody.

The petitioners subsequently raised further complaints regarding the handling of the case.

The District Police Chief (Thiruvananthapuram City) ordered the suspension of the officer following an inquiry in view of the serious lapse in duty.

World.title: VMRDA fast-tracks second Kailasagiri ghat road
World.content:
A second ghat road to Kailasagiri, may finally take shape, with the Visakhapatnam Metropolitan Region Development Authority (VMRDA) preparing a proposal to ease traffic and parking congestion to the popular destination, which has a high tourist footfall particularly on weekends. Tenders for the proposed 1-kilometre alternative road, estimated to cost ₹3 crores, are expected to be finalised soon. The road will provide an additional route to hilltop and ease pressure on the existing road.

VMRDA In-charge Commissioner Ketan Garg, along with his team, recently inspected the 380-acre hilltop park.

“We can no longer afford to choke our prime tourist destination with a single-lane road. We inspected the site and reviewed the proposal for the second alternative road,” Mr. Garg said.

“The growing number of visitors, especially with the new attractions such as the cantilever glass bridge draws large crowds, calling for immediate additional infrastructural expansion. We are fast-tracking proposals to ease traffic congestion so visitors no longer have to sit for hours hours in traffic jams,” he said

Authorities have also mapped out three dedicated parking zones strategically spaced along the route from the base of the existing ghat road to the Telugu Museum.

The picturesque park, known for its panoramic views of the Bay of Bengal and the 40-foot Shiva-Parvati statue, often witnesses heavy traffic congestion on weekends. This congestion also affects the movement of emergency vehicles.

Speaking to The Hindu, VMRDA officials said that pressure from political leadership and frequent complaints from the commuters has forced the administration to fast-track the project.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

World.title: Newly-wed couple found dead in Sasthamcotta Lake in Keralam
World.content:
In what the police suspect to be a case of suicide, a young newly-wed couple was found dead in Sasthamcotta Lake near the Ambalakkadavu area here on Sunday (September 6, 2026). The deceased have been identified as Rajeev, 26, and Abhirami, 19.

Abhirami’s body was recovered first from the lake on Sunday morning. Shortly after, the Sasthamcotta Fire and Rescue team located Rajeev’s body approximately 50 metres away during their search operations. Investigators suspect that both individuals jumped into the lake during the early hours of Sunday.

The couple had married four months ago after being in a relationship, despite strong opposition from both their families. Following their marriage, they lived in a rented house and had no active contact with their relatives. Rajeev was employed as a cleaning staff member at a nearby school. The police had met with the couple last month to address family-related concerns.

Following autopsy, the bodies were handed over to the relatives. The Sasthamcotta police have registered a case and are investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

(Suicide prevention helpline: DISHA – 1056, 0471-2552056)

World.title: Bodies of three family members who jumped into Godavari retrieved
World.content:
Three bodies have been retrieved from the Godavari river near Badava village in West Godavari district on Sunday, a day after a family of four jumped into the river, prompting authorities to conduct search operations.

The deceased have been identified as Namuburu Srinivas, 45, his 16-year-old son, and 12-year-old daughter, while Srinivas’s wife Padmini, 42, survived the suicide bid as she was rescued by the fishermen immediately after she, along with her family members, jumped into the river.

Srinivas sold milk for a living, and his wife Padmini ran a pan shop from their residence in Tanuku, while their son and daughter were still studying.

Yelamanchili Sub-Inspector M. Raj Kumar told The Hindu that the family had resorted to the extreme step due to “financial struggles”, as cited in a suicide note recovered from their residence.

They had sold their house and gold jewellery to meet their financial needs and mortgaged a house site in Palakollu town, Mr. Kumar said.

The Sub-Inspector said the dead bodies have been handed over to their family after a post-mortem was performed at Palakollu government hospital.

Those struggling with suicidal tendencies can dial the West Godavari District Police at 9490401725.

World.title: Demand for government arts and science college in Tiruchengode grows louder
World.content:
Demand for a government arts and science college at Tiruchengode in Namakkal district has grown louder, with academicians making a case for it.

Tiruchengode is a prominent taluk in Namakkal district and has witnessed a remarkable boom of private higher secondary schools. It also has eight government higher secondary schools and a government-aided one.

The Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department-run Tiruchengode Arthanareeswarar Arts and Science College is unable to meet the demand for higher education as it offers only four courses.

Educationist K. Pandiyan said that since 1991, nine self-financing arts and science colleges have been established in and around Tiruchengode. These developments clearly demonstrate the strong and sustained demand for higher education in the area. Against this backdrop, it is both surprising and concerning that successive governments in the State have not taken meaningful steps to establish a government arts and science college in Tiruchengode, he said.

Equally disappointing is the failure of successive political representatives and leaders to take up this long-standing demand in a serious and sustained manner. There was, however, an attempt by Periyar University, Salem, in 2016-17 to establish a constituent college at Tiruchengode.

The episode raises a larger question: why has Tiruchengode been repeatedly denied a government arts and science college despite the region’s educational potential and growing demand? Mr. Pandiyan asked.

The Association of University Teachers (AUT) Tamil Nadu vice-president M.S. Balamurugan said there is a perception that the strong political and social influence of private educational interests in the region has stood in the way of a government arts and science college coming to Tiruchengode.

With the constituency now represented by Minister for Health K.G. Arunraj, a prominent Minister in the TVK-led government, time has come to break this long-standing deadlock. “After decades of waiting, the region deserves a government higher education institution that serves students from economically and socially disadvantaged sections and meets the growing educational needs of the area,” Mr. Balamurugan added.

When contacted, Tiruchengode MLA and Minister for Health K.G. Arunraj said that Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay has allocated ₹15 crore for constructing permanent buildings for the Tiruchengode Arthanareeswarar Arts and Science College and that steps will be taken to bring in this college all the UG courses available in government colleges.

World.title: Police search realtor’s home in Madanapalle over alleged land grab
World.content:
Police conducted searches at the residence of a woman, Koneti Sulochana, in Madanapalle in connection with an alleged land-grab case involving properties worth crores. The search lasted from Saturday evening till the early hours of Sunday.

The searches followed court orders after a public complaint that she, a local realtor and an associate of a former Minister, illegally grabbed land, the police said.

Teams led by Deputy Superintendent of Police (Madanapalle) Bucchiraju searched her house and her brother Srinivasulu’s house.

Nearly 50 documents and 15 bond papers allegedly bearing forged signatures were said to have been seized during the searches. The documents would be sent to the forensic lab for analysis, the police said.

Records reportedly show a building on 502 yards at Bandakammapalle locality worth ₹60 crore, as well as 1.75 acres at Ponnutipalyam in her name. It is alleged that 47 cents worth ₹10 crore were grabbed using a forged power of attorney and gifted in the name of the former Minister’s wife through the Madanapalle sub-registrar office on June 13, 2023.

The search was based on a warrant issued following a complaint by Marpu Venkatesh Naidu. Sulochana was not at home as she was in Vijayawada at the time of the search. The seizure list was handed to her children. Fourteen cases are pending against her in Madanapalle One Town and Taluk stations, the police said.

World.title: ‘How can my press conference damage India-Bangladesh relations? I am not so powerful,’ says Sheikh Hasina
World.content:
Defending her right to hold press conferences and meet her Awami League party colleagues while in India, Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina says she had no intention of damaging India-Bangladesh ties. In an interview to The Hindu, including in written replies and an extensive telephone conversation, Ms. Hasina, who has been convicted of murder and sentenced to death in Bangladesh, says she is undeterred from returning to Bangladesh, as she has already announced. She also says that if her party decides she should step down, she would.Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina

Excerpts from the interview:

What can you tell us about the events of August 5, 2024, when you fled from Dhaka? Life away from home is never easy. So, leaving the country was extremely painful for me. On August 5 (2024), I did not leave Bangladesh by choice. When I heard that Tarique (Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman) had instructed his leaders that they needed [more human casualties] to topple the government, I realised that killing people had become their main objective. I did not want bloodshed. They were killing people indiscriminately and putting the blame on us. On July 18 (2024), I formed a Judicial Inquiry Commission to investigate the killings. I visited hospitals to see the victims. I met families who had lost their loved ones between July 15 and August 1 (2024). I offered condolences, gave assistance, and provided compensation to the families. I also strengthened the inquiry process by reorganising the Commission with three judges of the High Court. But the violence did not stop. The situation continued to worsen. Police officers were being killed. Police stations were attacked and looted. Government properties and the houses of Awami League leaders were burned. At that moment, the situation around me deteriorated very quickly. My security personnel, party leaders, and family members urged me to leave the Prime Minister’s residence. Their intention [on] that day was to kill me and my sister. Now they themselves are admitting those intentions. I was prepared to go to Tungipara (Ms. Hasina’s hometown), and I had expressed my willingness to leave and resign as Prime Minister. But I didn’t get the chance to resign. I did not even know that I was leaving the country. Only when I was in the helicopter did I learn from my staff that I was being taken to India. I said, “What?” I had no idea that was what they had planned, but they said they did it to keep me safe. India received me on very short notice and made arrangements for my security and stay. I am grateful for that. But it was very hard for me to accept that I had been taken out of my own country. They have tried to eliminate me several times, but I survived. This time too, I survived. Because of that, I can still speak to my people, to those who are suffering, to those who have lost family members, and to those who have been injured by the atrocities of the BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) and Jamaat (Jamaat-e-Islami). I believe it is because of the wishes of the people, and by the will of Allah, that I survived this attempt as well.

When you reached Delhi on August 5, did you intend to stay in India, or was there a plan for you to travel elsewhere? Have you applied for asylum or visas in any other country? No, I did not want to go anywhere else. I am next door to my country, as close as I can be to my people. From here, I can keep in touch with them. Where else would I go? How would I live somewhere else? I do not have any means to live abroad permanently. When my family was assassinated in 1975, I was in Germany. Mrs. [Indira] Gandhi called me and said I should come and stay in India. Then, in 1981, when I had taken shelter in India for six years, even then, [President] Gen Ziaur Rahman did not want me to return, but I did. In 2007 as well, the caretaker government didn’t want me to return, arrested me, but I went back anyway. So, I will go back again.

What about reports that you asked to travel to the U.S. and the U.K., or to a Gulf country? No, no that isn’t true. Why would I go anywhere else?

Given your personal equations with them, have you met Prime Minister Narendra Modi, or Mrs. Sonia Gandhi during your time here? Frankly, I did not want to try to meet them, given the circumstances. No doubt, I have good relations with them, but I decided I would only meet my party workers and relatives while here. Maybe a time will come when I will go home and then come again to India, and then meet everyone, including media (laughs).

Has any specific date, route or entry point been decided? Will other Awami League leaders return with you? Will there be any discussion with the Bangladesh government before your return? I will tell that in due time.

Are you sure the Bangladesh government will allow you to go back, and not stop you at the border? This is a peculiar situation. They repeatedly ask the Indian government to send me to Bangladesh [to face her sentence], but when I say they don’t need to send me, I will come myself, then that also seems to be a problem for them.

The Bangladesh government says your recent press conference (on August 5, 2026) has damaged the atmosphere for India-Bangladesh relations. Do you think your public remarks are affecting bilateral ties? When I heard this, I was surprised. How can a press conference damage India-Bangladesh relations? I did not know that I was so powerful that one press conference of mine could damage Bangladesh’s foreign policy. In 2007, Tarique Rahman gave a written undertaking that he would never engage in politics. But when he was in London and took up the BNP leadership, he gave online speeches, held video conferences and spoke at press conferences. Did my government write to the British government raising this issue? No. We did not ask another country to silence him. My intention was never to damage anything. I wanted to tell the truth. Freedom of speech and expression is part of democracy. But since Muhammad Yunus took power illegally, and after the sham elections of 2026, freedom of speech and expression has not merely declined, it has been destroyed. Since August 2024, 50 media houses have been vandalised or set on fire. Thirteen journalists have been killed, 38 journalists have been jailed, and more than 300 journalists face cases, including murder cases. So, the real question is not whether my press conference damaged relations. The real question is why truth and free speech are being feared so much.

In your time as PM, you also did ban the Jamaat-e-Islami. Was that a mistake? They are now the main Opposition in the country... Jamaat-e-Islami members were war criminals — they worked with the Pakistani army during the occupation; they were convicted of rape, murder and genocide. That is why they were banned. But later, they would be part of coalitions with other parties. In 2013, the courts cancelled their registration, and they could not stand for elections.

All that was years ago. Today, even the Indian High Commission and India’s Foreign Secretary (Vikram Misri) meets with them… If that is so, I have no comment on that.

Has the Indian government conveyed to you that you should not hold any more press conferences? What kind of support do you expect from India and the international community? It is important for the world to understand what Bangladesh is going through today. The largest political party, the party that brought independence to Bangladesh, has been banned. Political prisoners, detained in false cases, are being kept in horrible conditions. Today, bail is denied to most Awami League leaders. War criminals sit in Parliament. Freedom of speech is gone. My demands are simple. I ask the international community to support the lifting of the ban on the Awami League, the release of political detainees, the withdrawal of false cases, the safety and security of every citizen, especially women and girl children, freedom of movement, and freedom of speech and expression.

If the Bangladesh government were to revoke the ban on the Awami League on the condition that you step down as President, would you agree? Awami League is the only party in Bangladesh that works according to a Constitution. It is the party that decides who will be the leader. I was made President when I was in exile in India in 1981, when the party councillors decided that. I am prepared to step down, but who is the government or the BNP to decide who will lead the Awami League?

Has the government placed any restrictions or asked you not to hold more press conferences? I ask because, recently, on August 31, the police cancelled another event in Delhi where Awami League leaders were due to attend a conference. There was some misunderstanding over that event. Awami League was not involved in it.

Hundreds were killed during July-August 2024. It is alleged that these deaths occurred during police action ordered by you. Do you accept personal responsibility? Would you apologise to the families of those who died? When police are working in the field, how can they contact the Prime Minister for every action? Police operate under standard operating procedures. They are trained to handle emergencies, crowd control and violent situations. When police personnel were attacked and killed, and police stations were set on fire, they responded according to the situation. How could I personally order officers in those circumstances? Nearly 10,000 of our party workers have been killed, forcibly disappeared, or had their houses burned and vandalised. On July 16, Chhatra League leader Sabuj Ali was killed. Since then, our workers have been killed or arrested every day. Police personnel, journalists, cultural activists, freedom fighters, teachers, students, lawyers, judges, Awami League leaders and workers were targeted. Public buildings were destroyed and houses were burned. Have they apologised? No. They were given indemnity by Muhammad Yunus. The vandals have also publicly accepted that without burning down metro stations and killing police personnel, the movement would not have succeeded. So, who should apologise? I left the country on August 5. My people have faced brutal persecution since then. Who bears responsibility for that? Even now, the killings have not stopped. Women and children are tortured and raped in front of their family members, and videos are shared. Victims are not allowed to lodge complaints at police stations. Police stations also do not accept FIRs (First Information Reports) from Awami League workers. During the interim government, orders were given for arrests without cause. Murder cases and cases under the Explosives Act are filed so that bail cannot be obtained.

You refer to ‘them’ and to ‘my’ people. But you were PM for 15 years — aren’t all Bangladeshis your people? Many young protestors said they felt alienated when you called them ‘Razakars’… When I say my people, I mean my party workers — more than six lakh have had cases filed against them; so many have been arrested or harassed, tortured in jail without any legal procedures being followed. How can I forget them? Of course, the common people are all my people.

Do you still believe that U.S. agencies or foreign powers played a role in your ouster? In the context of your earlier remarks on St. Martin’s Island, what is your position now? When Muhammad Yunus went to the United Nations in September 2024, he attended a programme hosted by the Clinton Foundation. There, he proudly said that what happened in Bangladesh was not a spontaneous student protest, but a meticulously designed plan led by a mastermind. The so-called mastermind later also clarified in a news interview that the movement was not a student movement, but a movement to overthrow the government. Those words are important. They confirm what I had been saying: this was not an ordinary student protest. The Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean routes are peaceful and non-controversial routes. They are among the busiest routes for maritime trade and commerce. They have remained peaceful for a long time, and they should remain so. Bangladesh is a sovereign, independent country, and it must remain so. Our land, sea, islands and resources must serve the interests of the people of Bangladesh. Bangladesh must not become a field for geopolitical competition.

World.title: Students visit Devipattinam coastal police station ahead of police commemoration day
World.content:
Over a hundred students of Sri Vivekananda Matriculation Higher Secondary School visited the Devipattinam Coastal Police Station as part of an outreach initiative ahead of Police Commemoration Day.

The visit was organised under the orders of Coastal Security Group Superintendent of Police Rohit Nathan Rajagopal and the guidance of Additional Superintendent of Police Balakrishnan. It was led by Rameswaram Coastal Security Group Inspector V. Jhansirani.

During the visit, Ms. Jhansirani briefed the students on the functions and operations of the Coastal Security Group and demonstrated the safety gear and specialised equipment used during maritime police duties.

The interactive session also focused on creating security awareness among the students.

More than 100 students, accompanied by the school Principal Deenadayal and faculty members, participated in the programme. Sub-Inspector of the Coastal Police Station, Ayyanar, and Intelligence Wing Head Constable Saravanapandi were also present.

World.title: KP CM determined to hold Karachi rally as PTI convoy reaches Hyderabad
World.content:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi reached Hyderabad on Sunday and voiced his determination to hold his planned rally in Karachi as he alleged hurdles were being created in his convoy’s journey.

The KP CM, accompanied by PTI’s provincial President Junaid Akbar, has been on a five-day public mobilisation campaign in Sindh for the party’s September 27 nationwide protest for the release of its founder Imran Khan and his immediate medical treatment at Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital.

The PTI confirmed shortly after 5:30pm that the central leadership’s convoy led by CM Afridi had entered Hyderabad district.

Earlier, on his way to Hyderabad, Afridi addressed PTI workers in Tando Allahyar.

While thanking PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari for welcoming him to Sindh on social media, Afridi alleged that hurdles were being created for his convoy.

“My message for Bilawal Bhutto is that obstructions are being raised in our way,” the KP CM said, affirming that people were still with PTI despite those hurdles.

“Containers are being placed and craters are being dug,” he claimed.

“Is this being done by your [PPP] government or by someone else?” Afridi asked. “Will they host their guests in this manner?” he added.

The PTI leader urged party supporters and workers to join the planned September 27 rallies across the country.

In a video shared on X, CM Afridi said that it was “possible they might have created some hurdles in the way”, but the party convoy would defy them to reach Hyderabad, and then finally Karachi.

Thanking the people from Umerkot for their support yesterday, the PTI leader also asked the people of Hyderabad to be prepared for the PTI caravan.

“After Hyderabad, we will be in Karachi by the evening,” the KP CM declared.

‘No rallies allowed’

Karachi’s District East police, in a statement, said that “no public gatherings, rallies or processions will be allowed around Mazar-i-Quaid”, located at Shahrah-i-Quaideen, where the PTI has planned its rally.

“If any gathering is held despite the lack of permission, legal action will be taken in accordance with the law,” it warned.

Security arrangements at Mazar-i-Quaid had been “further strengthened in view of the current threat situation”, the police statement added, noting the deployment of additional police personnel.

“Surveillance at the entry and exit points of Mazar-i-Quaid has also been further tightened.”

Meanwhile, the Karachi Traffic Police detailed that some routes around Mazar-i-Quaid had been closed to vehicles.

As of 6pm, the traffic police said the both sides of Shahrah-i-Quaideen had been closed for traffic for “security”.

Routes blocked near Mazar-i-Quaid as of around 7pm on Sept 6, 2026. — screengrab via Google Maps

As an alternative, traffic from Noorani Chowrangi was being diverted towards Khalid Bin Waleed Road, while traffic approaching Allah Wali Chowrangi was being diverted towards Tariq Road.

Shortly after 4pm, New MA Jinnah Road and the road near the Corridor-III parking plaza towards PP Chowrangi and Jail Chowrangi had been closed to traffic from both sides for security.

Traffic was being diverted from Saddar Dawakhana towards the Star Gate side, while traffic from Jail Chowrangi was being diverted towards Kashmir Road and Tariq Road.

In a statement, the PTI condemned the alleged blocking of its caravan travelling from Hyderabad to Karachi and also claimed its party workers in multiple cities of Sindh had been taken into custody.

The statement marked a turn from Saturday’s cordial exchange on social media between CM Afridi and Bilawal.

“On the one hand, Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari welcomes Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and PTI’s visit to Sindh on social media; on the other hand, the Sindh government, under his influence, is using the police to block roads and arrest PTI workers,” the PTI said.

It termed the alleged actions a “manifestation of the PPP’s blatant political hypocrisy and fear”. “If the PPP truly believes in democracy and political freedom, then why is it so afraid of a peaceful PTI political rally?” PTI asked.

PTI asserted that the police deployments, barriers and arrests could not prevent its party workers and the people of Sindh from exercising their political rights.

“The PTI leadership made it clear that the people of Sindh are not slaves to feudal or dynastic politics. They have the right to welcome leaders of the political party of their choice, voice their concerns and express their political opinion,” the party maintained.

It demanded that the PPP chairman direct his Sindh government to ensure “political freedom in practice”.

“If the welcome is limited to Twitter while police arrest workers on the ground, this is not democracy but political theatrics.”

The party also demanded the immediate release of all workers allegedly taken into custody in Hyderabad, Karachi and other parts of Sindh, as well as an end to any obstruction to the PTI’s political activities.

PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh, who was accompanying the KP CM, shared a video of him driving a truck, which he claimed was placed to block his convoy’s route in Tando Allahyar.

Sheikh later shared videos of what he described as the people of Hyderabad welcoming the PTI convoy.

‘Politics of tolerance’

On Saturday night, Afridi thanked Bilawal after the latter wished him the best for the rest of his visit to Sindh.

In a post on X, the PPP leader welcomed Afridi to the “city of martyrs” after the KP chief minister reached Larkana.

“Best wishes for the remainder of your tour across Sindh. We must ultimately return to a politics of tolerance, respect and coexistence, the foundation of any democracy,” Bilawal wrote.

In response, Afridi thanked him and noted that the “beauty of democracy is in freedom of politics and expression, independence of judiciary, acceptance of public mandate, an independent parliament and press being free”.

He also expressed hope that a large crowd would come out on the PTI’s call in Karachi and Hyderabad, where he is due today.

Last time Afridi was in Sindh to mobilise people for a street movement, he had initially praised the PPP-led Sindh government’s reception, saying the democratic legacy of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and Benazir Bhutto still thrived in the province. However, he had later accused the Sindh government of not upholding the honour of the ajrak and topi and criticised its treatment of its “guests”.

Ahead of Afridi’s rally in Karachi on January 11, the party had alleged that the KP CM had to face obstacles on his way to the metropolis. The party also accused the authorities of violence against its workers and supporters.

World.title: FO condemns mosque demolition in India's Uttar Pradesh, terms it part of 'drive to erase Islamic heritage'
World.content:
Pakistan on Sunday condemned the demolition of a century-old mosque in India’s Uttar Pradesh, describing it as part of an “Islamophobic and Hindutva-driven campaign to erase the Islamic heritage” in the country.

Responding to media queries regarding the demolition, Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan condemned the move and described it as “a reprehensible action against a historic Islamic place of worship”.

He recalled that the demolition of the Babri Mosque in 1992 was an “enduring symbol of this ideology of religious intolerance, prejudice and hatred”.

“Pakistan calls upon the international community to take immediate cognisance of the systematic persecution of Muslims by Indian authorities,” the statement said, highlighting the “continued desecration and destruction of their places of worship under state patronage”.

Khan called for accountability of Indian authorities for actions against the religious freedom and cultural heritage of all minorities, particularly Muslims.

According to The Indian Express, the mosque, which was located inside a Collectorate in Saharanpur, was demolished a day earlier.

The demolition came three days after a district court had dismissed an appeal against an order holding that the structure stood on government land and was unauthorised.

The September 2 order did not itself mention demolition.

The Indian Express quoted mosque staff member Tanveer Ahmed as saying that the order was for eviction, not demolition. He claimed the mosque was around 150 years old, and maintained that the land was recorded in their names.

All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen president and Hyderabad lawmaker Asaduddin Owaisi condemned the demolition and questioned whether the constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion applied to Muslims, NDTV reported.

According to Owaisi, the mosque dated back to 1911, claiming that the Collectorate itself was constructed later.

In 2024, the Akhonji mosque, which was over 600 years old, was razed to the ground without any prior notice in Delhi’s Mehrauli district. In 1992, a Hindu mob destroyed the famous Babri mosque, triggering riots that killed about 2,000 people across India, most of them Muslims.

World.title: Dar, Saudi and Turkish FMs follow up on understandings reached in first Makkah Defence Alliance meeting: FO
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar held phone calls with Saudi Arabian and Turkish foreign ministers on Sunday and followed up on the understandings reached at the inaugural meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance last month, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

The joint defence pact was signed on August 7 and empowers the member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Its inaugural meeting was held on August 31 in Istanbul, where it was decided that the alliance’s secretariat would be initially headed by Pakistan for three years.

The three countries also agreed to work towards strengthening their defence capabilities and the cohesion of their armed forces through joint activities, robust defence industry cooperation, and joint technology development and production. Moreover, through the institutionalised and resolute implementation of the Makkah agreement, the three countries also agreed to provide essential contributions to regional peace and stability.

In a series of posts on social media platform X, FO said that DPM Dar held separate phone calls with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal Bin Farhan and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Sunday.

In the call with the Saudi FM, the two leaders discussed regional and international developments, including matters of mutual interest at multilateral fora.

“They also discussed follow-up on the understandings reached at the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee of the Makkah Defence Alliance, held in Istanbul, and agreed to remain in close contact,” FO said.

In a separate post, FO said that Dar also spoke to Fidan and thanked him for hosting the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Istanbul.

FO said the two leaders followed up on understandings reached and discussed ways to further advance cooperation under the framework.

“The two foreign ministers also exchanged views on regional and international developments. They also discussed matters of mutual interest and opportunities to further strengthen cooperation at multilateral fora,” FO added.

The tripartite agreement was signed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during a summit at Al-Safa Palace.

Pakistan has said that the pact is “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. And while Turkiye has said that there is a possibility of Egypt joining the pact, there has been no confirmation from Cairo.

Abdelatty invites Dar

Earlier in the day, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty invited DPM Dar to visit his country, FO said.

A statement issued by the FO said that the two held a telephone call in which they exchanged views on Egypt-Pakistan bilateral relations and regional and international developments.

Abdelatty invited Dar to “hold a bilateral visit to Egypt at his earliest convenience”, it added.

They also reaffirmed their commitment to remaining “engaged and involved” on regional security matters, agreeing to meet on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) this month.

Last November, the Egyptian foreign minister undertook an official two-day visit to Pakistan at DPM Dar’s invitation.

During the visit, he met Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, where the two discussed “defence and security cooperation, military exchanges, training collaborations and regional peace and stability”, FO said at the time. Abdelatty also met President Asif Ali Zardari during the visit.

Pakistan and Egypt are also members of a quadrilateral regional alliance known as the R-4 Group (Regional Four), an arrangement which also includes Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. The R-4 group has been focused on regional security and emerged in March amid mediation efforts between the US and Iran.

World.title: Pakistan dispatches humanitarian aid to Nepal after deadly floods, landslides
World.content:
Pakistan on Sunday dispatched 100 tonnes of humanitarian assistance to Nepal to support relief efforts following the recent deadly floods and landslides.

The glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,384 people and left more than 5,500 missing across the two countries. In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,341 bodies, while around 4,996 people remain missing.

The humanitarian aid from Pakistan was coordinated by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and sent by a chartered flight from Islamabad to Kathmandu, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement.

“The relief consignment comprised tents, blankets, mats, hygiene kits and medicines for the affected communities,” FO said.

The send-off ceremony for the humanitarian assistance was held at the Islamabad airport, and was attended by Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, Nepal’s Ambassador Rita Dhital, along with senior FO and NDMA officials.

“The assistance reflects Pakistan’s solidarity with the government and people of Nepal during this difficult time,” FO noted.

Sharing the development on X, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said: “Our thoughts and prayers are with the bereaved families and all those affected. Pakistan stands in solidarity with the Government and people of Nepal and remains ready to extend all possible support in this difficult hour.”

Rescue operations continue

In Nepal, rescuers faced challenging conditions on Sunday as search operations after catastrophic floods entered a 12th day, buoyed by the extraordinary rescues of four survivors.

Rescuers found two more people alive on Saturday, joining two saved the day before in what have been described as miraculous tales of survival.

Three of those have been found in hydropower tunnels where the government initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive.

“Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity,” Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told AFP.

Rescue workers were experiencing “multiple challenges”, he said.

The wall of icy water and debris tore through mountain districts on August 26, destroying roads, bridges and other infrastructure.

On Saturday, rescuers pulled a Chinese man alive from deep inside a hydropower tunnel, and a 64-year-old Nepali woman, Chandrika Shrestha, from her mud-covered home.

Nepal Police officers assist Chandrika Kumari Shrestha after she was rescued alive from a damaged house following deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Betrawati in Nuwakot district, Nepal on Sept 5, 2026. —Nepal Police/Handout via Reuters

Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the latter rescue had “given hope to the entire nation”.

A day earlier, two Nepali hydropower workers were rescued at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where searches continue alongside multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects affected.

Other examples of remarkable fortitude have emerged from Nepal, including Rajendra Dawadi, a school principal who quickly ordered an evacuation as the torrent approached, saving hundreds of students’ lives.

“If the information was wrong, we would lose a day of schooling,” he told AFP.

“But if it was true, we were going to lose our lives.”

Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said work was continuing to restore electricity in several areas.

“Places that have unreachable, we’ve tried to restore power with solar,” he told AFP.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has called the disaster a “Himalayan tsunami” and has warned reconstruction costs could run into the billions of dollars.

The United Nations has said the magnitude of the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge, and has launched a $50 million appeal to help more than 84,000 people.

With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves, after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to the police.

Only around 100 bodies have been identified and handed over to families.

Nepal will hold a national day of mourning on Monday, the 13th day since the disaster, in line with a traditional period of mourning in Hindu rituals.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melting worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

World.title: Scuffle in Karachi's DHA: Fresh case registered after inquiry report finds first FIR unsubstantiated
World.content:
KARACHI: A resident of Karachi’s Defence Housing Authority (DHA) has sought action against her neighbours and police personnel for allegedly beating her in a fresh case registered in connection with a scuffle outside her apartment last month, it emerged on Sunday.

The matter came to light when the CCTV footage of the physical altercation at an apartment building in DHA’s Phase 6 surfaced on social media last week. The footage showed police officials restraining a woman as another woman with a dumbbell attacked her.

However, the initial first information report (FIR) of the incident was registered against the woman who was assaulted and her brother. But an inquiry report later said that the allegations in the FIR were “not substantiated” by the findings and also recommended departmental action against police officials involved in the incident.

The report also said the first FIR should be disposed of, and subsequently, another was registered at the Darakhshan police station on September 5.

In the second FIR, a copy of which is available with Dawn, the complainant said she was a resident of a third-floor apartment in DHA, Phase 6.

The FIR quoted her as saying that on August 20 at 11:45pm, she was at her house with her brother and mother when a police officer rang the apartment’s doorbell and told her that her neighbour was calling them to the ground floor.

Shortly after, the complainant continued, her neighbour came upstairs while hurling curses and started banging on the door. “When I opened the door, she dragged me by the hair, snatched my phone, and threw it down,” she alleged.

“When my mother came out, she grabbed her by the hair as well and beat her,” the complainant claimed, adding that her neighbour then pinned her to a wall.

The neighbour then went to her apartment and came back with her daughter and some police officials and “attempted to take away our phones, […] and her daughter, who was carrying a dumbbell, hit us”, she alleged.

She further stated that she, along with her family, ran inside the house and called the police. “Meanwhile, the police officials outside broke the CCTV camera and later, the Darakhshan police broke into our house and took my and my brother’s cellphones away,” the FIR said.

The complainant sought action against the suspects for “beating me, stealing our mobile phones and damaging the security camera”.

The case was registered under Sections 147 (punishment for rioting), 148(rioting, armed with deadly weapon), 379 (punishment for theft), 427(mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees), and 337A(i) (whoever, by doing any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC).

Police official suspended

Meanwhile, Darakhshan Police Sub-Inspector Imran Khan was suspended with pay on Sunday, pending an inquiry into his conduct in the DHA scuffle case.

“He is shifted to PHQ Garden, South Zone Karachi, where he will attend daily roll call/parade, accordingly,” the suspension notice dated Sept 6 said, a copy of which is available with Dawn.

A show-cause notice issued to Imran by South Investigation Superintendent of Police (SP) Touheed Rehman Memon observed that Khan had “failed to collect the tangible evidence, video footage of the incident and conduct [an] impartial investigation purely on merit”.

His conduct reflected “a lack of professional diligence, negligence and dereliction of duty”, the notice stated, a copy of which is available with Dawn.
