World.title: US delegation lands in Kyiv amid Russia-Ukraine capitals ceasefire
World.content:
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have arrived in Kyiv as part of a push to revive peace talks in Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In joint statements to reporters after the first round of talks, Mr Witkoff said the US team had been "very encouraged" by what he described as a "substantive, important" discussion.

Russia, Ukraine to halt strikes on capitals during peace talks Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy have agreed to halt strikes on their respective capitals.

The visit by the emissaries follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday.

Mr Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks took place.

Mr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Kyiv was ready for a "constructive" discussion with US representatives.

"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared," he said in a post on Telegram.

European security advisors will participate in some of the talks, Mr Zelenskyy confirmed.

"We are expecting one session of our talks, and then another session will be held with the European NSAs (national security advisors)," he said.

No breakthroughs in Moscow talks

Saturday's meeting in Moscow lasted more than 3 hours behind closed doors and ended without announcements of any breakthroughs.

Mr Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described them afterwards as constructive, frank and useful but did not discuss specific outcomes.

Vladimir Putin greets Steve Witkoff prior to talks in Moscow on Saturday. (AP: Mikhail Metzel/Sputnik)

While Moscow offered its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, Mr Ushakov said the talks were not purely focused on the war in Ukraine.

"Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," he said.

Prior to these meetings, Washington's push to end the fighting had lost momentum, with the United States focused for the past six months on the Iran war.

The last known visit to Moscow by Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was in January when they also held talks with Mr Putin at the Kremlin.

Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire

Mr Putin and Mr Zelenskyy had agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks took place.

Still, the two traded fire overnight into Sunday in other regions, officials said.

Russian attacks across multiple Ukrainian regions killed one person and injured at least 10 others overnight into Sunday, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomes Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in Kyiv. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

In Zaporizhzhia, drone strikes killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three people, while a drone damaged an apartment building, injuring seven people, in the Khmelnytskyi region.

Ukraine's air force said on Sunday that it had intercepted 82 drones out of the 108 launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.

In Russia, a man was killed and a woman seriously wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a vehicle, local authorities in the Belgorod border region said.

The Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday that its air defences overnight shot down 258 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the waters of the Black and Azov seas.

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometre front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.

ABC/Wires

World.title: 'People were screaming': Qantas passengers tell of engine spitting fire
World.content:
People screaming and widespread panic are how passengers have described the moment they heard loud bangs and saw fire spitting from an engine on a Sydney-bound Qantas flight.

On Saturday afternoon, Flight QF122 had just left Queenstown in New Zealand when it had to be diverted to Christchurch in what the airline said was a "suspected engine issue".

Kriti Sethi was on her way home after her holidays, and was sitting towards the back of the plane where she "could see the fire" coming from the left-hand side.

"It happened around five times, so we hear bang, bang, bang and there was five times fire coming out," she told the ABC from Sydney Airport after spending the night in Christchurch.

"And then the people were screaming; people were like, 'Oh my God.' It was quite scary."

Kriti Sethi says she was sitting in the back of the plane and could see the fire. (Supplied)

Despite the cabin crew initially blaming the landing gear, Ms Sethi said that, because of her seat's location, she could see everything.

"So we were like, 'No, it's actually fire coming out of the engine, it's not landing gear'."

Adding to the panic and fear was the turbulence.

"So the plane was shaking as well. So it was fire and then went straight into shaking; it was just so scary," she said.

Announcements from captain

Sari-Elle Kraemer, who was sitting on the right-hand side of the plane, said there was a lot of nervous energy on board, especially after the lights went off.

The flight was forced to divert to Christchurch. (Supplied: Kriti Sethi)

While she could not see the fire, she could hear other passengers talking about it and did not know what to think.

"I've never experienced something like that," Ms Kraemer said.

"Just the noise and the fact that people could see fire on the plane was scary, but obviously the pilots are trained to deal with that, and I felt it was under control after a few minutes."

Throughout the ordeal, passengers were kept informed of what was happening.

Ms Sethi said the flight's captain told passengers in one announcement that the plane had experienced a chemical failure with the engines, forcing the aircraft to make an emergency landing in Christchurch.

Fire engines and emergency services were on hand at the tarmac.

Sari-Elle Kraemer says she has "never experienced something like that". (ABC News)

Both women have commended the professionalism of the cabin crew, praising their handling of the incident, and were grateful for the safe landing.

"The cabin crew were amazing, and the captain was amazing,' Ms Sethi said.

"Once we landed, everyone was clapping."

She was still nervous on her trip home, but again the captain "made an announcement, saying 'That we understand what happened yesterday. It was a traumatic experience for you guys'."

Incident under investigation

A spokesperson for Qantas said the plane had been grounded in Christchurch as engineers carry out an inspection and examination.

It will remain there until it is cleared to resume flying, with an investigation underway into what caused the fire.

Engine flames prompt diversion of Qantas flight The Sydney-bound Boeing aircraft left Queenstown in New Zealand after 3pm before it had to be diverted to Christchurch.

In a second incident in two days, another Qantas plane has been grounded temporarily and is under inspection after it was forced to return to Sydney Airport this morning.

Flight QF121 was en route to Queenstown when an incident took place halfway into the trip.

"A flight deck alert indicated a potential issue with the aircraft's anti-skid system," the airline told the ABC.

A recovery flight is being organised for Monday, with passengers forced to stay in Sydney overnight.

'Aircraft is designed for these sorts of things'

International aviation consultant Neil Hansford said that while it remained unclear what caused the issue, an engine blade might have detached.

"And obviously when it's a piece of metal going at that many revs, it's hit a fuel line and the fuel's ignited," he said.

"So the captain's able to shut the engine down, use the fire suppression system and put the fire out.

"The aircraft is designed for these sorts of things, so if an engine loses power on take-off, it's designed to fly on safely and continue to climb.

"These are all controllable circumstances, and you don't necessarily want them, but at least with the training of Qantas pilots, they totally know how to handle it; they're tested in the simulator."

World.title: Dozens of bushfires burn as Qld swelters through above-average temps
World.content:
A large bushfire has caused major disruptions on the Warrego Highway west of Brisbane, as dozens of fires burn in Queensland.

A Prepare to Leave warning was issued about 3:45pm for the blaze burning at Plainland in the Lockyer Valley, forcing the highway to close in both directions between Brisbane and Toowoomba.

The warning has since been downgraded to a Stay Informed advisory, and the highway fully reopened about 5:30pm.

The fire is expected to continue to burn for several days.

The Warrego Highway was closed earlier on Sunday and has since reopened. (ABC News)

There are 78 bushfires across south-east Queensland.

A 24-hour fire ban was imposed yesterday for Ipswich and the Lockyer Valley, set to end at midnight tonight.

Queensland Fire Department deputy chief officer Joel Gordon said hot, dry weather had created challenging firefighting conditions.

"We're currently watching three fires that have been burning for a little while … one up at Sandy Creek … we've also been monitoring [the] fire that started yesterday at Plainland, another one just a little bit further down at Prenzlau."

Homes under threat

Lockyer Valley Regional Council Mayor Tanya Milligan said up to 20 homes could have been at risk.

"They're the homes that the QPS [Queensland Police Service] went and doorknocked," she said.

"A lot of people voluntarily evacuated and left; some decided not to.

"We had some pain-in-the-backside northerly winds, which created some havoc and just made it really unpredictable. We had 26 appliances on site … we had two water bombers. The fire also … jumped across the highway."

Parts of the state sweltered through some of the hottest September temperatures in seven years today, with temperatures five to 10 degrees above average for the month in parts of the south-east.

Senior meteorologist Steven Hadley said the mercury in inland areas reached 34 to 36 degrees Celsius.

"That's the hottest we've seen in September since 2019," he said.

"We're getting into spring now so the sun's getting higher in the sky, [and] more intense, so it's able to heat the ground and air up more readily than it was in August."

World.title: Dockers AFLW star turns ruck coach after injury to assist victory
World.content:
Injured AFLW powerhouse Mim Strom was forced to play ruck coach on the bench as the Dockers steamrolled a Monique Conti-less Richmond by 25 points on the road.

Two-time All-Australian ruck Strom was in agony at Princes Park after a tackle from Tigers midfielder Emelia Yassir in the first quarter of Sunday's clash.

Recruit Eden Zanker was first cab off the rank in the ruck, while Gabby O'Sullivan kicked three goals to help lift the Dockers to a 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) win in Indigenous Round.

Later on Sunday, Aishling Moloney finished with four goals as Geelong posted a 13.5 (83) to 7.9 (51) result to pile the misery on a winless Essendon at Kardinia Park.

Lisa Webb's Dockers (2-2) can finish the fourth week of the 12-fixture competition in the top eight, but are bracing to lose Strom for part of their finals push.

Before Sunday, Strom had played 78 consecutive matches since making her debut in 2020.

"She's been on the bench with a big smile, so she's hard to get a read on, but I'll get a medical update," coach Webb told Seven Plus at three-quarter time.

"She's been a ruck coach on the side. She's been a warrior for us, and we'll look after her."

Gabby O'Sullivan (pictured) kicked three goals as Fremantle recorded a 25-point road win over Richmond. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Richmond, which, like Fremantle, has not reached finals since 2024, drop from sixth and could finish as low as 13th with a 2-2 record.

The Tigers are unsure of how serious Conti's injury is, with the 2023 league best-and-fairest managing Achilles soreness.

The five-time All-Australian midfielder was a late withdrawal alongside Fina Dethlefsen, with recruit Georgia Stubs and Kate Dempsey returning to the side.

Youngster Isabel Bacon (24 disposals, six clearances) led the game in Conti's absence, and Olivia Wolmarans kicked two goals.

Geelong's Mikayla Bowen (left) picked up a game-high 40 disposals in her side's 32-point win over Essendon. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

The Dockers took the early advantage after three lead changes in the opening quarter, pipping the Tigers by five points thanks to a goal from O'Sullivan.

Strom's absence did little to sap Fremantle's momentum, with O'Sullivan piling on back-to-back goals as the hosts were kept scoreless in the second term.

It was much the same after half-time, with the Dockers maintaining a perfect record against the Tigers across four meetings since season six in 2022.

At Kardinia Park, scores were level at 1.1 (7) for much of the first quarter before Chantal Mason gave away a free kick for a high tackle on Maggie Johnstone in Essendon's forward-50.

Johnstone converted after the quarter-time siren for a six-point lead, but the Bombers' ascendancy did not last long after Moloney came to life.

The star Irishwoman kicked four of Geelong's six goals in the second term, while the visitors managed just two to trail by 18 points.

Geelong improved its record to 3-1 to tighten its grip on a top-four spot, leaving Essendon languishing in 16th.

Mikayla Bowen had a monster 40 disposals, while Cats star Georgie Prespakis matched older sister and Essendon veteran Maddy with 27 disposals and five clearances.

AAP

World.title: Burnouts and drag races as Red CentreNATS takes over Alice Springs
World.content:
Sitting in the passenger seat as her dad lined up in his classic Ford Falcon XC 393 Stroker to drag race at the 12th annual Red CentreNATS, Montana Taylor looked jubilant, and proud.

The teen and her dad, Ben, had travelled from South Australia to be a part of the festival that celebrates all things horsepower.

"I love it so much, I'm so glad I get to come and experience this," she said, with a massive grin.

Ben and Montana Taylor travelled from South Australia to be at the Red CentreNATS. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

She said she could not wait to drive her dad's car.

"Maybe one day," Mr Taylor said.

The Red CentreNATS is held over four days. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

The event has been part of the Alice Springs calendar for 12 years. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

The Taylors are among the 700 registered entrants into this year's Red CentreNATS — more than half of whom come from interstate, boosting the local economy by about $5 million each year.

The weekend's program was huge, featuring street cruising, show and shines of the incredible array of vintage and new muscle cars, drag races, burnout competitions and a street parade that stopped the town.

The event drew about 700 entrants this year. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Labours of love

A pale blue 1984 Holden Kingswood ute shone bright against the red-brown of the dirt dragway.

It was right at home — it had been in Alice Springs its whole life, according to owner Paul Totani.

Paul Totani enters his Kingswood in the Red CentreNATS every year. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Mr Totani, whose family has been in town since the 1960s, is a licensed aircraft engineer and pilot. But on Saturday he swapped the sky for the dirt, tearing down the drag strip, dust flying.

"It's a family heirloom. It will go to the kids later on, but we get it out once a year for Red CentreNATS," he said.

People of all ages attended this year's Red CentreNATS. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Drag races were a popular event. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

At the show and shine car display, dozens of automobiles sparkled in the sun and inside the Alice Springs Convention Centre.

Proud owners stood beside their lovingly cared-for cars, excited to share their stories.

Heather and Laurie, pictured at the show and shine display, love their car. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Spectators also enjoyed the action from the stands (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Parading the past

Sitting on the back of utes, in deckchairs and on car roof-racks, Alice Springs turned out in force and lined the streets for the annual Red CentreNATS street parade.

It was a perfect day for the parade in Alice Springs. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Australian and Northern Territory pride was on show. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Hundreds of cars rolled around the town's largest roundabout at the base of the MacDonnell Ranges, which glistened in the afternoon sun.

Plenty of old utes were on display. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

These kids watched the parade from a good vantage point. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

It was a family affair for many locals watching the parade. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

One of the spectators was Alice Springs local Lisa Morgan, who said events like the Red CentreNATS helped Alice Springs to shine.

She has volunteered for the event for years.

"Everyone bands together for the excitement, and the rumbles," she said.

World.title: Canadian woman dies in moped crash on Magnetic Island
World.content:
A woman has died after the moped she was riding collided with a car on Magnetic Island in north Queensland.

Emergency services were called to Horseshoe Bay just before 12pm.

A 74-year-old woman, a Canadian national, died at the scene.

The driver of the car was not physically injured.

A Queensland Police Service spokesperson could not confirm whether the woman was a tourist visiting the island.

Horseshoe Bay resident Simone Wall told the ABC multiple bystanders tried to save the woman.

"Everyone, including residents, tourists and lifeguards, worked tirelessly trying to save her," Ms Wall said.

"They never gave up. CPR was commenced immediately and when the lifeguards arrived the defibrillator was applied.

"Our deepest condolences go to her family."

The forensic crash unit is investigating and anyone with information or dash cam footage is urged to contact police.

World.title: Who knew there was an AFLW double-header on?; Daisy Pearce’s Eagles slump to 0-4
World.content:
Sunday at Ikon Park showcased an action-packed day of footy with a double-header that saw Fremantle triumph over Richmond, and Carlton continue their winning streak with a resounding victory over Collingwood.

It’s a shame more people weren’t there to see it.

Blues and Pies during Sunday’s double-header. Getty Images

A crowd of 1931 fans showed up to watch the Richmond game at 12.30 at Ikon Park for the second week of Indigenous Round. The Carlton versus Collingwood clash at 3pm had an attendance of 3892 (an accumulative figure that counts fans who came for the first game, but might not have stayed for the second).

This is obviously a nuanced conversation.

Mother’s Day has traditionally been a dead fixture for AFL men’s with significantly lower attendance records, so it makes sense the women’s league would experience a similar decrease for Father’s Day.

It’s also important to note we’re in the middle of the men’s finals season – a time when many fans could be experiencing footy fatigue or aren’t paying attention to the women’s league.

But walking around Ikon Park, you couldn’t help feel this weekend was a missed opportunity. Most of the stands were empty, and the green space outside the suburban stadium was fairly barren.

Fremantle triumphed over Richmond by 25 points in the first double-header on Sunday. Getty Images

A double-header typically means you want to encourage fans to stay at the stadium for both games, which means the following need to be on offer: music, entertainment, activation stands and numerous food options and stalls.

There was none of that on Sunday, except a few merch stands and one gourmet burger stand.

Longtime AFLW fan Amy Stephens has only missed two Collingwood games since 2018 and was cheering for the Pies from the boundary line on Sunday.

However, the supporter said she had no idea there was a double-header on today, citing the lack of advertising around the event.

Stephens said only realised there was a double-header when she checked the fine print on her Ticketmaster account, but she’d already left home and missed the game.

“I think there needs to be more advertising for AFLW in general, let alone a double-header,” she said.

Stephens said it would be good to have activities or entertainment between the two games, to “break up the day” and encourage people to stay.

She also wanted to see a bigger advertising push on social media and on television, so fans could actually know a double-header was on.

Several other fans this masthead spoke said they had no idea a double-header was on today.

Sunday’s attendance at Ikon Park is made more bleak by the fact double-headers – when advertised and publicised properly – do really well. Footy fans have voted with their feet over the first three rounds, with AFLW attendances up by more than 50 per cent compared with the same stage last season. The growth has been driven largely by five double-headers, with the men’s game, which have drawn crowds as big 20,000, in tier one stadiums.

Carlton coach Matthew Buck reiterated his support for the double-header concept after the Blues won by 39 points – their fourth consecutive win this season.

When asked if he was hoping for more  around the double-header, Buck didn’t specify his thoughts, but said he thought there was “a great vibe within the crowd”.

“I’m all for it [the double-headers],” he said. “I think we could take those to Marvel as well, and fill Marvel up with them, it’d be fantastic.

“But what we know is when we play at Ikon Park and our Carlton fans turn up, that it’s a great place to be. And I think Freo, Richmond might have felt a little bit of that towards the end of their game.”

Double-header are proven to work.

But if the AFL want to meet their attendance benchmarks and fill stadiums for W games, they need to make sure fans actually know when the games are on.

World.title: The not-so-golden handcuffs costing workers $2500 a year
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalWage growth The not-so-golden handcuffs costing workers $2500 a year Shane Wright September 6, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Contractual handcuffs that prevent people on less than $190,000 from moving to a better-paying or more interesting job would be banned under proposed laws to be unveiled by the federal government on Monday. The ban on so-called non-compete clauses, part of the government’s plans to boost productivity across the economy, follows growing evidence their use by some firms is having a “chilling effect” on workers whose skills may be better rewarded with another employer. Bricklayers, childcare workers and nurses have been caught in non-compete clauses which economists argue reduce wages and slow productivity. Craig Abraham Assistant Productivity and Competition Minister Andrew Leigh said banning non-competes was aimed at making the economy work more efficiently while delivering better wages. “Workers shouldn’t need their old boss’s permission to take a better job. Non-compete clauses can act like a padlock on opportunity, holding down wages and keeping people from jobs where their skills are worth more. We’re cutting that padlock,” he said.



Related Article Opinion

Industrial relations The bizarre way bosses are treating cooks and hairdressers like CEOs Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent Research by the Australian Bureau of Statistics has found almost 47 per cent of businesses use some type of non-compete clause. The most common are bans on non-disclosure agreements. But the bureau found other restrictions, which have a direct impact on workers’ ability to use their skills in a better paying job, are widely employed by businesses including client non-solicitation clauses (25.4 per cent), non-compete clauses (20.8 per cent) and bans on the solicitation of co-workers (18 per cent). Separate research by the e61 think tank has found that banning non-compete clauses could lift the wages of affected workers by up to $2500 a year. Submissions to an inquiry into non-competes last year revealed the extent to how they are being used to reduce the ability of employees to move to new jobs.



In one case, a person on less than $80,000 a year was barred from taking a job in the same industry in Australia and New Zealand. In another case, a graduate engineer on $63,000 found a clause in their contract that prevented them from working anywhere else in Victoria for the next year if they left the company. Bricklayers, nurses and retail workers were revealed to have non-compete clauses that had traditionally been used in high-income professions in which trade secrets may have a particularly high value. Apart from the draft legislation on non-compete clauses for people earning less than $190,000, the government will also consult on a series of related employment restraints including non-solicitation and no-poach clauses and wage-fixing arrangements. The government plans to offer “appropriate exemptions and safeguards” to protect what are considered legitimate business interests. This may include the transfer of corporate secrets with some businesses concerned that staff they have trained may take those skills to a competitor or set up their own firm. Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth said non-compete clauses were hurting the entire economy.



“Labor is determined to help boost job mobility for more than three million Australian workers constrained by a non-compete clause, including childcare workers, construction workers and hairdressers,” she said. Consultation on the legislation will run until October 2.

World.title: Government closes in on $100m social media fines
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCyber bullying Government closes in on $100m social media fines Shane Wright September 6, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Social media companies could be slugged with fines of more than $100 million if they fail to do more to keep under-16s off their sites under an Albanese government bill set to go before the Senate on Tuesday. The fines are part of a push to give more power to eSafety Commission chief Julie Inman Grant to target sites such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok for not lifting efforts to abide by Australia’s ban on young people accessing social media. Communications Minister Anika Wells is urging all sides of politics to fast-track the government’s heavy fines on social media companies. Dominic Lorrimer It forms a key part of a broader assault on social media platforms with draft laws that would force companies to take action that would prevent the platforming and sharing of harmful content, including illegal pornography, on their sites. At the start of July, the government introduced to parliament an urgent bill it said would boost the eSafety Commission’s information gathering powers. That bill was sent to a Senate committee that, despite misgivings by non-government members, ticked off its approval.



Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Hanson, Coalition ready to fight Labor’s plan to tame social media feeds That bill, which includes fines of $109.2 million for breaching new laws to prevent under-16s from accessing social media sites, will go to the Senate on Tuesday. The government has come under fire over the large number of young people still on social media sites, despite its mandating of age verification. But Communications Minister Anika Wells said more than five million under-16s accounts had been removed. She urged the upper house to back the bill as quickly as possible. “Australian kids and parents needed these laws eight weeks ago, but the Coalition and Greens teamed up to send our four-page bill to an eight-week inquiry,” she said.



“The Coalition and the Greens ignored the pleas of parents who want social media companies held to account for harming Australian kids. “We have to put politics to the side and pass this bill this week, so the eSafety Commissioner can hold social media companies accountable.” The large fines at the heart of the under-16 ban will form part of the so-called “digital duty of care” reforms that the government is expected to release for public comment later this week. The proposed legislation has the potential to split the Coalition between those who want to protect free speech and those who believe some social media outlets are deliberately causing harm among young people. Liberal leader Angus Taylor on Sunday said while he had not seen the draft laws, he was worried about an “attempt by government to censor social media”.



He was more focused on the laws going to the Senate this week, noting the continued use by under-16s of social media. Editor's pick City life ‘Blows the pavement up’: How freezing water and car tyres create a pothole in just days “It’s not working. So then going off and starting off on some other thing, which risks being censorship of the internet, enormous ministerial discretion around censorship on the internet … If that’s what’s being proposed, we’re sceptical,” he told News24. Opposition communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson expressed deep reservations about the proposal and how it would give more powers to the government to regulate Australians’ freedom of expression. “While we will consider the government’s exposure draft, the proposal for new ministerial powers to make regulations governing categories of online harms without parliamentary oversight is a serious threat to free speech,” she said.



“While tougher action is required to combat serious online harms and empower Australians to take greater control over what they see online, the digital duty of care, as currently proposed, appears to be a dangerous step in the wrong direction. But opposition home affairs spokesman Jonathan Duniam said there might be merit in users not being force-fed an algorithm for their social media. “Provided the detail stacks up and it doesn’t unnecessarily impede on people’s rights and freedoms, empowering individuals to make a choice about what they consume is absolutely where we should be at,” he told the ABC’s Insiders program. “Empowering parents to do the same for those that are in their custody, their kids, should absolutely be something we consider.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: You need Uncle Samistan
World.content:
“Trump’s patriotic re-naming of parts of the world is intriguing,” thinks George Manojlovic of Mangerton. “I’m waiting for something more imaginative than Gulf of America or Lake America. American Mayan Yucatán rolls off the tongue, as does Unclesamoa and Unclesamistan. How about Yankee Chewing Guam or Southern Fried Türkiye? Londonald has a familiar ring to it, too.”

The Bee Gees’ Easter Show gig (C8), has notoriety, according to Andrew Cohen of Glebe: “I remember when a handsome young man about 17, brought my 15-year-old sister home to Pymble about 6pm from the Easter Show with his two young brothers in the back of his yellow FC Holden. He politely apologised to my scary fuming father, ‘My brothers and I had commitments’. Dad: ‘I know who you are Mr Gibb. You’re one of those singers on Bandstand. How dare you bring my daughter home after dark. Get back in your car. Don’t go near her again.’ Maurice and Robin saw me watching from a window and their eyes were messaging me their alarm. My sister remains none too pleased about this.”

Marjie Williamson’s pill-popping enquiry (C8) has flooded our mailbox to the extent that it’s challenging to find material on any other subject. It led Nola Scott of Wagga Wagga to say, “I’m right-handed, so I open tablets in a foil pack from the left, just as I write from the left. I don’t think I could do it going backwards.” Michael Johnston of Corlette starts “each of my four foil sheets of tablets in a random spot and congratulate myself when they all finish on the same day. Being right-handed I open them with my left hand as an anti-dementia strategy.”

All very instructive, but maybe it’s worth heeding Col Burns of Lugarno: “I may be ambidextrous or just disorganised, but if I noticed that I was selecting tablets other than at random, I’d assume that those tablets were treatment for my OCD.”

“Lyndall Dawson succinctly and incisively describes the genius of Cathy Wilcox (C8),” says Robyn Cashman of Fernhill. “The suggestion of a book of her work is welcome. It would make a great addition to every school’s modern history reading list. So much food for thought.”

World.title: Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney councils Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening Rachel Rasker September 6, 2026 — 8:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A portion of the roof of North Sydney Olympic Pool blew off on Saturday, almost a month to the day since the embattled $122 million project opened its doors on August 7. Photos circulated online showing what appeared to be roof flashing trailing along the street on Saturday afternoon, after powerful winds that reached more than 80km/h pummelled Sydney. North Sydney Pool’s flashing appeared to have blown off on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre Residents expressed disappointment at the damage, and questioned how much it would add to the troubled pool’s repair bill. North Sydney residents already face a 52 per cent jump in rates over three years to help fund the project. “I think it’s horrible because this is not the first time that’s happened,” said resident Gregory Barros, referring to the power supply issue that forced the pool to shut its doors a week after opening.



He said someone “needs to be accountable for the hundred million” spent on the beleaguered project, which had an initial estimated cost of $58 million. “Think about if someone was there. It would have been a very big issue,” Barros said. Pool staff confirmed no one was hurt in the incident. North Sydney pool on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre “North Sydney experienced significant wind conditions on Saturday, along with many other areas across Sydney. The strong winds resulted in minor damage to a section of roofing at North Sydney Olympic Pool,” a spokesperson for North Sydney Council said in a statement. “The area was made safe and contractors attended the site promptly to undertake repairs. Pool operations were not affected.”





The council was also mired in a separate legal battle with Brewster Hjorth over costs and delays caused by the roof, which was pulled down in 2023 and later replaced. Brewster Hjorth Pty Limited, the corporate trustee behind the architectural practice, has since entered liquidation. While the damaged section had been removed by Sunday, the roof’s blue underlay was exposed to the elements. North Sydney Pool was back open on Sunday, with a section of the roof’s edge missing. Rachel Rasker “It’s a great pool and it’s a shame they have repairs already, when it’s only been open a couple of weeks,” said Matt, a regular swimmer and local who declined to provide his surname. North Sydney Living posted photos on their Facebook page on Sunday, and questioned whether another closure was likely. “No word yet from pool management or council about the extent of the damage or potential disruption to opening times,” the post read.

World.title: Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney councils Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening Rachel Rasker September 6, 2026 — 8:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A portion of the roof of North Sydney Olympic Pool blew off on Saturday, almost a month to the day since the embattled $122 million project opened its doors on August 7. Photos circulated online showing what appeared to be roof flashing trailing along the street on Saturday afternoon, after powerful winds that reached more than 80km/h pummelled Sydney. North Sydney Pool’s flashing appeared to have blown off on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre Residents expressed disappointment at the damage, and questioned how much it would add to the troubled pool’s repair bill. North Sydney residents already face a 52 per cent jump in rates over three years to help fund the project. “I think it’s horrible because this is not the first time that’s happened,” said resident Gregory Barros, referring to the power supply issue that forced the pool to shut its doors a week after opening.



He said someone “needs to be accountable for the hundred million” spent on the beleaguered project, which had an initial estimated cost of $58 million. “Think about if someone was there. It would have been a very big issue,” Barros said. Pool staff confirmed no one was hurt in the incident. North Sydney pool on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre “North Sydney experienced significant wind conditions on Saturday, along with many other areas across Sydney. The strong winds resulted in minor damage to a section of roofing at North Sydney Olympic Pool,” a spokesperson for North Sydney Council said in a statement. “The area was made safe and contractors attended the site promptly to undertake repairs. Pool operations were not affected.”





The council was also mired in a separate legal battle with Brewster Hjorth over costs and delays caused by the roof, which was pulled down in 2023 and later replaced. Brewster Hjorth Pty Limited, the corporate trustee behind the architectural practice, has since entered liquidation. While the damaged section had been removed by Sunday, the roof’s blue underlay was exposed to the elements. North Sydney Pool was back open on Sunday, with a section of the roof’s edge missing. Rachel Rasker “It’s a great pool and it’s a shame they have repairs already, when it’s only been open a couple of weeks,” said Matt, a regular swimmer and local who declined to provide his surname. North Sydney Living posted photos on their Facebook page on Sunday, and questioned whether another closure was likely. “No word yet from pool management or council about the extent of the damage or potential disruption to opening times,” the post read.

World.title: Questions about safety of disabled school transportation after review
World.content:
Questions have been raised about the safety of school transport services for disabled students, after an independent review.

The Ministry of Education commissioned the independent operational review of the Specialised School Transport Assistance (SESTA) scheme, following concerns about new transport contracts.

The review drew on a national survey, interviews and discussions with students, whānau and caregivers, schools, transport providers, drivers, disability organisations and Ministry of Education staff. The survey received more than 800 survey responses.

It identified several recurring issues requiring attention, including problems with communication, supervision arrangements, driver capability and wheelchair transport safety.

"The review heard consistent evidence that successful outcomes depend not only on the commitment of drivers, schools, families and providers, but also on effective oversight, coordination, communication and problem solving across the wider system," the report said.

The independent review panel said maintaining a safe transport system required more than responding to incidents when they occurred.

"It requires ongoing investment in system stewardship, proactive risk management, capability development, monitoring and learning. As expectations of safety, accessibility and responsiveness continue to grow," it said.

"The Panel therefore invites the Ministry to consider whether sufficient capability, capacity and resources currently exist across the SESTA system to maintain and continuously improve a safe, reliable and responsive service. This consideration should not be limited to the Ministry itself but should also include the broader system of support involving providers, schools and those responsible for stewardship, monitoring, safety oversight, training and continuous improvement," it said.

The independent review also found that stakeholders reported differing interpretations of responsibilities, particularly during service changes, incidents, information sharing, student handovers, and the implementation of Safe Travel Plans.

"Lack of clarity can lead to confusion, inconsistent practice and increased safety risks," it said.

The review panel's recommendations include:

Improvements to safety planning

A review of training provided to SESTA drivers

Involving the Children's Commissioner in monitoring SESTA trends.

In a statement, Ministry of Education services and programmes manager Andrea Williams said it accepted the findings, and it had begun work on the recommendations and priority actions.

"Some students and whānau told us their experience of the service did not consistently meet their needs or expectations. Their feedback has helped identify where improvements are needed and has directly shaped the actions we are taking in response," Williams said.

The ministry's focus was now on improving communication, safety planning, driver training and support, supervision, wheelchair transport, service monitoring and information management.

"A project to improve the quality and currency of information in our systems and the processes for sharing this is well advanced," Williams said.

"Work to improve communication is also well underway with the Ministry establishing regional contacts for all schools with SESTA services."

Williams said the ministry had initiated a review of SESTA roles and responsibilities, and would be taking concrete actions to make sure these are understood.

"The review recognises that student Safe Travel Plans are central to effectively managing each student's safety needs. We have now made these mandatory for all students, and we are working on a process to ensure that the information held in these is kept up to date and accurate," she said.

"We will report on our progress, while ongoing feedback from the people who use and deliver SESTA helps shape these improvements.

World.title: Future of Duffy Books in limbo as Ministry of Education considers 'competitive tender process'
World.content:
The Ministry of Education is considering opening its contract with the Duffy Books in Homes programme to competitive tender.

A briefing paper shows it renewed the contract for providing free books to children in poor communities until the end of 2027, but intended to "explore a competitive tender process ahead of any further contract renewals".

The ministry said its contract was with the Alan Duff Charitable Foundation, which funded the Duffy Books programme.

It provided at least 550,000 books to over 550 schools and about 40,000 books to more than 200 early childhood centres.

The programme also ran theatre shows and school assemblies with role models, it said.

"We want to be assured that we are getting the highest possible value for money with this contract. A procurement process will help us determine if there are other suppliers interested and capable of delivering these services," the ministry said.

It said the whole-of-life value of the contract since July 2025 would be $16.6million.

Duffy Books in Homes general manager Linda Vagana said the ministry's funding covered about a third of the organisation's work.

General Manager of Duffy Books in Homes, Linda Vagana. RNZ / Talei Anderson

She said it paid for two free books for each child in participating schools in term two each year, and bridged the gap when schools could not find a partner to fund half the cost of books for their pupils.

Vagana said a competitive tender was unusual but she understood the ministry's funding was tight.

"This is obviously something that's now part of the process," she said.

Vagana said the programme had been running for 32 years and communities needed it. She said it was about more than just dropping books at schools.

"It's also about telling the stories and having kids see themselves in the role models that we send out to all the schools," she said.

World.title: Warriors fall short of minor premiership, will play Dolphins at Mount Smart
World.content:
The Warriors have fallen just short of what would have been their second-ever minor premiership.

Going into the 27th and final round of the regular season, the Warriors were clear of the Panthers by just one on points differential.

After defeating the Sea Eagles 31-30 in Auckland last night to keep their place on top of the NRL ladder, the Panthers were left needing to beat the Tigers by two or more to finish in first.

They did just that, hammering the 15th-placed Tigers 38-10 in Sydney.

Penrith ran in seven tries including a hat-trick to Kiwi forward Casey McLean.

The result sees the Warriors finish in second, on 42 points with 18 wins and six losses.

However, coach Andrew Webster has maintained his side is chasing a much bigger carrot in 2026.

"There will be no one prouder if we happen to be minor premiers. It's a historical trophy and we'd be proud of it but not at the expense of what we need to do," Webster told media this week.

The Warriors will meet the Redcliffe Dolphins in week one of the finals at Mount Smart at 6.05pm on Saturday night.

World.title: No-confidence motion against Solomon Islands PM withdrawn
World.content:
Prime Minister Matthew Wale Pacific Islands Forum

The motion of no confidence filed against the Prime Minister of Solomon Islands has been withdrawn.

The motion against Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who has only been in the top job for over three months, was set for debate in parliament on Monday, 7 September.

Manasseh Maelanga, who lodged the motion against Wale a week ago, announced Sunday afternoon that he is withdrawing the motion.

Manasseh Maelanga Facebook / O.U.R Party Solomon islands

SBM Online reports Maelanga also signed the required documents for the formal withdrawal of the motion and submitted them to the National Parliament this afternoon.

"I have not taken this decision lightly, the motion was never about professional ambition, personal interest or creating division in our country, it was not a decision I took in isolation," Maelanga said.

In response to the announcement, Prime Minister Wale thanked Maelanga for withdrawing the motion.

"I have been quite concerned since I aware .. the time I landed in Palau.. emotions and public opinion, I think, also a rising level of public anger in terms of how leaders behave in these situations, and this something not good in the public mind."

I welcome the spirit with which he [Maelanga] has acted...and he informed me on Friday afternoon that this is what he would do over the weekend," Wale said.

A week in Solomon Islands politics

The motion came as a shock to Matthew Wale, who was in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting when the news broke.

Mr Wale left Palau early the next day to return home and deal with the domestic political crisis.

On his return to Solomon Islands last week, he faced the resignations of three Cabinet ministers.

Last Thursday, Wale then sacked the Finance Minister, Gordon Darcy Lilo, who also shares a political party with Maelanga.

Lilo told RNZ Pacific that he had no involvement with the motion against the prime minister.

World.title: Pet shop letter fails to keep man out of jail after he bashed brother with a bowl
World.content:
A man who repeatedly struck his brother over the head with a ceramic bowl, leaving him needing 13 stitches, hoped a glowing reference from a pet shop about his care of a rare African grey parrot might help keep him out of jail.

"I know that I could trust him with my flock," the store owner wrote of Anthony Gugich.

The letter of support was among the material put before the court, alongside a Corrections report revealing that Gugich had declined to provide an address for home detention, saying he wanted to "keep his affairs to himself".

This week, Gugich appeared in the Whangārei District Court for sentencing via audio-visual link from Pukekohe District Court before Judge Greg Davis on one charge of injuring with intent to injure.

Judge Davis recently found Gugich guilty at a judge-alone trial for the assault at the family home in Pukekohe.

On August 12, 2025, Gugich arrived at the home to find his belongings on the driveway.

When his brother arrived, the pair argued, and Gugich hit him on the head several times with a ceramic bowl. The brother suffered a serious cut requiring 13 stitches.

Gugich took his case to a judge-alone trial, claiming he was acting in self-defence.

But Judge Davis rejected his defence and, after finding him guilty, warned he would go to prison if he did not find an address at which to serve a sentence of home detention.

Pre-sentence reports were ordered, but Gugich told Corrections he was unwilling to provide an address as he wanted to "keep his affairs to himself", the judge said.

Gugich's lawyer, Kerrie Scott, said he was "taken by surprise" when he read the report, which had left Gugich with limited options.

However, Scott pushed for a reconciliatory approach, submitting that the case could be referred to restorative justice and that community work could be an appropriate sentence.

"I made it pretty clear at the end of the hearing that this was serious, that I wanted electronically monitored options, and he's seen fit not to see it as being that serious community-wise," Judge Davis responded.

"We're having a serious disagreement as to the gravity of this offending here. And sorry, I win these arguments."

Judge Davis said Gugich did not appear remorseful, despite the victim providing a victim impact statement that said he loved his brother and did not want to see him go to jail.

Gugich then addressed the court.

"I have thought about what happened, and I'm very shocked and very sorry about it," he said.

"I have wanted to apologise personally, but the no-contact order prevented me from doing so.

"Since the passing of our mother, we have become closer. Having Craig in my life is something I want very much, as we do get along in a positive way and also we do need each other, especially now."

"I know that I could trust him with my flock," the pet store owner wrote of Anthony Gugich, who cares for a rare African grey parrot. AFP

The letter from the pet shop was given to the court, in which the owner said Gugich owned a rare African grey parrot called Blue, which belonged to his mother, and often brought it in for treats.

"Tony and a selection of other customers buy a toy or treat for their feathered friends as payment for a wing clip," she wrote.

"I also have birds, but not as big as Blue. In the time that I have known Tony, I have found him to be very easy to chat with, and I know that I could trust him with my flock if I needed someone to take care of them."

In sentencing Gugich, Judge Davis did not comment on the letter from the pet shop, but said the assault was significant, given that it involved repeated blows to the head with a weapon and required hospital treatment.

The judge also said the victim had revealed in his statement that there had been no offer of reconciliation and Gugich breached his bail "almost every day" by not keeping his distance from him.

"You broke those conditions nearly every day, he says," Judge Davis said.

"You refused to provide electronic monitoring options to the court, not that I would have adopted them anyway. Your view was this should be dealt with by way of community work. You should keep your affairs to yourself, so to speak.

"However, this offending, in my view, is significantly beyond the scope where community work would be the appropriate sentencing outcome."

He sentenced Gugich to two years and six months' imprisonment.

At that point, Gugich slumped forward and put his head in his hands.

Gugich was also issued a strike under the three-strikes law.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Disabled teen loses deportation appeal, ordered to leave New Zealand
World.content:
A teenager who uses a wheelchair and needs help with daily tasks such as eating, bathing and dressing has been ordered to leave the country or face deportation.

Her resident family will likely have to leave New Zealand with her, after the teen's appeal against deportation on humanitarian grounds failed.

The teen, who has cerebral palsy, spastic quadriplegia, vision impairment and an intellectual disability, arrived in New Zealand from the Philippines in December 2024, having been granted a special visitor visa after a failed first attempt.

She then overstayed her visa by almost a year, making her liable for deportation.

An appeal lodged on her behalf was declined.

The Immigration and Protection Tribunal found last month that the teen, whose name and identifying details are suppressed, had not established that there were exceptional circumstances of a humanitarian nature.

However, given her dependence on family for daily care, the tribunal allowed the family four months to make arrangements for the teen's departure and "potentially their own".

The family also needed time to arrange care for the teen on her return to the Philippines, tribunal member Natalie Small said.

The teen's father arrived in New Zealand in late 2017 on an essential skills work visa, followed by her mother and two siblings in 2020 on work and student visas.

The high-needs teen remained in the Philippines while the family sought ways for her to join them in New Zealand.

In November 2021, the father lodged an application for a resident visa under the Accredited Employers category and included his wife and all three children.

The application was withdrawn a few months later and replaced with one under the "Special" category.

The application included medical evidence disclosing the teen's condition.

Small said the father withdrew the teen from the application in August 2022. In March 2023, the parents and two siblings were granted resident visas and became permanent New Zealand residents in 2025.

Special visitor visa granted on second attempt

An application was lodged on the teen's behalf in January 2024 for a six-month visitor visa but was turned down when Immigration New Zealand found she did not have an acceptable standard of health because she required fulltime care.

The family tried again in May 2024. Four months later, the Minister of Immigration granted her a nine-month special visitor visa.

In evidence presented to the minister, it was noted that the teen's mother had travelled back to the Philippines in 2023 to take care of her daughter.

The pair then travelled to New Zealand in December 2024.

Small said the teen's visitor visa expired on September 7, 2025, meaning she had been unlawfully in New Zealand since then while being cared for by her family.

The tribunal said the evidence suggested the family had been able to make adequate care arrangements for the teen in both NZ and the Philippines. NZ Herald / Supplied

Teen's case 'did not meet statutory test'

In making its decision, the tribunal focused on whether exceptional circumstances of a humanitarian nature would arise from deportation.

Small said the teen's case did not meet the statutory test.

"This is because it has not been demonstrated that the appellant's health needs, or any inability to provide for those health needs, has arisen out of, or as a consequence of her liability for deportation."

Small said the teen appeared to have been adequately cared for in the Philippines after her mother and siblings left in 2020, possibly by the parents' large, extended families who were still there.

"There is nothing exceptional about a person who arrives in New Zealand with a pre-existing medical condition who has had adequate support in their home country," Small said.

She said it appeared that the teen's cerebral palsy had been a constant feature in her life and that of her family, and that she would need ongoing assistance.

"That is true whether she is in New Zealand or in the Philippines."

Small said the evidence suggested the family had been able to make adequate care arrangements for her in both countries.

"In this case, there is no evidence to establish that the appellant cannot access daily support and/or medical support in the Philippines should she require it."

Small said the teen's family, as permanent residents, could leave New Zealand and return at any point.

The fact that her parents were faced with difficult choices was a result of their earlier decisions to move to New Zealand and obtain residence status here.

"They have long known that the appellant will not meet the eligibility requirements for residence and so there is nothing unexpected or uncommon in the requirement that the appellant must go home while they have the ability to remain in New Zealand," Small said.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Dental bills lead surge in requests to Christchurch charity fund
World.content:
Christchurch's Mayor's Welfare Fund has paid more than $200,000 to assist people with dental and electricity payments as the cost of living bites.

Those numbers have nearly doubled from the year prior.

Councillor Yani Johanson, the chair of the advisory fund committee, said the fund has paid out $122,474 for dental work so far in 2026, with a maximum of $2000 given out to any individual.

Dental expenses were previously counted as part of the medical category, but this year the fund had dental as a separate category due to the high number of requests.

"There is a huge need - the tragedy is of course that the more people don't go to the dentist, the longer they leave it, the higher the cost for treatment," Johanson said.

Poor dental health had a huge impact on a person's quality of life, self-esteem and health, he said.

"It's a damning indictment on our society and country that we have such huge need because it has become completely unaffordable for so many people and that's why we are seeing such an increase in demand," Johanson said.

The medical category accounted for $55,702 last year, including dental.

Requests for help with electricity bills had also jumped, with the fund paying out $109,599 so far this year, compared with $58,000 last year and $38,000 in 2024.

"Power prices are just going up and up and up, and people's income is just not meeting the cost of living. So we are seeing a significant increase in requests for help," Johanson said.

The Christchurch City Council's Mayor's Welfare Fund started as the Mayor's Coal and Blanket Fund in 1897 and was renamed in 1973.

In 1992 the Mayor's Welfare Fund Charitable Trust was created to administer the fund.

Johanson said the city has a proud tradition of helping those most in need.

"It's a fund of last resort to help people when there is no other option for funding to meet the basics that are needed to provide for their well-being."

The fund covers specific categories, and applications are assessed by an administrator on a case-by-case basis.

Items covered include electricity and rent arrears, firewood, medical costs, childcare arrears and funeral costs.

In the past year requests for help with child and adult learning assessments were added to the eligible criteria.

The fund gave out $54,876 for adult assessments and $39,936 for child assessments so far in 2026.

In the past year the fund received 702 applications with 447 approved, 98 declined, 129 withdrawn and 28 yet to be decided.

Johanson said the number of applications to the fund had increased hugely, as had the amount of money given out.

The fund is likely to pay $700,000 in grants by the end of this year compared with $371,000 last year.

Councillors had agreed to pay their directors' fees to the fund.

World.title: Osaka apologises to children after struggling with Achilles issue at US Open
World.content:
Naomi Osaka continued to impress with her style and staying power at the US Open on Saturday as she shrugged off a late Achilles problem to beat Belgian Elise Mertens 6-3, 3-6, 7-5 and reach the fourth round.

For her latest eye-catching walk-on look, the four-time major champion blended boardroom and locker-room aesthetics in a grey checked blazer-hoodie and wide-leg pants, putting a tailored twist on traditional pre-match attire.

She looked on course for a business-like win after the first set but was dragged into a battle in the third, where she had to fight through the Achilles niggle to advance.

"I wouldn't say it's a huge injury," Osaka told reporters. "I'd say it's this ongoing problem that I've had since the grass season.

"I don't know why it hasn't gone away. I feel I've done a lot of things in order to make it better, but maybe the time off wasn't enough. I'm not really sure what the reason is, but the medical timeout was to address that.

"You know, she massaged my leg and stuff, so that seemed to help, and gave me Tylenol."

The 28-year-old, a two-time champion at Flushing Meadows, reeled off three games in succession to take a 4-1 lead in the first set under the lights of Louis Armstrong Stadium, clinching it with a battling hold thanks to a string of booming serves.

Naomi Osaka was pushed hard by Elise Mertens (right) but eventually prevailed in a three-setter. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Osaka pushed the 23rd seed hard at the start of the next set with some heavy hitting from the baseline before pouncing with a break in the third game, only to surrender the lead by dropping the next two games.

"Honestly, I can't believe I won this match," Osaka said on court after sealing victory, thanking the crowd for the energy it provided.

"There was a certain point where I put my heart on the court and kept trying in every point. Thank you so much, but honestly, I'm shocked I won. I'm not going to lie."

After levelling the match to force a decider, Mertens capitalised on several unforced errors by a frustrated Osaka to gain the upper hand, but there would be another momentum shift in the match after a medical timeout for the Japanese player.

"I didn't play amazing and it was getting me down, sorry about my behaviour, for the little kids watching," said Osaka, who threw her racket to the floor at one point.

"This is my favourite tournament. I wanted to play well in front of you. I'm just that glad I have the opportunity to play another match.

"I thought I was going to be OK, but clearly I was shaky."

After recovering a break late on, Osaka fired a huge ace to take a 6-5 lead and revved up her forehand in the following game to complete the win and earn a meeting with Elena Rybakina in the next round.

Reuters

World.title: Swans star 'shattered' after skipper's heartbreaking knee injury
World.content:
Sydney star Tom Papley says he is "shattered" for Swans skipper Callum Mills as Mills braces to miss the club's push for an unlikely AFL premiership.

Mills's feared ACL rupture added a sour note to Sydney's remarkable 53-point qualifying final demolition of reigning premiers Brisbane at the SCG on Saturday.

Scans are expected to confirm the major knee injury for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss and has dealt with numerous untimely injuries across his 197-game career.

But Sydney have an opportunity to make amends for previous grand final losses, with a preliminary final at the SCG against either Fremantle or Geelong to come.

Papley admitted it "didn't look great" for Mills following the resilient skipper's first-quarter knee injury.

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the club amid the dramatic fallout from the events at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne last month.

"He is an amazing captain," Papley told the Nine Network of his skipper on Sunday.

"[He's] been amazing over the last few weeks.

"He puts this club on his back and wears his heart on his sleeve. It's just shattering for him.

"I'd love nothing more than to win a premiership and have him by my side, albeit he might not be there [playing].

"He deserves it more than anyone."

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Sydney were given little chance to knock off the Lions, even though they finished the home-and-away season second.

Even club chairman Andrew Pridham conceded the Swans' premiership hopes had been "torpedoed" after suspending the five players.

But all cylinders of the Swans machine fired on Saturday despite those major absences, with Errol Gulden calling the shots in the engine room as Harry Cunningham directed the defence.

Logan McDonald may have led with six goals, but Sydney enjoyed an even contribution from their forward line, with Charlie Curnow and Papley slotting five each.

Tall forward Hayden McLean's three-goal haul is set to further complicate coach Dean Cox's selection conundrum, with Joel Amartey (Achilles) nearing full fitness.

Star winger Justin McInerney is also expected to return from a hamstring strain for the preliminary final.

Errol Gulden (right) marshalled Sydney's engine room in style against Brisbane in the absence of some of his star teammates. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They should both be available … and that'll be a decision, like we do every week," Cox said of Amartey and McInerney.

Cox said Saturday's win felt like the most complete four-quarter performance in his tenure.

"With the quality of opposition that we were playing and the ability of the match-winners that they have all over the ground," Cox said.

"I was really proud when we've got some of the young kids that come into our football team to be able to execute the roles they had to play at the right time."

AAP

World.title: NRL finals schedule confirmed, Panthers claim minor premiership
World.content:
The Penrith Panthers have a fourth NRL minor premiership in the last seven seasons after battering the Wests Tigers 38-10 at Western Sydney Stadium.

Thomas Jenkins scored a first half double to join Alex Johnston on top of the NRL try-scoring charts for the year with 30 to share the Ken Irvine medal, while Casey McLean nabbed his first career NRL hat-trick.

The Wests Tigers briefly showed some life at the start of the second half, with PNG-bound via Parramatta five-eighth Jarome Luai benched by Benji Marshall after the break.

The lively Latu Fainu ensured the Tigers immediately lifted, amplifying the sense of disappointment fans must have felt at the underwhelming Luai era that had promised so much.

Penrith's victory ensures the Panthers will host the Roosters at Western Sydney Stadium on Sunday in the first week of the finals.

NRL finals schedule week 1 Friday Elimination Final: South Sydney Rabbitohs vs Newcastle Knights at Sydney Football Stadium — 7:50pm AEST Saturday Qualifying final: New Zealand Warriors vs Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium — 4:05pm AEST

Elimination final: Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks vs North Queensland Cowboys at Sydney Football Stadium — 7:50pm AEST Sunday Qualifying final: Penrith Panthers vs Sydney Roosters at Western Sydney Stadium — 4:05pm AEST

The Rabbitohs and Knights will open the weekend with their elimination final at the Sydney Football Stadium on Friday night (7:50pm AEST).

The second-placed Warriors will take on the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium on Saturday afternoon (4:05pm AEST) before the Sharks play the Cowboys at the Sydney Football Stadium that evening at 7:50pm AEST.

The Sharks had hoped to host the match at Shark Park but the 45,500-capacity Moore Park stadium got the nod.

The Cowboys will likely be without star forward Reuben Cotter, who will miss at least week one of the NRL finals after being charged for a high tackle against the Raiders.

The Maroons forward was handed a grade two careless high tackle charge for his contact on Josh Papali'i in the first hit up of the match.

Earlier, Tyrell Sloan scored a 45-metre field goal to secure the Dragons a thrilling 24-22 victory over the Parramatta Eels in Wollongong.

"I guess it's the stuff you dream about," Castleford-bound Sloan told ABC Sport after the match.

"The fans turned up … they stuck with us through a tough year and just to repay them there is the best feeling ever."
